More practically: you could fold Axiom into Assumption, but you'd lose the signal that these particular assumptions are non-negotiable within the current logic frame rather than provisionally adopted to proceed.

usage.intended: statement accepted as true without proof, foundational in current logic frame.
usage.broad_contexts: mathematical axioms, ethical first principles, constitutional declarations, API contracts, system-level invariants, organizational values.
usage.every_context_needs: statement text, scope of applicability, non-negotiability semantic.
usage.varies: provability outside the frame (some axioms are provable in wider frames), frame identity, dependent-derivation tree.

tensions: Non-negotiable within a frame vs revisable across frames — an axiom feels absolute locally but is chosen, not discovered.
Foundational stability vs paradigm lock-in — the same axiomatic bedrock that makes reasoning possible also makes paradigm shifts structurally painful.
Community acceptance vs individual verification — 'accepted as true' hides the question 'by whom, and why did they accept it?'
tradeoffs: Gains: a termination condition for proof chains, a shared foundation for community reasoning, a marker that distinguishes 'this cannot be argued here' from 'this hasn't been argued yet.'
Gives up: the pretense that reasoning is ever fully grounded — every axiom pushes the justification problem up one level.
critique: Very thin mechanism — almost a role marker. The interesting work all happens at frame boundaries (Paradigm, Reframe) where the choice of axioms is renegotiated.
No way to mark strength or centrality — all axioms look the same even though some are load-bearing and others vestigial.
Risks becoming a dumping ground for 'I don't want to defend this.' The pattern has no invariant forcing the user to justify why this particular claim deserves foundational status.

Axiom.family_discussion: The stable anchor of the epistemic-stance family. Assumption is provisional, Hypothesis is under test, Datum is observed, Axiom is foundational. Where the family gets interesting is at the boundary with Paradigm — paradigm shifts are essentially axiom replacements, and the pattern library treats them as distinct events rather than smooth continuations of normal reasoning.

motivation.why_it_exists: Contention reduction as a typed primitive — every retry loop needs exponential delay with jitter and a cap, and reinventing it per call site produces inconsistent behavior (different multipliers, missing jitter, unbounded growth). Backoff pins the minimum mechanism so every retry loop in the library inherits the same shape.
motivation.removability: No. Referenced by Retry, ReAttempt, StateLock, Mutex, Lock, Throttle, and every other pattern that has to handle contention. Removing would force each site to re-declare the delay mechanics.

usage.intended: exponential delay to reduce contention — multiplier growth + jitter + cap.
usage.broad_contexts: retry backoff, thundering-herd prevention, rate-limit recovery, connection retry, TCP congestion, SaaS API integration.
usage.every_context_needs: initial delay, multiplier, jitter, cap.
usage.varies: multiplier value, jitter distribution, cap value, reset-on-success semantic, per-target vs global.

tensions: Deterministic policy vs jitter: the mechanism mandates jitter to prevent thundering herd, which is inherently non-deterministic. Callers who need reproducibility have to seed or disable jitter — the pattern doesn't expose the seed.
Exponential growth vs cap: unbounded growth is catastrophic; bounded growth degrades the 'exponential' property at the cap. The pattern requires the cap but doesn't say what value is reasonable.

Reset-on-success vs sticky state: the mechanism says reset on success. Some production systems want to keep the backoff growing across independent operations on the same resource (adaptive throttling). That is a descendant concern.
tradeoffs: Exponential buys rapid contention reduction at the cost of slow recovery from transient failures (a single failed attempt takes exponential time to retry).
Jitter buys herd prevention at the cost of predictability — the precise retry times are randomized.
Finite retry budget buys crash-loop prevention at the cost of surrendering on persistent failures that would eventually resolve.
critique: Only one failure mode (Starvation). Missing: Thundering Herd Despite Jitter (jitter-bounded collisions at very high contention), Exhaustion Before Recovery (budget runs out while the service is still warming up), Retry Amplification (cascading retries across a service chain multiply load).

The invariant 'retry budget must be finite' is correct but the pattern does not say who owns the budget — caller? descendant? The distinction matters: a global-budget Backoff differs operationally from a per-attempt-budget Backoff.

'Multiplier (typically 2)' is advisory; no invariant pins the minimum or maximum multiplier. Descendants (`FibonacciBackoff`, `AdaptiveBackoff`) diverge from 2 without a parent-level constraint to check against.

Backoff.family_discussion: The contention-reduction primitive for every retry loop in the library. Composed with `Cooldown` (minimum inter-event gap), `Throttle` (rate cap), and `Hysteresis` (asymmetric thresholds). Used by `Lock`, `Mutex`, `StateLock`, `Retry`, `ReAttempt`, `CircuitBreaker` at the contention layer.

motivation.why_it_exists: Forward reasoning (facts → conclusions) is natural but undirected; given a goal, most forward paths don't lead to it. BackwardChain reverses the flow: start from the desired end-state, ask what's required to get there, recurse. This gives planning a pruning heuristic — you only expand prerequisites of goals you care about.
motivation.removability: Not removable without losing goal-directed planning as a named capability. You can simulate it with forward chaining plus search, but you pay the cost of exploring branches that don't lead anywhere useful. Removing BackwardChain would leave only generic search patterns.

usage.intended: goal-first decomposition — recursively identify prerequisites from desired end-state.
usage.broad_contexts: goal-oriented planning, Prolog-style inference, dependency resolution, project planning (start from deadline), reverse engineering, medical treatment planning.
usage.every_context_needs: goal/end-state, recursive prerequisite identification, termination at known facts or actionable steps.
usage.varies: depth limit, cycle detection, fact-database lookup method.

tensions: Goal anchoring (focus) vs discovery (openness) — backward chaining is blind to goals you didn't know to want.
Causal sufficiency (hard requirement) vs real-world contingency — step T being 'sufficient' for T+1 assumes a cleaner causal structure than most domains offer.
Termination at leaves vs infinite regression — the invariant says leaves must be actionable or known, but that requires a well-specified ground truth that often isn't there.
tradeoffs: Gains: planning efficiency, an interpretable chain from goal to action, natural integration with deductive reasoning.
Gives up: serendipity (no room for noticing unrelated opportunities) and robustness (brittle if the causal chain has gaps or competing pathways).
critique: Assumes causality is a clean DAG; real decisions involve feedback loops that backward chaining can't represent natively.
The 'sufficient condition' invariant is too strong for soft-causal domains (most of cognition) where prerequisites are typically necessary-not-sufficient.
No built-in handling for alternative paths — backward chaining picks a path and commits; exploring alternatives requires a separate BeamSearch or equivalent.

BackwardChain.family_discussion: Paired with ChainOfThought (execution substrate) and Deduce (each step is a deductive move). Its opposite number is ForwardChain (fact-first). The solver family (PolymorphicSolver, RootSolver) uses backward chaining implicitly when decomposing a goal into subtasks. For multi-path exploration, reach for BeamSearch or TreeSearch instead — BackwardChain commits to a single line.

motivation.why_it_exists: The typed container for a decision proposal — question + options + rules + deadline, immutable once cast. Without Ballot as a pattern, every voting protocol invents its own shape; cross-protocol interoperability suffers.
motivation.removability: No. Vote, Consensus-via-Ballot, and governance workflows all reference Ballot. Removing would force protocol-specific vote containers with no shared invariants.

usage.intended: immutable container for a decision proposal.
usage.broad_contexts: democratic votes, governance ballots, consensus rounds, delegated voting, poll artifacts, veto records.
usage.every_context_needs: question being decided, options, voting rules, deadline, immutability once cast.
usage.varies: option count, voting rules (majority, supermajority, unanimity, weighted), anonymity, delegation chains, cryptographic proofs.

tensions: Immutability vs amendment: cast Ballot is immutable — amendments require new Ballot. This is principled but operationally costly for iterative decisions.
Decision rule field vs rule enforcement: Ballot carries the rule (majority/unanimity/...) but doesn't enforce it — that is Vote's job. The Ballot is data; the enforcement is process.
Spoiled ballot failure vs schema validation: 'ambiguous or invalid select format' shouldn't happen if the Ballot is well-typed. The pattern acknowledges the failure mode but doesn't prevent it.
tradeoffs: Completeness invariant (question + options + rule) buys self-contained voting artifacts at the cost of needing careful authoring.
Immutability buys tamper-resistance at the cost of forbidding in-flight revisions.
Data-structure framing (Infrastructure) correctly reflects Ballot's nature — it's the shape, not the protocol.
critique: Two invariants, two failure modes. Missing: Deadline Validity (deadline must be future-tense at creation), Option Disjointness (options should be mutually exclusive unless the rule permits multi-select).
Double Voting as a Sybil risk is mentioned but the pattern has no signing requirement — a signed Ballot wouldn't eliminate Sybil but would eliminate replay.
The 'voting rules' field is informally listed (majority/supermajority/unanimity) — no enum definition. Different implementations use different strings.

Ballot.family_discussion: The vote-proposal data structure. Consumed by `Vote` (the protocol), enforced via `Quorum` (the threshold). Pairs with `Decision` (what the vote produces) and `Ballot` is the input; `Decision` is the output of the voting process.

motivation.why_it_exists: The most reliable bias in human and LLM reasoning is base-rate neglect — vivid, specific details systematically overwhelm statistical priors. BaseRateInclude is the named counter-reflex: before weighing the particulars of this case, ask how often this class of thing happens. Agents without this primitive will confidently over-index on narrative detail.
motivation.removability: Could be folded into BayesUpdate as 'step one: set prior.' Keeping it separate is a deliberate redundancy — the failure mode is so pervasive and so easy to skip that elevating the anchor step to its own pattern gives it a slot in checklists and audit trails.

usage.intended: anchor prior probability before evaluating specific case (outside view).
usage.broad_contexts: forecasting, medical diagnosis, startup evaluation, strategic planning, anti-anecdotal-reasoning discipline, Fermi estimation.
usage.every_context_needs: base rate for the reference class, adjustment rule for case-specific evidence, resistance to vivid details.
usage.varies: reference class definition, evidence weighting, subjective base-rate estimation when data is sparse.

tensions: Reference class relevance vs availability — the most relevant reference class is often one you don't have data for, and the one with good data is often loosely analogous.
Outside view (base rate) vs inside view (this case) — both matter, and the pattern forces the outside view first, but agents often resist because the inside view feels more informative.
Static prior vs evolving situation — last year's base rate may not apply to this year's class; the pattern has no freshness mechanism.
tradeoffs: Gains: an anti-narrative counterweight, forced humility about typical outcomes, a shared reference for calibration across agents.
Gives up: speed (setting the prior is extra work) and sometimes relevance (poorly chosen reference classes give misleading anchors).
critique: Reference class tennis (the named failure mode) is hard to prevent with an invariant alone — determining what's 'relevant' is itself judgment-laden.
The pattern commands 'vivid details don't change base rates' but in reality they should sometimes (new information can legitimately update the reference class); the rule is coarse.
Doesn't specify where the base rate comes from — agents can invent plausible-sounding priors and call the pattern satisfied.

BaseRateInclude.family_discussion: The sibling of BayesUpdate — BaseRateInclude is 'set the prior properly,' BayesUpdate is 'revise it with evidence.' Together they form the disciplined probabilistic-reasoning backbone. Also adjacent to SteelmanCheck (outside view on the alternative) and RedTeam (actively seek the reference class that would undermine your case).

motivation.why_it_exists: Belief revision is the single most common epistemic operation, and doing it informally is systematically biased (base-rate neglect, conservatism, over-updating on vivid evidence). BayesUpdate names the disciplined version so agents can at least recognize when they're deviating from it.
motivation.removability: Not removable as a concept — belief revision is unavoidable — but you could argue the named pattern adds little over 'just do Bayes.' The value is less in the math and more in the invariants: never update to 0 or 1, anchor on the prior, cite the likelihood ratio. Remove the pattern and those invariants lose their place to live.

usage.intended: mathematically rigorous belief revision via likelihood weighting.
usage.broad_contexts: probabilistic reasoning, diagnostic updating, A/B test analysis, prediction market updates, scientific hypothesis revision, spam filtering, medical diagnosis.
usage.every_context_needs: prior probability, observed evidence, likelihood ratio computation, posterior.
usage.varies: prior representation (point, distribution, ensemble), likelihood estimation method, base-rate handling, clamp thresholds to avoid 0/1 collapse, incremental vs batch.

tensions: Mathematical rigor vs tractability — exact Bayesian updating requires P(E|H) and P(E|¬H) you usually don't have; agents approximate and then pretend they didn't.
Never-update-to-certainty vs needing to act — strict Bayesianism forbids P=1, but decisions require commitment. BayesUpdate refuses the degenerate case but doesn't solve the commit/update tension.
Single update vs dependent evidence — multiple correlated observations tempt agents to update as if they were independent, inflating the posterior.
tradeoffs: Gains: a calibrated framework, a named boundary (never 0 or 1), a forcing function to cite base rates.
Gives up: fluency under real uncertainty (exact numbers often aren't available) and accessibility (agents without probability background struggle to invoke it correctly).
critique: The 'never update to 0 or 1' invariant is the right rule but collides with computational limits — in practice agents clip to 0.001/0.999 and then treat those as effective certainty.
No mechanism for correlated evidence — the pattern describes a single update in isolation, but most real agent loops involve streams of non-independent observations.
Assumes the agent has explicit priors to anchor on, which is often false; the BaseRateInclude invariant helps but doesn't close the gap when no reference class exists.

BayesUpdate.family_discussion: Sits at the center of the belief-revision family with BaseRateInclude (anchor the prior), BeliefTracking (log the update), SurprisalUpdate (measure the magnitude), and Evidence (the trigger). It's the mathematical spine; the others are the scaffolding that makes the math usable. Compare with AcceptSpec — BayesUpdate revises internal beliefs; AcceptSpec revises external commitments. Both are 'legal change of mind' patterns, at different layers.

motivation.why_it_exists: Naive depth-first search blows up on branching graphs; breadth-first runs out of memory. BeamSearch names the pragmatic middle: keep a fixed-size frontier of the k most promising nodes, explore them in parallel, prune the rest. Without it, agents either over-commit to one path (depth-first) or lose themselves exploring equally uninteresting alternatives (breadth-first).
motivation.removability: Removable — the algorithm is elementary enough for agents to re-invent. Naming it earns consistency (beam width becomes a named parameter) and composability (beam search can be used as a subroutine in PolymorphicSolver, BackwardChain, UniversalSolverTree). The cost of removal is mostly in shared vocabulary, not capability.

usage.intended: width-limited heuristic search — expand top-k most promising nodes.
usage.broad_contexts: ML beam search (NLP decoding, speech recognition), game-tree search with width cap, research-direction beam pruning, hypothesis beam testing.
usage.every_context_needs: queue of size k, successor generation, ranking, top-k selection per step.
usage.varies: beam width k (PositiveInteger per §3.17), ranking heuristic, pruning criteria, diversity constraint.

tensions: Beam width trade-off — too narrow and you miss good paths; too wide and you might as well run breadth-first.
Ranking quality vs search progress — the whole algorithm is only as good as its ranking function; a misleading ranker prunes the correct answer early.
Optimality (invariant) vs diversity — always selecting the top-k by score means similar candidates crowd out exploration of structurally different paths.
tradeoffs: Gains: bounded memory, predictable compute cost, explicit parallelism in exploration.
Gives up: completeness — beam search can miss the optimal solution if it falls outside the top-k early. This is the fundamental cost of fixed-width search.
critique: 'Optimality: the K nodes selected are the highest ranked' is a weaker optimality than it sounds — it's local optimality within the ranking, not global optimality in the search space.
No mechanism for diversity preservation — similar candidates crowd the beam, and the algorithm has no built-in reward for distinctness.
The ranker is treated as given; in practice designing the ranker is the actual problem, and the pattern offloads it.

BeamSearch.family_discussion: Search-family sibling of Bisect (O(log n) partition), TreeSearch (depth first), and Discover (the parent verb). Used as a subroutine by PolymorphicSolver when evaluating multiple strategies in parallel. Compare with MonteCarloTreeSearch — BeamSearch is deterministic breadth-limited, MCTS is stochastic with an exploration/exploitation balance.

motivation.why_it_exists: Identity-based authorization requires every actor to re-authenticate at every checkpoint, which is expensive and couples authorization to identity infrastructure. BearerToken decouples the two: possession grants rights, without identity check. This makes delegation (agent-to-agent, human-to-agent) composable — you can hand over capability without handing over identity.
motivation.removability: Removable in systems where identity-based authorization is sufficient and delegation is rare. The pattern earns its weight in agent ecosystems where capabilities flow across trust boundaries frequently — in those settings, re-authenticating at every hop is untenable.

usage.intended: possession-based authorization — "do you have the token?" not "who are you?"
usage.broad_contexts: OAuth bearer tokens, API keys, session cookies, access tokens, movie theater tickets, transit passes.
usage.every_context_needs: signed token payload, rights encoding, delegation semantic (freely passable).
usage.varies: signature algorithm, expiry, scope encoding, revocation mechanism.

tensions: Possession equals access (convenience) vs possession equals risk (theft) — the same property that makes tokens composable makes them the target of every credential stealer.
Fine-grained scope vs token management burden — narrow-scoped tokens minimize blast radius and multiply management overhead; wide-scoped tokens are convenient and dangerous.
Expiry too short (constant refresh) vs too long (theft window) — the pattern names revocability/expiry as invariant but doesn't prescribe the window.
tradeoffs: Gains: composable authorization, clean delegation, separation of identity from capability, offline validation (verifier only needs the issuer's public key).
Gives up: identity binding — if the token is stolen, the attacker has exactly what the legitimate bearer had, and the pattern provides no way to distinguish them.
critique: Theft is listed as a failure mode but there's no built-in mitigation (proof-of-possession keys, token binding to TLS session, sender-constrained tokens are all external to the pattern).
Replay attacks require nonce or expiry, as the pattern notes, but neither is listed as an invariant — only expiry/revocation-ID is mandated, which is insufficient against replay.
'Scope Creep' is a failure mode with no structural mitigation — token scope is whatever the issuer wrote, and over-issuance is a social problem the pattern doesn't address.

BearerToken.family_discussion: Capability-auth sibling of Permission (the general access primitive), Card (the capability-advertisement artifact), and IdentityBasedAccess (the opposing model). In agent systems, BearerToken is the natural primitive — agents delegate frequently and have weak identity in any case. Compare with Contract — BearerToken is ad-hoc, contract is negotiated; both confer rights with different ceremony.

motivation.why_it_exists: Typed epistemic state — claim + confidence + evidence pointer. Distinct from Fact (objective) by being subjective and mutable. Essential substrate for Bayesian reasoning, confidence-weighted decisions, and any pattern that reasons about what an agent knows vs believes.
motivation.removability: No. BayesUpdate, ConfidenceCalibrate, BeliefTracking, TraceBelief all reference Belief. Collapsing into Fact would lose the subjective/mutable distinction that reasoning patterns depend on.

usage.intended: a subjective epistemic claim with confidence and evidence.
usage.broad_contexts: LLM prior beliefs, scientific hypotheses, agent mental models, world models, prediction-market positions, user-intent inferences, probabilistic assertions.
usage.every_context_needs: a claim, a confidence score [0.0, 1.0], a pointer to supporting evidence; mutability via `BayesUpdate` or similar.
usage.varies: evidence representation (citation, linked data, derivation), confidence update rule (Bayesian, heuristic, frequency-based), superseding semantics, audit trail.

tensions: Confidence-as-scalar vs richer uncertainty: [0, 1] scalar excludes uncertainty distributions (where you have evidence but it's spread across options). Descendants could specialize; the parent is scalar-only.
Evidence pointer vs evidence itself: referencing evidence rather than carrying it keeps Belief lightweight but means evidence lifecycle is decoupled — a Belief can outlive its evidence.
Subjective vs inter-subjective: Belief is per-agent. Shared/group beliefs need a separate pattern; the library doesn't mint one directly.
tradeoffs: Scalar confidence buys comparability at the cost of hiding multimodal uncertainty.
Evidence pointer buys lightweight Beliefs at the cost of requiring evidence resolution.
Mutability (distinct from Fact) buys accurate epistemic modeling at the cost of harder-to-verify claim chains.
critique: Zero invariants and zero failure modes. For a substrate pattern this central, missing: Confidence Range (0 ≤ c ≤ 1), Evidence Existence (referenced evidence must exist at creation time), Monotonic Update (confidence changes should be tied to evidence changes).
The subjectivity is named but not operationalized — an agent can hold contradictory Beliefs without detection.
Evidence-backed is structurally implied (pointer to evidence) but not enforced — a Belief with null evidence pointer is technically a Belief, operationally useless.

Belief.family_discussion: The epistemic-state substrate. Updated by `BayesUpdate`, tracked by `BeliefTracking`, calibrated by `ConfidenceCalibrate`, traced by `TraceBelief`. Paired with `Evidence` and distinguished from `Fact` by subjectivity.

motivation.why_this_layer: epistemic version control within one mind
motivation.why_it_exists: Agents update beliefs constantly but usually without a record — the posterior silently overwrites the prior, destroying the history of learning and enabling hindsight bias. BeliefTracking names the discipline of keeping old beliefs around, linking updates to their triggers, and treating the belief state as version-controlled. Without it, agents can't explain how they got from A to B.
motivation.removability: Unremovable in any serious multi-step reasoning system. Downstream audit, supersession, and debugging all depend on the belief graph being traversable backwards. You can weaken it (less frequent commits, coarser triggers), but removing it entirely turns every agent into an opaque oracle.

usage.intended: epistemic version control — track what was believed before and after evidence.
usage.broad_contexts: prediction markets, forecasting calibration, scientific hypothesis tracking, debugging belief-state machines, mind-change provenance for auditing.
usage.every_context_needs: prior state pinning, posterior tracking, `supersedes` edge on belief shift, surprisal quantification.
usage.varies: shift threshold, compression policy (full history vs delta), access control, replay support.

tensions: Non-destructive history vs storage cost — perfect tracking explodes the graph; coarse tracking loses the fidelity that makes tracking worth doing.
Over-sensitive (epistemic thrashing) vs under-sensitive (silent update) — the threshold for 'significant shift' is judgment-dependent and the pattern doesn't specify it.
Explicit commits vs cognitive fluency — requiring a commit before each ingestion slows thinking, but skipping the commit loses the causal link.
tradeoffs: Gains: auditable reasoning, immune response against hindsight bias, explicit evidence-to-belief linkages, supersession history.
Gives up: speed and implicit ease — belief updates become first-class operations rather than silent state changes.
critique: The threshold for 'significant shift' is left to the caller; in practice this becomes a judgment call that is itself subject to motivated reasoning.
Non-destructive update is a principle; enforcement requires discipline the pattern can't provide on its own. Many 'belief tracked' graphs are actually silent-updated with token commit ceremony.
Storage and traversal costs grow without bound; the pattern provides no principled pruning mechanism for low-value history.

BeliefTracking.family_discussion: The epistemic version-control layer for the whole reasoning stack. Pairs with BayesUpdate (mathematical revision), SurprisalUpdate (magnitude measurement), and the supersession primitives at the graph level. Compare with AuditTrail — BeliefTracking is the internal analogue, tracking belief changes; AuditTrail is the external analogue, tracking action and state changes.

motivation.why_it_exists: Before committing to execute a task, a solver should be able to declare what it will cost, how confident it is, and which parts it can handle. Bid names that pre-execution artifact, making commitments auditable and allowing the caller (or a compute market) to compare offers. Without it, agents either just start working (no price discovery) or argue informally (no comparability).
motivation.removability: Removable in settings where one solver just does one task (no contest, no budget concerns). The pattern becomes load-bearing when multiple solvers compete, when budgets are finite, or when confidence calibration matters for downstream decisions. Removing it collapses the multi-solver coordination story.

usage.intended: binding offer from solver to execute a task.
usage.future: any commitment offer in a negotiation.
usage.broad_contexts: solver auctions, procurement, crowdsourcing, API rate-limit bidding, resource auctions, milestone proposals, contracts-for-work.
usage.every_context_needs: bidder identity, offer content (cost, confidence, capability match), commitment semantics ("if accepted, bidder is bound").
usage.varies: currency/unit, confidence representation, capability-match structure, withdraw semantics, expiry timing.

tensions: Binding commitment vs real-world uncertainty — bids promise what the solver will do; real work frequently exceeds estimates, and the pattern makes that overrun expensive.
Confidence as honest estimate vs confidence as signaling — confidence theater is the named failure mode, and it's hard to counter without calibration history.
Verifiable (invariant) vs subjective components — time and tokens are measurable; 'capability match' is judgment, which resists verification post-hoc.
tradeoffs: Gains: price discovery across solvers, ex-ante cost transparency, a target for confidence calibration, a basis for budget management.
Gives up: the ability to quietly revise — once bid, you're committed. This is correct for market discipline, painful for legitimate re-scoping.
critique: Underestimation vs Overestimation are symmetric in the pattern but asymmetric in practice — overestimation just loses work, underestimation blows up execution.
Confidence Theater is the most dangerous named failure mode and the pattern has no mechanism to prevent it. Calibration requires history the pattern doesn't carry.
Capability Match is vague — 'which parts the solver can handle' is useful conceptually, specified poorly. In practice it becomes a free-text field and the guarantees evaporate.

Bid.family_discussion: The offering unit that feeds AuctionMechanism, ComputeMarket, Award, and AtomicBid (the fire-and-log variant). Sibling of BoundedTask (which packages the outputs) and Solver (the bidder). Compare with AcceptSpec — Bid is the solver's commitment to cost; AcceptSpec is the evaluator's commitment to quality criteria. Both live before execution and shape it.

motivation.why_it_exists: Many investigation and debugging tasks reduce to 'find the item in a space.' Linear search scales with space size; binary partition scales with the logarithm. Bisect names the discipline so agents can recognize when the structure permits it and can commit to the logarithmic strategy rather than drifting into linear sweep.
motivation.removability: Removable — bisection is elementary enough that agents can re-invent it. Keeping it named provides a slot for invariants (≥40% elimination per step) and for the connection to RecursiveRootCause, which frequently delegates its search step to Bisect.

usage.intended: logarithmic search via binary splitting.
usage.future: any "split search space in half" narrowing mechanism.
usage.broad_contexts: git bisect, 20-Questions, binary search in sorted arrays, medical diagnostic narrowing, debugging (which commit broke it?), diagnostic decision trees.
usage.every_context_needs: possibility space, partition question, elimination rule, recursion on remaining half.
usage.varies: question-selection heuristic, partition fairness (exactly half vs approximate), fallback on indivisible space.

tensions: Requires an ordered or divisible domain — in unstructured spaces the splitting question can't be constructed, and attempting to bisect is actively harmful (the false-negative failure mode).
Splitting question quality vs availability — the ideal split is 50/50 informative; the available split is often uneven, reducing bisection to near-linear in pathological cases.
Speed vs false confidence — logarithmic search feels clean and finished; agents can mistake 'I bisected' for 'I solved,' ignoring that the splitting function itself may have been wrong.
tradeoffs: Gains: O(log n) search in well-structured spaces, a named discipline for debugging and root-cause investigation.
Gives up: robustness in unstructured domains and the qualitative information that a linear scan would surface along the way.
critique: The ≥40% invariant is a floor, not a guarantee — in practice many splits underperform and the pattern offers no escape hatch other than 'the question was flawed.'
No handling for multiple correct answers — bisection collapses the space assuming one target; multi-answer search needs a different pattern.

False negative (discarding the half that contained the answer) is the canonical failure and is unrecoverable without restarting; the pattern doesn't require a verification step on the eliminated half.

Bisect.family_discussion: Lives in the search family with BeamSearch (multi-path parallel search) and TreeSearch (branching depth-first). Bisect is the cheapest, most disciplined member — applicable only when structure allows. Frequently invoked by RecursiveRootCause as its core search step, and by Debug. The Bisect-RecursiveRootCause pairing is one of the most reliable debugging combinations in the library.

motivation.why_it_exists: The irreducible two-valued truth type. Minted as a pattern (rather than assumed as a language primitive) so agents sharing the library have a byte-identical, content-addressed definition of 'exactly two members.' Also gives Validate a named output type that is not confused with Status or Decision.
motivation.removability: Probably not cleanly. Could argue Boolean is so universal it doesn't need a Sema pattern — English and every programming language already define it. But the content-addressing principle applies even to 'trivial' types: giving Boolean a hash lets Validate's output be verifiable rather than assumed. Removal would force Validate to reference a non-Sema type, breaking the invariant that every dependency is a pattern.

tensions: Triviality vs rigor: Boolean's mechanism is almost tautological. But the alternative — leaving it implicit — means every caller hand-wires its own Boolean representation (int 0/1? string 'true'/'false'? enum?). The library trades verbosity for typed consistency.

No middle value vs real-world nuance: the Exhaustive invariant forbids intermediate values. Real verification often lands in 'true with low confidence' — that belongs on Judge or Check, not Boolean. Callers who reach for a tri-valued Boolean are signaling the wrong type.

Minted vs imported: most languages provide Boolean as a primitive; Sema duplicates it. The justification is content-addressing — a Validate that yields `sema:Boolean#981e` is byte-verifiable against the caller's expected type.
tradeoffs: Explicit pattern buys typed verifiability at the cost of looking pedantic (why a whole pattern for true/false?).

Exhaustive + Exclusive invariants rule out extensions (maybe, indeterminate). If later needs require a three-valued case, descendants cannot relax the invariants — a new pattern (Status, Decision) is the right move.
The absence of failure modes is honest (what could fail about a two-element set?) but leaves the impression the pattern is vestigial.
critique: No failure modes and no preconditions/postconditions. For a primitive, this is defensible, but the pattern doesn't assert that the only valid members are the two constants — technically, an invalid-byte Boolean (neither true nor false) could be produced and the spec has no explicit rejection.
The three-way distinction from Decision and Status is asserted in prose but not enforced by type — it lives in caller discipline.
Boolean's purpose is primarily to give Validate a typed output; yet the pattern's mechanism doesn't mention Validate. The relationship is implicit via Validate's yields declaration.

Boolean.family_discussion: The degenerate case in the verification-stack taxonomy: two-valued (Boolean) vs three-valued epistemic (Status) vs three-valued operational (Decision) vs graded scalar (Score). Output of Validate. Simplest of the four; maps most directly to host-language primitives.

motivation.why_it_exists: Unbounded tasks run forever, cost arbitrarily, and never gate on quality. BoundedTask is the minimum viable civilized form: wrap Task with Budget (economic bound) and AcceptSpec (quality bound). Without this specialization, every caller re-derives the 'here's the task, here's when to stop, here's what good looks like' combo, often incompletely.
motivation.removability: Technically removable — callers can compose Task + Budget + AcceptSpec themselves. The named bundle is a reminder that tasks without both bounds are irresponsible in deployed systems. Keeping it earns default-safe scheduling and a clear signal that these are the minimum ceremonies expected.

usage.intended: specialized Task enforcing budget + AcceptSpec for economic + quality boundaries.
usage.future: any "Task with must-have budget and acceptance" variant.
usage.broad_contexts: budgeted solver calls, SLA-bound assignments, grant-funded research tasks, time-boxed projects, deliverable-with-deadline.
usage.every_context_needs: underlying Task, budget (required here), AcceptSpec, enforcement of both.
usage.varies: budget type (compute, time, money), AcceptSpec strictness, overrun behavior.

tensions: Budget as hard ceiling vs soft guidance — real work sometimes legitimately exceeds estimates; a hard ceiling kills good work, a soft one erodes the discipline.
AcceptSpec as pre-committed criteria vs evolving understanding — quality bars should reflect what you learn during execution, but allowing mid-task revision breaks the commitment.
Bundling (convenience) vs expressiveness — BoundedTask fixes the bound types (Budget and AcceptSpec); callers who need a different bound structure have to drop back to composing primitives.
tradeoffs: Gains: default safety for task execution, forcing function for quality and cost specification, clean vocabulary for 'the task you're willing to deploy.'
Gives up: flexibility. BoundedTask picks two specific bound types; tasks that need different bounds (time-bounded, adversarially-bounded, resource-bounded) have to use other patterns.
critique: Very thin — the mechanism is a one-sentence specialization of Task. Invariants now state the specific claims (previously they were bare labels — 'Budget Enclosure' and 'Quality Gate' with no statement — which rendered as noise in the manual).
Pairs Budget and AcceptSpec as if they're symmetric — they're not. Budget is an input constraint; AcceptSpec is an output criterion. The bundle flattens this asymmetry.
No handling for budget overrun / spec failure interaction — does overrun halt the AcceptSpec check, or does the check still run on a partial result?
`derived_from` updated from stale Task sema_id (aa452d4a...) to current (b32808db...).

BoundedTask.family_discussion: A specialization of Task, with Budget and AcceptSpec as companions. Sits alongside other specialized tasks like Investigation (epistemic work) or MicroTask (minimum unit) in the task family. Consumed by the solver family (PolymorphicSolver, RootSolver) which expects bounded tasks by default. Compare with SelfContainedTask — same family, different specialization axis.

motivation.why_this_layer: engineered conditional-fork primitive — authored, not substrate
motivation.why_it_exists: The two-way conditional fork is a mechanical primitive — if-else. Making it a pattern avoids reinvention and establishes a shared handle for 'exactly two mutually exclusive paths,' distinct from Route (N-way classifier) and Gate (conditional halt with Decision output).
motivation.removability: Probably yes at the library level — Branch is semantically equivalent to a Gate yielding a two-option Decision. The library keeps it as its own pattern because 'if C then A else B' is so universally recognized that the abstraction cost of routing it through Gate would hurt readability. A pragmatic retention rather than a necessity.

usage.intended: conditional fork — if C then A else B (mutual exclusion).
usage.broad_contexts: if-else programming, decision gates, binary state transitions, A/B experiments, diagnostic forks, binary game moves.
usage.every_context_needs: condition, A-branch, B-branch, mutual exclusion.
usage.varies: condition evaluation, evaluation cost, short-circuit semantics.

tensions: Minimalism vs informativeness: the mechanism is one sentence. For a primitive, that is appropriate, but it leaves a lot implicit (does Branch have an output? Does it yield something?) — downstream callers have to infer.
Exclusive-two-path vs real-world ternary (if / else-if / else): multi-way branching is Route's territory, but the boundary is fuzzy when an else-if chain is essentially a Route with poor ergonomics.
Mutual exclusion vs both-branches-execute: the mechanism forbids simultaneous execution but many real implementations (speculative, parallel both) violate it. The pattern is opinionated.
tradeoffs: Minimal mechanism buys universality at the cost of precision.
Mutual-exclusion invariant rules out speculative/parallel variants — they need descendants.
The lack of explicit output shape (no yields declaration in the spec shown) leaves composition implicit.
critique: Zero invariants and zero failure modes listed. For a primitive this thin, that might be acceptable, but at minimum: Exhaustive (A and B together cover the condition space); Deterministic (same C → same branch).
The boundary between Branch and Route is not articulated in the pattern — readers looking at both have to infer that Route is N-way and Branch is 2-way.
No mention of what Branch yields. If it passes through the chosen side's output, that's worth stating; if it yields a Decision, it overlaps Gate.

Branch.family_discussion: The 2-way case in the flow-control family. Sibling to `Route` (N-way classifier dispatch) and `Gate` (conditional halt producing a Decision). The simplest member of the family; most other control-flow patterns specialize or combine these three.

motivation.why_it_exists: Decomposition patterns have no natural stopping rule for how many branches to spawn. Without a governor, agentic systems fork-bomb themselves — every subtask becomes N subsubtasks, the tree explodes, and the parent loses the ability to integrate. BreadthGovernor names the upper bound and the truncation/clustering rules for staying under it.
motivation.removability: Removable in single-agent depth-first settings. Becomes essential the moment parallelism is possible, because nothing else in the library bounds fan-out. Miller's Law (7±2) is the implicit ceiling; without a governor, agentic systems routinely blow past it without noticing.

usage.intended: Parsimony-bounded expansion — limit max parallel branches (fan-out) at a node.
usage.future: any "how wide can we spread this search" governor.
usage.broad_contexts: tree search pruning, beam search width, brainstorming fan-out control, research question diversification, parallel-experiment count bounding.
usage.every_context_needs: max breadth bound, distinctness + expected-value prioritization, truncation (top-K) or clustering (merge similar).
usage.varies: K value (PositiveInteger per §3.17), distinctness metric, value-estimation method.

tensions: Breadth limit vs exploration — fixing the cap at 7±2 honors cognitive limits but may be far too narrow for genuinely branchy search spaces.
Distinctness invariant (orthogonal branches) vs exhaustiveness — forcing cosine<0.8 ensures exploration spans the space but may leave good clustered variants unexplored.
Truncation vs clustering — top-K discards alternatives; clustering merges them. The pattern names both but doesn't say when each is appropriate.
tradeoffs: Gains: bounded fan-out, parent integrability, a structural defense against fork-bombs.
Gives up: search completeness. Some problems legitimately need >7 branches; BreadthGovernor will either truncate or merge them, and the right move depends on context the pattern can't see.
critique: Miller's Law is a result about working memory in humans, not a law of distributed systems; using it as the parallelism ceiling for machine agents is a rhetorical transfer, not a derivation.
Distinctness-by-cosine is a cheap proxy for semantic orthogonality; two branches with cosine 0.75 can still be near-duplicates on the dimensions that matter.
No provision for reviewing merged branches later — once clustered, the suppressed alternatives are typically lost from the trace.

BreadthGovernor.family_discussion: The counterpart to DepthGovernor (depth limit). Part of the decomposition governance cluster with ConceptualDecomposition, FractalIntelligence, UniversalSolverTree. Invoked by any pattern that spawns parallel subtasks — particularly PolymorphicSolver when running strategies in parallel. Compare with BeamSearch: BeamSearch picks top-K and moves on; BreadthGovernor is a system-wide policy that applies across decompositions.

motivation.why_it_exists: Coordination failure is inevitable in distributed agent systems, and silent failure is catastrophic. Break names the protocol for announcing 'I can't continue' with enough structure (severity, reason, recoverability) that partners know how to respond. Without it, failure is either silent (partners wait forever) or chaotic (partners interpret the same failure differently).
motivation.removability: Not removable without losing the graceful-failure story for multi-agent work. You can substitute Failed as a terminal state but lose the recoverability distinction. Break is specifically the 'pause, partners acknowledge, decide whether to recover or escalate' flow.

usage.intended: protocol for announcing coordination failure — {severity, reason, recoverable}.
usage.future: any "coordination failed, we need to stop/pause" signal.
usage.broad_contexts: saga break events, distributed-transaction aborts, emergency stops in multi-party coordination, cascading failure propagation, ejection events.
usage.every_context_needs: severity, reason, recoverability flag, ACK requirement, escalation-on-no-ACK.
usage.varies: broadcast scope, severity levels, default termination vs pause, integration with CircuitBreaker/EjectionSeat.

tensions: Severity classification vs simplicity — severity levels give useful routing but force callers to make a judgment they may not be well-positioned to make under stress.
ACK collection vs liveness — requiring partners to acknowledge the break is safer but blocks progress when a partner is itself failing.
Cascading Breaks vs true failure — if Break itself fails to deliver (meta-failure), the protocol breaks down at exactly the moment it's most needed.
tradeoffs: Gains: explicit failure semantics for multi-agent coordination, severity-based routing, a clear interface between Break and retry logic.
Gives up: simplicity. The protocol (broadcast → ACK → escalate on timeout) is heavier than just setting a status field, and the weight doesn't always pay off.
critique: The 'No data loss during interruption' invariant is aspirational — the pattern has no mechanism that enforces it, only a naming.
ACK timeout tuning is the named failure mode and it's genuinely hard; too short and transient network issues look like failures, too long and partners pile up work on a dead agent.
Recoverable vs non-recoverable is a binary; real failures are frequently 'recoverable with compensation,' 'recoverable with user input,' etc. The pattern flattens that.

Break.family_discussion: Lives in the failure-handling cluster with FailClosed, FailFast, FailSafe, Retry, and Compensate. Break is specifically the multi-party announcement flavor; FailClosed is single-actor. Pairs with AuditTrail (the durable record of the Break event) and Handoff (which a recoverable Break may trigger).

motivation.why_it_exists: Multi-party coordination frequently fails mid-commit, leaving participants in inconsistent states. Bubble names the isolation pattern: try the coordination inside a sandbox (copy-on-write, snapshot-isolated), commit to reality only if all participants reach READY. It's a transactional pattern imported into agent coordination.
motivation.removability: Removable if you accept the costs of partial-commit cleanup or if coordination is naturally idempotent. Bubble is the right primitive when the coordination is complex, the participants are diverse, and partial outcomes are expensive to roll back. Simpler settings don't need it.

usage.intended: isolated sandbox with copy-on-write state and soft resource reservations.
usage.future: any "try coordination without real consequences" environment.
usage.broad_contexts: distributed transaction sandboxes, rehearsal spaces, multi-party negotiation sandboxes, dry-run environments, game scenarios.
usage.every_context_needs: isolation, copy-on-write state, soft reservations, 2-phase commit for merge.
usage.varies: TTL, isolation level, nesting (child bubbles), participant count.

tensions: Isolation guarantees vs resource holds — soft reservations during a long-running bubble starve other work; releasing them early breaks isolation.
Snapshot freshness vs bubble duration — the longer the bubble runs, the more the outside world drifts from the snapshot; commit-time conflict becomes likely.
Nested bubbles vs complexity — bubbles-within-bubbles are powerful for hierarchical coordination and a source of intricate failure modes.
tradeoffs: Gains: transactional semantics for coordination, safe trial of multi-party flows, compositional isolation via nesting.
Gives up: latency (all-or-nothing commit is slower than partial execution), simplicity (the protocol is intricate), and freshness (snapshots age during the bubble).
critique: Copy-on-write snapshot isolation is well-known at the database level; lifting it to agent coordination is conceptually clean but operationally expensive (agent state is rarely cheap to snapshot).
The stale-snapshot failure mode is fundamental: if the outside world changed during the bubble, the bubble's outcome may be invalid even after successful internal commit.
Resource starvation from long-running bubbles is noted but unmitigated — no built-in timeout or preemption story.

Bubble.family_discussion: Transactional sibling of LatticeCommit (CRDT-style eventual consistency), AnchorDrop (emergency checkpointing), and Handoff (atomic transfer). The copy-on-write/READY-then-COMMIT shape is directly borrowed from two-phase commit protocols. Compare with AtomicBid — Bubble is heavy (all-or-nothing), AtomicBid is light (fire-and-compensate); they're opposite ends of the coordination-safety spectrum.

motivation.why_this_layer: arithmetic ledger with floor constraint — no cognition required; strategy of allocation is separate (ComputeBudget/MVR live in Mind)
motivation.why_it_exists: A typed resource allocation — 'you have this much compute/time/energy for this task.' Without Budget as a pattern, resource limits live as implicit parameters that fragment across every pattern needing them. Budget makes the constraint a first-class artifact.
motivation.removability: No. Task budget semantics, ComputeBudget, BoundedTask, and every stopping-rule pattern depend on Budget. Removing forces each to re-invent the conservation semantics.

usage.intended: quantified allocation of a resource constraining execution.
usage.broad_contexts: compute budgets, time budgets, energy budgets, token budgets, attention budgets, monetary budgets, risk budgets, retry budgets.
usage.every_context_needs: an allocation (how much), a consumption/refund tracking mechanism, conservation (total tracked value is preserved across transactions).
usage.varies: strict non-negative (BoundedBudget) vs. overdraft-allowed (OverdraftBudget), monotonic vs rebalancing (RollingBudget), refund semantics, multi-resource aggregation.

tensions: Single conserved quantity vs multi-resource budgets: Conservation invariant (Allocated + Remaining = Total) assumes one quantity. Real budgets mix compute, time, and money — needing multiple Budgets or a multi-dimensional specialization.
Hard limit vs soft targeting: the mechanism says hard limit. Soft-target budgets (prefer under X but allow overrun with warning) need a descendant; parent is strict.
Pre-allocated vs accumulating: Budget is pre-allocated ('constrains execution'). Pay-as-you-go models need a different pattern.
tradeoffs: Hard limit buys predictable bounds at the cost of no graceful-degradation pattern.
Single-quantity simplicity buys clean accounting at the cost of requiring separate Budgets per resource type.
Conservation invariant buys book-keeping rigor at the cost of needing a trusted accounting mechanism.
critique: Only one invariant, zero failure modes. Missing invariants: Monotonic Consumption (used resources don't un-use themselves), Non-negativity (Remaining ≥ 0). Missing failure modes: Accounting Drift (sum-to-Total invariant violated), Budget Exhaustion (consumption exceeds limit despite check).
'Hard limit on consumption' is declarative but has no enforcement mechanism — the pattern is a contract, not a check.
The resource type is free-form ('compute, time, energy'). A typed resource field would let Budget-compatibility checks happen at compose time.

Budget.family_discussion: The resource-allocation primitive. Composed with `Conservation` (the invariant basis), `ComputeBudget` (the cognitive-scoped variant), `BoundedTask` (budget-carrying Task). Consumed by `MarginalValueRule` (the stopping-rule condition).

motivation.why_it_exists: Full rollout is expensive and frequently fails on assumptions that could have been tested cheaply. Build names the prototype-before-commit pattern: construct a low-cost artifact that specifically addresses the risky assumptions, read the result, then decide on full rollout. Without it, agents either over-commit (betting the full plan on untested assumptions) or under-commit (never building anything).
motivation.removability: Removable if assumptions are truly low-risk or if rollout itself is cheap. Keeping it as a named pattern is a forcing function — it asserts that prototype-then-commit is a default move, not an optional flourish. Removing it leaves agents free to charge straight at full rollout.

usage.intended: construct low-cost prototype to verify critical assumptions before full commitment.
usage.future: any "make something cheap to learn" operation.
usage.broad_contexts: MVP construction, POC development, architectural spikes, breadboard circuits, UX prototyping, experimental drafts.
usage.every_context_needs: spec with critical assumptions, low-cost artifact construction, verification against spec.
usage.varies: prototype fidelity, construction cost bound, iteration count before commit.

tensions: Prototype fidelity vs cost — low-fidelity prototypes cost less and carry the risk of false-negative (the pattern names this failure mode); high-fidelity prototypes edge toward the full product.
Risk-specific prototypes vs general exploration — the invariant demands the prototype 'address specific risks,' but in practice exploration often reveals risks the original plan didn't name.
Build vs plan — overengineering during build is the dominant failure mode because agents find it easier to build more than to stop.
tradeoffs: Gains: cheap de-risking, empirical validation of specific assumptions, a bounded experiment with clear termination.
Gives up: speed-to-full-rollout and the option of 'just ship' when the prototype's overhead isn't warranted.
critique: The Marginal Value Rule is cited but not specified — what counts as marginal value, how to decide when further build is worth it, is left to the caller.
Over-engineering is the most common failure and the pattern has no structural mitigation; 'build less than the full product' is a guideline.
False negatives (prototype fails due to low fidelity) are particularly dangerous because they kill good plans; the pattern doesn't specify how to distinguish prototype failure from plan failure.

Build.family_discussion: Sibling of Plan (the precursor) and Rollout (the successor). Part of the deliberate-execution family with FirstPrinciples, Sketch, and Experiment. Compare with Canary — Build is a prototype of the artifact itself; Canary is a prototype of the execution path. Both de-risk before committing, on different axes.

motivation.why_it_exists: Recomputation is the single largest source of wasted compute in agent loops, and most computations are deterministic functions of their inputs. Cache names the pattern of storing (input → output) pairs so repeat lookups skip the computation. The named foundation ensures consistency and freshness aren't afterthoughts — they're invariants.
motivation.removability: Removable if compute is free and determinism is absent — neither is common. In practice every agent system caches something; the pattern earns its weight by making the cache's contract explicit (consistency, freshness) rather than implicit.

usage.intended: temporary high-speed storage to avoid recomputation.
usage.future: any key-value store with staleness semantics.
usage.broad_contexts: memoized functions, RAG retrievers, pathway memory, routing decisions, computed heuristics, embedding caches, session state, prompt caches.
usage.every_context_needs: a way to store keyed values and look them up. Storage semantic is the definitional floor.
usage.varies: eviction policy (LRU, LFU, FIFO), TTL, size limits, consistency model, distributed vs local, invalidation strategy.

tensions: Consistency (Cache(Key) == Source(Key) if valid) vs staleness — the invariant holds only while the cached value is valid; determining 'valid' is the hard part.
Freshness vs hit rate — aggressive invalidation keeps data fresh and trashes the cache; lazy invalidation keeps the hit rate and risks staleness.
Keyed lookup vs semantic lookup — caches work great on exact keys and badly on near-matches; semantic caching is a different pattern entirely.
tradeoffs: Gains: massive speedup on repeat lookups, reduced load on the backing source, a clean place to instrument hit/miss rates.
Gives up: data freshness and simplicity — every cache becomes a new source of staleness bugs. 'There are only two hard things in CS' applies.
critique: Staleness is called out as a failure mode but the pattern has no invalidation protocol — 'write-behind, invalidation discipline' are described as 'descendant concerns.' The hardest problem is deferred.
Thrashing (frequent evictions) has no built-in monitoring; a cache too small for its workload just silently hurts performance.
No semantics for partial results or incremental updates — caches either hit or miss, which is a coarse view of actually-useful intermediate states.

Cache.family_discussion: Core infrastructure primitive, paired with Source (the backing store), Invalidation (the freshness mechanism), and Key (the lookup handle). Compare with PathwayMemory — PathwayMemory is a memoization pattern for reasoning traces rather than values. Compare with HeuristicSnap — both speed up reasoning by avoiding work, but Cache is faithful repetition, HeuristicSnap is approximate lookup.

motivation.why_it_exists: Running a full coordination path with real resources is expensive and destructive to roll back. Canary names the expendable-probe pattern: spawn a small agent with bounded blast radius, run the full path, read telemetry, decide. The key invariant is the canary must fail before the main system — without that, it's not testing, just adding load.
motivation.removability: Removable if you're willing to test in production (which is often fine for low-stakes work). Essential when the real path's failures are expensive or destructive. Canary is essentially A/B-testing for multi-agent coordination — you can build it by hand but the named pattern codifies the invariants.

usage.intended: expendable agent tests full coordination path before committing real resources.
usage.future: any "test in limited scope first" pattern.
usage.broad_contexts: canary deployments, tasters (historical kings), pilot programs, beta-tester cohorts, A/B tests with small initial exposure.
usage.every_context_needs: bounded blast radius, full coordination path test, telemetry emission, proceed/caution/abort recommendation.
usage.varies: resource bound, telemetry detail, lifecycle (destroy/recycle/promote), canary count (single vs multiple).

tensions: Fidelity (canary matches production) vs cost (canary is cheap) — the closer the canary is to real, the more expensive it becomes; the further it is, the less useful its signal.
Canary gaming — if agents can tell they're being canaried, they can behave differently. The pattern names this failure mode but can't prevent it at the agent level.
Predictive vs retrospective — canaries test whether the path works before commit; non-deterministic paths may canary-pass and production-fail.
tradeoffs: Gains: cheap path validation, bounded blast radius for failure, telemetry without cost of full commitment.
Gives up: confidence — canary success is necessary but not sufficient for production success. The pattern honestly owns this limitation.
critique: The 'canary fails before main system' invariant is the whole point and also very hard to enforce without fidelity; cheap canaries fail in different ways than real workloads.
Non-determinism is called out as a failure mode with no mitigation — statistical canary testing (run many canaries, compute failure rate) is needed but isn't part of the pattern.
The canary/real distinction degrades over time: patterns that worked at canary scale fail at real scale (distributed systems corollary), and the pattern doesn't account for scale-sensitive failures.

Canary.family_discussion: Safety-testing sibling of Build (prototype the artifact), Probe (measure-specific-property), and Witness (produce an attestation). Compare with Bubble — Canary is lightweight sacrificial, Bubble is heavyweight transactional. Both test coordination before commit, at different cost/confidence points.

motivation.why_it_exists: Agents with unbounded capacity memorize; agents with pressured capacity abstract. CapacityPressure names the regularization pattern — artificially constrain resources until the agent is forced to compress signal. Without it, agents default to exact replication whenever possible, which is useless for generalization.
motivation.removability: Removable in classical ML setups where regularization is handled by other mechanisms (weight decay, dropout). As a pattern for agent design, it's a rare but load-bearing primitive — there's no other pattern that names 'force abstraction by starving capacity.' Removing it leaves the technique nameless.

usage.intended: forced abstraction via resource starvation — create bottleneck Capacity < Information.
usage.broad_contexts: ML bottleneck regularization (variational autoencoders), educational summarization requirements, emergency resource rationing, legal word-limit drafting, haiku constraints.
usage.every_context_needs: resource constraint creating bottleneck, pressure to compress/generalize, selective signal retention.
usage.varies: `compression_ratio` (principled [0.0, 1.0] per §3.17), `resource_type` (enum), pressure shape.

tensions: Tight bottleneck (abstraction forced) vs too tight (collapse, underfitting) — the knife-edge between productive pressure and destructive starvation is narrow.
Adversarial encoding — a sufficiently clever agent finds ways to 'zip' noise rather than abstract it, satisfying the bottleneck without the intended behavior.
Utility preservation (invariant) vs measurability — 'retains predictive power for the target task' requires a task to measure against; generic agent loops often lack such a task.
tradeoffs: Gains: forced abstraction, better generalization, a pressure-relief valve against over-memorization.
Gives up: performance on within-distribution tasks. CapacityPressure is specifically not for tasks that benefit from exact replication.
critique: Adversarial Encoding is the hardest failure mode and the pattern has no structural defense — preventing 'zip instead of abstract' requires measuring the compressed representation's generalization, which is exactly what the bottleneck was supposed to force.
False Abstraction (hallucinating patterns to satisfy the bottleneck) is the second-hardest failure mode, and similarly unprevented by the mechanism alone.

Bottleneck sizing is an art; the pattern offers no principle for choosing it beyond 'Capacity < Information Content,' which is too coarse to be actionable. Failure modes were previously jammed into one list entry (Collapse + Adversarial Encoding + False Abstraction run together); now split into three distinct entries.

CapacityPressure.family_discussion: Information-theoretic sibling of Compress (explicit reduction), Abstraction (the output), and Parsimony (the goal). Compare with EntropyPump — both manipulate information content to drive cognition; EntropyPump injects, CapacityPressure constrains. Sits in the rare corner of the library devoted to representation engineering.

motivation.why_it_exists: The typed capability advertisement that makes agent discovery before contact possible. Without Card (or something like it), agents that want to coordinate must either enumerate each other's capabilities by trying them (expensive, error-prone) or rely on a central registry (defeats decentralization). Card lets agents publish 'here is what I claim to do' in a structured form that can be filtered, ranked, and verified.
motivation.removability: No. Card is the Manifest surface of the Solver contract — every PolymorphicSolver uses it. Agent-discovery protocols (AgentDiscover, ToolDiscovery) reference Card. Collapsing would force each protocol to reinvent the capability-advertisement shape.

usage.intended: structured capability advertisement enabling agent discovery before contact.
usage.broad_contexts: agent cards (A2A protocol), LinkedIn profiles, business cards, DMP agent-capability manifests, API capability documents, MCP server metadata.
usage.every_context_needs: agent_id, endpoint, protocols, capabilities, constraints, metadata.
usage.varies: publication mechanism (registry, broadcast, DHT, well-known endpoint), TTL, verification/signing.

tensions: Immutable after issue vs capability evolution: the invariant forbids changing a Card after issue. But real agents add capabilities, deprecate features, update rate limits. The pattern's answer is TTL + new issuance — the old Card expires, a new one is published.
Claimed vs actual capability: False Claims is a named failure, mitigated by Probe. But Probe-free deployments take claims at face value. The pattern does not enforce verification.

Self-published vs certified: a Card is self-published by the advertising Agent. In low-trust contexts, that invites fraudulent claims. Certification (a trusted third party signs the Card) lives outside the pattern.
tradeoffs: Structured schema buys filterability (agents can query for 'who can do X') at the cost of a shared schema dependency (agents must agree on the capability vocabulary).
Immutability-after-issue buys byte-stable caching (Cards can be cached and reused) at the cost of forcing re-issuance for every real change.
Discovery-before-contact buys efficiency at the cost of trusting claims — until Probe is invoked, the caller is operating on unverified self-descriptions.
critique: One invariant, two failure modes. Missing invariants: Signed-by-Issuer (Card must carry the issuing Agent's signature), Non-Empty Capabilities (a Card with no claimed capabilities is operationally vestigial).
Stale Cards is a named failure with TTL as the mitigation, but TTL is advisory — the pattern doesn't enforce stale-Card rejection on the consumer side.
The metadata block (version, ttl, publication info) is described in prose but not schema'd. A caller implementing Card needs to invent field names; discovery protocols may diverge.

Card.family_discussion: The Manifest surface output of the Solver contract. Consumed by `AgentDiscover`, `ToolDiscovery`, `SpectralTune`. Paired with `Probe` (verifies claimed capabilities), `Identity` (the issuer), and the agent-protocol family for structured coordination.

motivation.why_it_exists: Most patterns describe value-extracting or goal-directed action. Care names the opposite stance: work applied to reduce disorder in a target without pulling value out. It's the pattern for maintenance, curation, nurture — activities that are load-bearing and systematically under-named in goal-oriented vocabularies.
motivation.removability: Removable if you accept that agent systems shouldn't engage in non-extractive work. That assumption breaks down quickly — caring for the graph itself (pruning stale nodes, resolving ambiguities, refreshing stale context) is Care, and without naming it these activities get mislabeled as 'maintenance overhead' or skipped entirely.

usage.intended: non-transactional maintenance energy — Work applied to reduce target's Entropy without Value extraction.
usage.broad_contexts: stewardship (Gardener), relationship maintenance, codebase refactoring (no feature delivery), janitorial work, system hygiene, ecosystem tending.
usage.every_context_needs: target, Work application, Entropy reduction, absence of Value extraction.
usage.varies: intensity, frequency, measurement (or lack thereof), reciprocity structures.

tensions: Entropy reduction vs closed-system thermodynamics — local entropy decrease requires export of disorder elsewhere; the pattern doesn't account for where the disorder goes.
No value extraction vs resource consumption — Care costs Work but produces no direct return; this is at odds with optimization pressures in most agent systems.
Buffer against volatility vs intervention overhead — caring well is frequently invisible; the pattern's value is noticed mainly in its absence.
tradeoffs: Gains: a named slot for non-extractive work, explicit recognition that maintenance is distinct from production, a frame for curation/nurture/attention.
Gives up: simplicity of the 'every action extracts value' model. Care forces the library to admit that not all work is ROI-shaped.
critique: Very thin mechanism — the pattern is almost a philosophical stance. 'Application of work to reduce entropy' fits thermodynamics but is vague for programming.
'Without explicit value extraction' is hard to enforce; agents optimizing for some utility will often rationalize Care as value-extractive in disguise.
No composition story — how Care interacts with Maintain, Curate, Nurture, or Tend isn't specified; there's risk of overlap or nominal confusion.

Care.family_discussion: Philosophical sibling of Maintain, Nurture, Curate, Attend. Contrasts with Extract, Exploit, Consume. Compare with Entropy (the target Care reduces) and Work (the resource Care consumes). Part of the small 'stance' family that names non-instrumental modes of action — patterns about why, not just how.

motivation.why_it_exists: Taxonomy depends on a primitive for 'these items are members of the same group.' Category is that primitive — a named bin, inclusion criteria, members. Without it, every taxonomy or classification re-invents membership semantics. It's the foundational noun behind Classify, Bin, Group, and Taxonomy as verbs.
motivation.removability: Could be folded into Set or Group, but loses the taxonomic semantics (Category implies inclusion rules, not just a collection). Essential for any pattern that reasons about types, classes, or kinds — which is most of the vocabulary.

usage.intended: specific grouping/bin for objects — equivalence class.
usage.broad_contexts: taxonomic categories, type categories, product categories, email folder categories, research field categories.
usage.every_context_needs: grouping criterion, equivalence semantic for certain ops.
usage.varies: mutual exclusion (category A excludes B), hierarchy integration, fuzzy membership.

tensions: Crisp inclusion (clear rules) vs fuzzy reality — real categories often have graded membership (Wittgenstein's family resemblance); the pattern defaults to set-like crispness.
Hierarchical structure vs flat organization — categories naturally nest, but the pattern doesn't prescribe a hierarchy, leaving it to callers.
Fixed taxonomy vs evolving classification — as new items appear, categories must grow, split, or merge; the pattern has no evolution story.
tradeoffs: Gains: a reusable primitive for grouping, explicit inclusion criteria, clear equivalence semantics for operations within a category.
Gives up: fuzzy and graded membership (supported only by explicit extensions), and taxonomic evolution (the pattern is static).
critique: Very thin — barely more than a named set. The interesting work happens in Taxonomy, Classify, and Tag (which use Category as substrate); Category itself is almost a stub.
No semantics for category boundaries — membership is binary, which fits some domains and distorts others.
Treats category membership as a property of the item; some theories treat it as a property of the observer (category as lens), and the pattern can't express that.

Category.family_discussion: Substrate for Taxonomy, Classify, Tag, Bin. Compare with Type (a more formal variant with richer semantics) and Schema (which combines types with structure). Category is the minimum viable grouping primitive; the others build richer structure on top.

motivation.why_this_layer: buffers until causal dependencies met — causal-cone physics
motivation.why_it_exists: In async agent systems, messages arrive in order of delivery, not order of causation. Without a barrier, an agent can observe an effect before its cause — an 'impossible state' that violates the agent's model. CausalBarrier buffers messages until their causal dependencies are met, guaranteeing the agent never sees a paradox.
motivation.removability: Removable in synchronous systems or systems where causality is naturally preserved. Distributed/async agent systems need it; without it, debugging becomes impossible because 'impossible states' appear intermittently in traces. The alternative is making every pattern causality-aware, which is much worse.

usage.intended: buffer messages until causal dependencies met (never see impossible state).
usage.broad_contexts: distributed systems (vector clocks), eventual consistency stores, message queues with causal order, game-state replication, collaborative editing (OT/CRDT).
usage.every_context_needs: buffer, dependency tracking per message, release rule (all predecessors seen).
usage.varies: dependency representation (vector clock, happens-before, explicit edges), buffer size limits, timeout policy, stale-dependency garbage collection.

tensions: Strict ordering (safety) vs throughput — buffering messages until dependencies arrive is slower than processing in arrival order.
Buffer size vs stall — a small buffer overflows on dependency delays; a large buffer adds latency to every causal chain.
Causal dependency detection vs false ordering — the barrier needs to know which events depend on which; getting that wrong either stalls progress (phantom deps) or violates ordering (missed deps).
tradeoffs: Gains: freedom from impossible-state bugs, simplified reasoning for every pattern downstream, a clean separation between event ordering and event processing.
Gives up: latency and memory. Messages wait in the buffer for dependencies to arrive, which accumulates end-to-end delay and buffer pressure.
critique: Buffer overflow (the named failure mode) is fundamental — dependencies that never arrive stall forever. The pattern has no timeout/drop mechanism.
Requires every sender to tag causal dependencies correctly; a misbehaving sender breaks the barrier's guarantees invisibly.
Doesn't distinguish strict from weak causality — happens-before ordering is stronger than needed in many cases, and the pattern has no weaker mode.

CausalBarrier.family_discussion: Lives in the causation family with Causation, HappensBefore, and TemporalOrder. Implementation-oriented counterpart to Causation's theoretical role. Compare with StateLock — both use locking to preserve invariants, but StateLock protects state while CausalBarrier protects ordering. Pairs with EventQueue and AuditTrail as the infrastructure for async agent processing.

motivation.why_this_layer: directed causal edge obtains regardless of any author — a relationship in reality
motivation.why_it_exists: The distinction between causation and correlation is foundational for any reasoning that intervenes in the world (not just observes). Minting Causation as a pattern pins intervention-responsiveness as the defining property — which is the right distinction to carry through dependent patterns (Correlation, Experiment, Abduction).
motivation.removability: Probably not. The library has multiple patterns that invoke causation (Correlation contrasts with it, Experiment is the inference tool, CausalBarrier enforces ordering). Without a shared pinned definition, each usage can drift. The structured-thinking criterion applies strongly.

usage.intended: a relationship where one event directly forces another.
usage.broad_contexts: physics causation, statistical causal inference, legal causation, economic causal models, scientific experimental causality, debugging (A caused B).
usage.every_context_needs: cause event, effect event, directness semantic (manipulating cause alters effect), distinction from Correlation.
usage.varies: causal strength, directness (direct vs chained), counterfactual semantics, confidence.

tensions: Directed edge framing vs richer structures: causal graphs can have feedback, multi-path effects, and probabilistic edges. The mechanism names a 'directed edge,' which is right for the minimal case but elides the richer structure.

Intervention-responsiveness vs counterfactual: the definition is operational (what happens when you intervene?) rather than counterfactual (what would have happened?). Different philosophical grounds; the library picks operational.

Physics placement: Causation obtains in reality regardless of author, making it substrate. But cognitive causal inference (the attribution task) is Mind. The pattern in Physics is about the relationship; attribution mechanisms live separately.
tradeoffs: Intervention-responsiveness buys empirical handle-ability (you can test causation by intervening) at the cost of circumscribing natural-occurrence cases where no one can intervene.
Directed-edge framing buys graph-theoretic tractability at the cost of hiding feedback loops.
Substrate placement buys stability (the relation doesn't depend on who names it) at the cost of ignoring the observer effects in Measurement.
critique: Zero invariants and zero failure modes. For a pattern this philosophically-loaded, at least: Directedness (cause precedes effect; not symmetric); Non-Inverse (A causing B does not imply B causes A); Testability-Under-Intervention (the edge is falsifiable by an intervention experiment).
The mechanism mentions 'external change to the cause alters the effect' as the definitional property but doesn't say what counts as external. Internal feedback loops blur this.
No cross-reference to Correlation, despite the library minting both and defining them against each other. A 'Distinguished From' block is warranted.

Causation.family_discussion: The causal-structure anchor in Physics. Paired with `Correlation` (the contrast anchor — what you have when you don't have Causation).
