critique: No failure modes. Missing: Boundary Drift (closure boundary changes during the transformation so pre/post cannot be compared), Hidden Source (an apparent violation turns out to reflect an unmodeled boundary flux).
'Closed system' is a load-bearing concept but the pattern doesn't define what qualifies — total energy isolation? Controlled material flux? The library assumes the concept is known.

The three listed domains (energy, charge, information in a sealed channel) are illustrative but uneven — information conservation in a sealed channel is less familiar than energy conservation and arguably deserves its own pattern.

Conservation.family_discussion: Substrate law linked with `Entropy` (the quantity that is not conserved under general dynamics), `Measurement` (which extracts conserved information), and `Reversibility` (which preserves everything, including entropy).

motivation.why_this_layer: immutable rule set binding a group
motivation.why_it_exists: The structured governance document — principles, rights, penalty rules — serving as the static input for oath binding. Without Constitution as a pattern, 'foundational rules for a group' is a free-form concept; governance patterns need machine-verifiable rules.
motivation.removability: Probably retain. OathBind, enforcement patterns, and governance workflows reference Constitution. Collapsing into generic AcceptSpec loses the 'this is the fundamental rule set' distinction.

usage.intended: immutable rule set defining principles for an agent group.
usage.broad_contexts: DAO constitutions, corporate bylaws, software rule sets (e.g., Claude's Constitutional AI), community charters, API governance rules, federation rules.
usage.every_context_needs: structured principles (immutable once ratified), binding semantics (via `OathBind`), identity of ratifying parties.
usage.varies: amendment mechanism (rigid vs. flexible), enforcement mechanism (automated vs. delegated), penalty specifications, inheritance from parent constitutions.

tensions: Clarity invariant (machine-verifiable) vs interpretive flexibility: real constitutions have intentional ambiguity (principles that require judicial interpretation). The pattern is strict — if it can't be machine-checked, it's not a valid Constitution entry.
Stability invariant (no runtime self-modification) vs adaptive governance: some governance needs runtime amendment. The pattern forbids it — amendment is out-of-band, via a separate process.
Penalty rules are automated. But 'fair enforcement' is a judgment call — the pattern commits to algorithmic penalties, which may be blunt.
tradeoffs: Machine-verifiable invariant buys automated enforcement at the cost of excluding interpretive rules.
Runtime immutability buys stability at the cost of agility in changing contexts.
Automated penalty rules buy consistency at the cost of case-specific judgment.
critique: Two invariants, zero failure modes. Missing: Ambiguity (a rule technically machine-verifiable but semantically underspecified), Penalty Proportionality (rules fire proportional to offense), Consistency (rules don't contradict each other).
The relationship to OathBind is one-way (Constitution is the input to OathBind) but the pattern doesn't declare this dependency explicitly.
Modification process ('formal out-of-band') is mentioned but unspecified — what constitutes 'formal' and 'out-of-band' is a governance question the pattern leaves open.

Constitution.family_discussion: The governance-layer rule set. Paired with `OathBind` (binding agents to constitutions), `AuditTrail` (for enforcement logging), penalty-automation patterns. Sibling to `Contract` (bilateral/multi-party) — Constitution is group-level rules, Contract is inter-party agreement.

motivation.why_it_exists: Optimization without bounds produces nonsense — best answer on the wrong axis. Constraint names the boundary condition: a hard limit that valid solutions must satisfy, explicitly typed (resource/safety/legal/physical). The non-compensatory invariant is crucial — you can't trade off one constraint violation against excess on another, which is exactly where naive optimization goes wrong.
motivation.removability: Non-removable. Every constrained optimization — which is most real-world optimization — needs this primitive. Removing it collapses Solve, Optimize, Plan, and AcceptSpec to unconstrained form, which they aren't.

usage.intended: non-negotiable boundary condition that valid solutions must satisfy.
usage.broad_contexts: resource budgets, safety bounds, legal compliance, physical laws, organizational policies, API rate limits, regulatory constraints.
usage.every_context_needs: boundary condition, non-compensatory semantic (can't offset one violation with another surplus), constraint type (Resource/Safety/Legal/Physical), Holographic Inheritance.
usage.varies: inheritance mechanism, violation-detection timing, override protocol (who can lift constraints).

tensions: Non-compensatory (hard) vs soft constraints (graded) — the invariant forbids compensation, but real-world constraints are often graded (slight budget overrun is different from catastrophic overrun).

Explicit (invariant) vs implicit constraints — the pattern demands all constraints be stated; real deployments always have hidden constraints that reveal themselves at failure time (the named failure mode).
Inheritance rule vs modular design — child constraints must include parent's, which is safe and makes modular design painful (you can't reduce constraints in a subtype).
tradeoffs: Gains: principled solution rejection, typed constraint categories, guaranteed parent-inheritance of constraint bounds.
Gives up: flexibility. Constraint relaxation (the named failure mode) exists because real-world solutions often need just a little give, and the pattern's non-compensatory invariant forbids it.
critique: 'Explicitness' invariant is aspirational — hidden constraints always outnumber named ones, and the pattern has no mechanism for surfacing them.
Constraint conflict (no solution exists) is called out as a failure mode but there's no built-in detection; agents discover conflicts by failing to satisfy, which is late.
Type taxonomy (Resource/Safety/Legal/Physical) is reasonable but non-exhaustive; ethical, aesthetic, social constraints don't fit neatly.

Constraint.family_discussion: Foundational optimization primitive. Pairs with AcceptSpec (constraints as quality bars), Budget (resource constraint specifically), and Solve (the consumer of constraints). Compare with Invariant — Constraint is a bound on valid solutions; Invariant is a property preserved across operations. Both are 'things that must hold,' at different operational points.

motivation.why_it_exists: Generating content first and checking constraints later is the default agent behavior and the source of most policy violations — safety, format, length. ConstraintFirst names the inverse: define the container first (safety rules, format requirements), then generate within it. Without this pattern, constraint violations are post-hoc rejections rather than structural impossibilities.
motivation.removability: Removable — you can always generate-then-filter. ConstraintFirst earns its weight when violations are expensive to filter post-hoc (leaked unsafe content, unrecoverable format errors, expensive re-generation). Remove it and you accept higher violation rates or more generate-filter iterations.

usage.intended: generate negative space (constraints) before content — rigid container then fill.
usage.broad_contexts: structured writing with word limits, regulatory-compliant drafting, safety-first software design, constitutional drafting, code with type signatures first.
usage.every_context_needs: constraint-set generation first, content generation second, form-vs-function separation.
usage.varies: constraint granularity, sequence rigidity (can iterate back to constraints?).

tensions: Rigid container (safety) vs creative expression — constraint-first can over-constrain, ruling out valid but unexpected outputs.
Constraints immutable during operation (invariant) vs learning — if the generation reveals a constraint was wrong, the pattern forbids updating in-flight.
Separation of form from function — the two are coupled in interesting artifacts; forcing them to be specified independently sometimes produces form that functionally can't be filled.
tradeoffs: Gains: violation-prevention at generation time, auditable constraint specification, reduced rejection cycles.
Gives up: generative flexibility (over-constraining is the named failure mode) and adaptability (constraints frozen during operation can't respond to what's discovered during generation).
critique: Over-constraining is the dominant failure mode and the pattern has no built-in relaxation step — constraints are set once and enforced forever within the operation.
Constraints immutable-during-operation is a clean-room invariant; real generation legitimately surfaces constraint issues that need mid-operation revision.
The 'negative space first' framing is poetic but under-specified — how you construct a constraint container for a free-form creative task isn't obvious.

ConstraintFirst.family_discussion: Pairs with ContextFirst (read shared state first) as the pair of 'before you act' primitives. Uses Constraint as substrate. Compare with AcceptSpec — AcceptSpec is a post-hoc quality bar, ConstraintFirst is a pre-hoc container. Both enforce quality, at different operational points.

motivation.why_it_exists: Before you can reason about a domain, you need to know what the terms are and how they relate. ConstructOntology names the primitive for building that structure from raw data or seed axioms — the 'physics' of a domain. Without it, every agent working in a new domain has to re-derive the taxonomy, leading to divergent concepts for the same territory.
motivation.removability: Removable when ontologies are pre-built and handed to agents. The pattern's value is specifically for the construction phase — adversarial ontology construction, iterative refinement, ontology bootstrapping. Remove it and you're left with static taxonomies that can't adapt to new domains.

usage.intended: build structured set of concepts and relationships from raw data/axioms — define domain's "physics."
usage.broad_contexts: domain-specific ontology construction (medical, legal), taxonomic schema design, world-building in fiction, API-schema evolution, scientific-classification construction.
usage.every_context_needs: raw data or seed axioms, FirstPrinciples grounding, structured output with concepts + relationships.
usage.varies: formality, domain specificity, collaborative vs solo, revision cadence.

tensions: Completeness invariant (all referenced terms defined) vs open-world reality — every ontology has unreferenced terms; full completeness forces closure the world doesn't have.
Consistency invariant (no contradictions) vs legitimate tensions — real domains include productive contradictions (wave-particle duality) that the consistency invariant would forbid.
Seed axioms vs emergent structure — starting from axioms biases the ontology toward the axiom-holder's worldview; starting from raw data produces structure that may not match any existing framework.
tradeoffs: Gains: named primitive for ontology construction, explicit completeness and consistency checks, a substrate for Adversarial Ontology Construction.
Gives up: pragmatism. Full completeness and full consistency are rarely achievable for real domains; the pattern holds them as invariants anyway.
critique: Incoherence (the named failure mode) is the bare minimum — real ontologies have deeper failures (over-specification, missing middle, wrong abstraction level) that the pattern doesn't name.
The 'constructive counterpart to Adversarial Ontology Construction' framing is useful but the relationship between the two isn't fully specified.
No mechanism for ontology evolution — once constructed, what happens when the domain shifts? The pattern doesn't prescribe versioning or revision.

ConstructOntology.family_discussion: Foundational epistemic primitive paired with Taxonomy (the output), Category (the building blocks), and AdversarialOntologyConstruction (the methodology that uses it). Compare with ConceptBlend — ConstructOntology builds from foundations; ConceptBlend fuses existing ontologies into a third.

motivation.why_it_exists: Portable execution-environment container — constraints, tools, memory, identity. Without Context as a shared structure, every agent handoff invents its own serialization. The Holographic Inheritance property (child contexts add but never remove constraints) is the safety invariant that makes delegation auditable.
motivation.removability: No. Every agent-protocol, every nested Task, every solver-tree traversal needs Context. Removing would force each pattern to re-invent the serialization, breaking cross-protocol compatibility.

usage.intended: portable execution environment — constraints, tools, memory, identity.
usage.broad_contexts: agent contexts, LLM conversation contexts, multi-turn dialogue state, subprocess environments, database transaction contexts, session state.
usage.every_context_needs: inherited constraints, available capabilities, working memory, identity claims.
usage.varies: persistence, serializability, transferability between agents, clone/fork semantics.

tensions: Constraint Monotonicity vs flexibility: children can add, never remove. But legitimate use cases (reducing scope on trusted delegates) want constraint removal. The library is strict — any relaxation requires re-rooting.
Serializability invariant vs rich in-memory state: everything must serialize to JSON. Callable references, live connections, and cached computations break serializability — they live outside Context.

Identity claims vs capability scoping: Context carries identity claims (who you are) but capabilities live elsewhere (what you can do). The relationship is underspecified — a Context with claimed admin identity doesn't imply admin capabilities.
tradeoffs: Constraint Monotonicity buys downward safety (delegates can't exceed parent authority) at the cost of upward rigidity (no delegate-relaxation).
Serializability buys portability at the cost of excluding live resources.
Bundled structure (constraints + tools + memory + identity) buys transport convenience at the cost of per-field lifecycle coupling.
critique: Two invariants, two failure modes — good coverage. Context Contamination and Context Poisoning are real and well-named.
Context Poisoning mitigations not specified — InputGuard is a separate pattern that would compose, but the pattern itself doesn't declare the composition.
The four-part structure (Constraints, Tools, Memory, Identity) is prescribed but the field names are not enforceable — different implementations may use different keys.

Context.family_discussion: The execution-environment container. Composed with `Constraint` (the inheritance-monotonic half), `Identity`, `Tool` (capability set), working memory. Pairs with `Task` (context flows with task dispatch) and `Card` (context travels with capability advertisements).

motivation.why_it_exists: Agent contexts grow — every tool result, every message, every intermediate thought accumulates. Without active compression, agents hit context-window limits, forget early information, or spend tokens replaying old state. ContextCompress names the memory-management step that reduces the context footprint while explicitly preserving constraints and unresolved goals.
motivation.removability: Removable in short interactions where the context naturally fits. Long-running agents — multi-turn conversations, extended sessions, research tasks — depend on it. Without compression, long sessions degrade to 'remember only the last N turns,' which breaks continuity.

usage.intended: semantic compression for long-running contexts preserving constraints and unresolved goals.
usage.broad_contexts: LLM context-window management, human meeting-notes distillation, knowledge-base summarization, conversational memory compression.
usage.every_context_needs: token/memory footprint reduction, active-constraints preservation, unresolved-goals preservation.
usage.varies: compression ratio, what's preserved beyond constraints+goals (preferences, open threads), recall-support.

tensions: Compression fidelity vs token savings — the more aggressive the compression, the greater the token savings and the greater the information loss.
Active constraints (preserved) vs historical constraints (potentially discarded) — distinguishing which constraints are still active is itself judgment.
Unresolved goals (preserved) vs completed goals (discarded) — 'unresolved' is a present-tense property that needs re-evaluation on every compression pass.
tradeoffs: Gains: sustained long-running agent sessions, bounded token usage, explicit preservation of load-bearing context.
Gives up: perfect recall. ContextCompress specifically loses information; the pattern's value is that it loses the right information.
critique: Very thin — the mechanism defers to Compress for the actual reduction, adding only the 'retain active constraints and unresolved goals' criterion. That criterion is the hardest part and is under-specified.
No mechanism for detecting when compression has been too aggressive — a lost constraint reveals itself only when a later step violates it.
Compression frequency is unspecified — compressing every turn is expensive; compressing rarely loses the smooth-degradation property.

ContextCompress.family_discussion: Agent-session-management primitive built on Compress, paired with ChunkMerge (structural compression) and SummarizeContext (higher-level compression). Compare with Cache — Cache stores results for retrieval; ContextCompress transforms the working context itself. Relies on Constraint and Goal patterns for the preservation criteria.

motivation.why_it_exists: Agents with stale state act on phantom facts — they imagine what must be true instead of looking. ContextFirst names the mandatory read-before-write discipline: before generating tokens or acting, refresh the shared state. Without it, hallucinated-state bugs are constant, especially in long-running multi-agent settings where other agents have changed the world since last read.
motivation.removability: Removable in single-agent short-session contexts where nothing else changes the state. Essential in any multi-agent or long-running deployment — the pattern's 'action timestamp > context refresh timestamp' invariant is the one defense against context-blindness in distributed agent systems.

usage.intended: operational invariant — MUST read before writing.
usage.broad_contexts: agent orient phase, CRUD ordering, informed consent (load context before decide), diagnostic workflows.
usage.every_context_needs: pre-action read operation, blind-action prohibition, Warmup or read-cycle before write.
usage.varies: read scope, freshness requirement, cache-hit shortcut.
notes: §3.20 wires callers to ContextFirst — broad-use test confirms.

tensions: Read-before-write (safety) vs latency — every action pays a refresh tax, which compounds in hot loops.
Freshness threshold — 'recent enough' is fuzzy; too strict and agents refresh constantly, too lax and stale data slips through.
Cost of Warmup vs benefit — initial graph skeleton + search is expensive for cold start; the pattern recommends it anyway, which is correct and sometimes painful.
tradeoffs: Gains: freshness guarantees, defense against hallucinated state, explicit operational invariant that reviewers can check.
Gives up: action latency and sometimes autonomy (agents that want to act confidently from memory are structurally prevented).
critique: The timestamp invariant (action > refresh) is elegant and easy to violate — caching layers, memoized results, and 'just this once' shortcuts routinely skip the refresh.
The pattern says 'execute a Read operation' but doesn't specify how thorough — a partial read can satisfy the invariant while missing the state that matters.
Hallucinated State is the named failure mode, and ContextFirst is the primary defense; the pattern doesn't specify what to do when the context fetched is itself inconsistent.

ContextFirst.family_discussion: Core operational invariant paired with ConstraintFirst ('define the container first'), Warmup (the initial context load), and ContextPropagation. Compare with the graph_skeleton tool in sema's MCP server — it's the literal implementation of ContextFirst for the sema vocabulary. Foundational for any agent loop that hopes to stay grounded.

motivation.why_this_layer: explicit mode toggle between interacting agents
motivation.why_it_exists: Agents need to change the interpretation rules mid-conversation — entering debug mode, switching to formal proof mode, handing off to an expert. ContextSwitch names the stack-based protocol: signal the change, push the new rules, revert to pop. Without it, mode changes are ambient ('from now on, treat me as X') and leak across conversations unpredictably.
motivation.removability: Removable by using multiple sessions or explicit ruleset passing. The value of the pattern is the stack semantics — nested switches compose cleanly because Revert pops the topmost. Without the stack, managing multiple mode changes becomes manual and error-prone.

usage.intended: explicit mode toggling via Switch signal — subsequent messages interpreted under new ruleset.
usage.broad_contexts: multi-modal API mode switches, communication-style switching (formal vs casual), trading-system regime switches, military rules-of-engagement changes, game-mode changes.
usage.every_context_needs: explicit Switch signal, new ruleset, Revert signal support, all-subsequent-messages-reinterpreted semantic.
usage.varies: ruleset scope, nested switches, revert protocol, audit trail.

tensions: Stack depth vs comprehension — nested context switches compose structurally but tax the reader's mental model.
Revert semantics — the pattern pops on Revert, which is clean for LIFO but awkward when you want to skip back multiple levels.
Explicit signal vs implicit context — requiring an explicit ContextSwitch prevents silent drift but adds ceremony to simple mode changes.
tradeoffs: Gains: composable mode changes, unambiguous reversion, explicit scope for rule changes.
Gives up: lightweight mode hints. 'From now on, be more formal' is easier than 'ContextSwitch: formal mode,' but more ambiguous.
critique: Stack semantics are fine for nested switches and awkward for cross-cutting mode changes (orthogonal modes — formal + detailed + adversarial — don't compose by stacking).
No timeout or bounded-duration semantics — a Context pushed without Revert persists until explicit pop, which in long sessions can be forgotten.
The pattern doesn't specify what happens when Revert is called without a matching Push (underflow); this is a common mistake in manual implementations.

ContextSwitch.family_discussion: Protocol pattern paired with ContextCompress (size management), ContextFirst (refresh discipline), and Context as the underlying object. Compare with Handoff — ContextSwitch changes interpretation rules; Handoff transfers responsibility. Both are mode-changing, at different axes.

motivation.why_it_exists: Plans fail under conditions the planner anticipated at authoring time — the question is whether the response was anticipated too. ContingencyPlan names the pre-computed backup: for each critical assumption, a trigger condition and a pre-made response. When the trigger fires, execution skips deliberation (which is slow and unreliable under stress) and runs the pre-made response.
motivation.removability: Removable at the cost of ad-hoc improvisation when plans fail. For adversarial, high-stakes, or time-sensitive failures, ContingencyPlan is essential — the few seconds you buy by not deliberating under stress are the difference between graceful degradation and cascading failure.

usage.intended: pre-computed If-Then responses to critical failure — avoid deliberation under stress.
usage.broad_contexts: disaster-response plans, military contingencies, financial-market tail-risk plans, IT disaster recovery, personal-crisis plans, project contingency budgets.
usage.every_context_needs: critical assumption identification, trigger condition, pre-computed response, store-before-need semantic.
usage.varies: response depth, trigger-condition specificity, update cadence, rehearsal frequency.

tensions: Planning effort vs likelihood of use — most contingencies never fire; the effort put into planning them is speculative investment.
Specific triggers (actionable) vs generic triggers (reusable) — specific triggers match one failure mode but miss neighbors; generic triggers fire on too many things and become noise.
Disjoint trigger invariant vs overlapping realities — real failures often trigger multiple contingencies; the pattern's disjoint-ness invariant is a clean-room assumption that breaks under real load.
tradeoffs: Gains: fast response under stress, reserved resources, explicit 'what if' planning that surfaces assumptions before deployment.
Gives up: planning time, plan-book maintenance (contingencies rot when the main plan evolves), and sometimes the flexibility to improvise (pre-made responses can be wrong).
critique: 'Maginot Line' failure mode is the dominant one — you plan for the disaster you imagined, and the real disaster is different. No built-in defense against imagination failure.
Resource reservation is an invariant but often unfunded — contingency reserves get reallocated during normal operation and aren't there when needed.
The disjoint-trigger invariant is too strong — overlapping triggers are normal; the pattern forbids them rather than specifying priority.

ContingencyPlan.family_discussion: Planning family, paired with Plan (the main), PreMortem (the trigger-discovery move), and Recover. Compare with Compensate — ContingencyPlan is pre-planned response to anticipated failure; Compensate is generic rollback after unanticipated failure. Both handle failure, at different planning points.

motivation.why_it_exists: Discrete auctions (one-shot, bid-and-done) don't fit resources that need ongoing pricing — compute time, bandwidth, state slots — where holding past a use should cost. ContinuousResourceAuction names the pattern of continuous-pricing, holding-cost-bearing allocation. Without it, rivalrous resources get hoarded (no holding pressure) or dropped at auction boundaries (discrete pricing artifacts).
motivation.removability: Removable in systems with abundant resources or static allocation. Essential for scarce, ongoing resources (compute cycles, attention, connection slots). The holding-cost invariant is the pattern's core discipline; without it, the auction collapses to discrete-timed variants.

usage.intended: algorithmic continuous pricing for rivalrous resources.
usage.broad_contexts: compute-resource markets, EIP-1559 gas pricing, Dutch auctions, ad auctions, spectrum auctions, API-credit markets.
usage.every_context_needs: resource supply, pricing function, continuous-bid acceptance, allocation mechanism.
usage.varies: pricing model (congestion, Dutch, linear decay), granularity, fairness constraints, price-discovery latency.

tensions: Circulation pressure (holding cost) vs planning stability — forcing non-zero holding cost prevents hoarding and makes long-term resource commitment expensive, which discourages planning.
Price discovery (continuous) vs volatility — aggressive pricing curves make prices responsive and unpredictable; moderate curves are stable and slow to reflect demand.
Monopoly lockout — wealthy agents can sustain hoarding if holding cost is low relative to their capital; the pattern names this without resolving it.
tradeoffs: Gains: continuous resource pricing, explicit circulation pressure, principled holding cost for ongoing resources.
Gives up: planning horizon. Continuous pricing is fair but hard to budget against; agents can't commit to long-term resource use without accepting price uncertainty.
critique: Price Instability as a failure mode is intrinsic to continuous pricing — the pattern names it without fully mitigating; damping the curve reduces price discovery.
Monopoly Lockout is avoided by making holding cost high enough to deter infinite hold, but 'high enough' scales with wealth, which is exogenous.
T_cycle for clearance is a parameter with no default or derivation rule; tuning is caller-dependent.

ContinuousResourceAuction.family_discussion: Market-mechanism sibling of AttentionMarkets (priced bandwidth), AuctionMechanism (discrete auction), and ComputeMarket (compute-specific). Uses StateLock to serialize bids. Compare with Token/BearerToken — ContinuousResourceAuction prices the resource; Tokens authorize usage. Both are capability-management, at different abstraction levels.

motivation.why_this_layer: immutable record artifact (the artifact is Infra; agreement semantic is Society)
motivation.why_it_exists: Multi-party commitment device — all named parties sign, terms are immutable after signing. Different from Constitution (group-level rules) and from AcceptSpec (solver-boundary contract): Contract is the specific bilateral-or-multilateral binding agreement.
motivation.removability: No. Every pattern that involves named-parties-agree-to-terms invokes Contract semantics. Collapsing into AcceptSpec loses the multi-party signing aspect.

usage.intended: immutable record of binding agreement between identities.
usage.broad_contexts: legal contracts, smart contracts, SLAs, API service agreements, employment contracts, insurance policies, escrow terms, bilateral MoUs.
usage.every_context_needs: identities of parties, conditions/obligations (terms), signatures from all parties, immutability.
usage.varies: signature algorithm, dispute-resolution clause, termination semantics, amendment mechanism, jurisdictional binding.

tensions: Consent invariant (all parties sign) vs partial-consent scenarios: some real contracts become valid when a quorum signs rather than all. The pattern is strict — all or nothing.
Immutability vs amendment: terms cannot change. Amendment requires a new Contract — clean but costly.

Ambiguity failure mode vs machine-verifiability: the pattern names ambiguity as a failure but doesn't require machine-verifiable terms (that's Constitution's requirement). Contracts can be machine- or human-interpretable.
tradeoffs: All-party consent buys integrity at the cost of requiring explicit assent (no 'assumed agreement').
Term immutability buys tamper-resistance at the cost of forbidding in-flight revision.
Ambiguity tolerance (unlike Constitution) buys expressive power at the cost of ambiguity risk.
critique: Two invariants, two failure modes. Missing: Expiration (Contracts may have a validity window; pattern is silent), Breach Detection (terms violated — who notices, how?), Enforcement Binding (contract → enforcement mechanism is implicit).
Multi-party with no ordered-signing: the spec requires all sign, but doesn't say if order matters. In some contexts, one party signs before another (offer/acceptance); the pattern flattens this.
'Binding foundation for economic/cooperative interactions' is the intent but the pattern doesn't specify what happens on breach — enforcement lives elsewhere.

Contract.family_discussion: The multi-party commitment artifact in Infrastructure. Composed with `Identity` (signers), `Condition` (terms), `Sign` (the signing op), `CommitmentDevice`. Used by `LatticeCommit`, governance, and economic-exchange patterns.

motivation.why_it_exists: Per-action minimum-interval enforcement — some actions must not repeat faster than a fixed rate regardless of load or retry logic (account-lockout cooldowns, re-auth gates, safety interlocks). Different from Backoff (which spaces retries exponentially) and Throttle (which caps a rate across a window): Cooldown enforces a hard minimum gap between individual invocations of one action.
motivation.removability: No. Cooldown and Throttle are genuinely distinct: Throttle bounds rate across many events in a window; Cooldown bounds the gap between consecutive events of one action. Collapsing them would lose the per-action-gap semantics that safety interlocks rely on.

usage.intended: mandatory delay between repeated actions.
usage.broad_contexts: API rate limits, UI button debouncing, game ability cooldowns, retry-after headers, service-request throttling, anti-spam measures, circuit breakers.
usage.every_context_needs: action identity, minimum interval duration, timer start event.
usage.varies: per-action-type independent vs shared, queue-on-violation vs reject, global vs user-scoped, adaptive.

tensions: Per-action vs global: Cooldown is per-action, so a system with 1000 action types maintains 1000 timers. Scalability of this state is a deployment concern the pattern does not address.

Blocked-vs-queued during cooldown: the mechanism says attempts are rejected or queued — but that is a significant policy choice. A rejected-by-default Cooldown differs operationally from a queued-by-default Cooldown.

Monotonic timer vs clock drift: the Monotonic invariant is trivial locally but harder distributed; clock-skew between Cooldown enforcers creates windows where the effective cooldown is shorter or longer than intended.
tradeoffs: Hard minimum gap buys safety (no rapid-fire actions) at the cost of liveness (legitimate urgent repeat is blocked).
Per-action timers buy granularity at the cost of state overhead.
Timer-starts-on-completion (vs starts-on-invocation) buys correctness for long-running actions at the cost of making the effective rate depend on action duration.
critique: Only one failure mode (Deadlock on critical action during cooldown). Missing: Timer Drift, Undefined Behavior Between Instances (which timer wins for multiple Cooldown enforcers on the same action), Queued-Queue Overflow (queued attempts accumulate unboundedly).
'Attempts during cooldown rejected or queued' is an OR — the pattern should pick one or parameterize, rather than leave it ambiguous.

The relationship to Throttle is stated in prose ('acts as the enforcement mechanism for throttle policies') but the patterns are separate. Deciding when to use which requires understanding both — the library could benefit from a distinguishing chart.

Cooldown.family_discussion: Sibling to `Backoff` (exponential growth between retries) and `Throttle` (rate cap). Where Backoff is 'wait longer after each failure' and Throttle is 'N per window,' Cooldown is 'gap ≥ D between individual invocations.' Uses monotonic time; composes with action-level safety gates.

motivation.why_it_exists: Co-movement is everywhere; causation is rare. Correlation names the weaker claim explicitly, with the coefficient in [-1, 1], so analysts don't accidentally promote it to causation. The single most common reasoning bug in data-driven claims is conflating these two; having distinct named patterns makes the conflation detectable.
motivation.removability: Non-removable for any principled data analysis. The distinction from Causation is the whole epistemic load — patterns that would otherwise conflate the two now have a clean way to refer to each. Removing Correlation collapses reasoning about co-movement into causation talk, which is the failure mode.

usage.intended: shared movement between variables, without implying cause.
usage.broad_contexts: statistical correlation, market co-movements, feature correlation in ML, symptom co-occurrence, meme spread patterns.
usage.every_context_needs: two variables, co-movement measure, explicit non-causal semantic.
usage.varies: correlation method (Pearson, Spearman, etc.), lag, directionality, confidence intervals.
notes: §3.18 flagged Correlation's mechanism as gloss-restatement. The broad-use sketch gives a concrete rewrite target: distinguish from Causation by structure (two variables, no directed edge), not by naming the fallacy.

tensions: Symmetric (undirected) vs directed — Correlation is symmetric by design, Causation is directed; the temptation to upgrade correlation to causation based on narrative plausibility is constant.
Coefficient in [-1, 1] (linear) vs nonlinear relationships — Pearson correlation misses nonlinear dependencies that are structurally present but orthogonal in the linear sense.
Correlation as evidence (for hypothesis testing) vs as proof (it isn't) — correlation is a signal worth investigating; it is not a conclusion.
tradeoffs: Gains: honest naming of the weaker claim, coefficient-based quantification, resistance to accidental causal upgrading.
Gives up: the false comfort of 'we see it moving together so we know how to intervene' — Correlation explicitly refuses this, which is honest and sometimes frustrating.
critique: Limited to linear co-movement via the coefficient — real dependencies are often nonlinear and Correlation has no expression for them.
Doesn't distinguish spurious correlation (confounded) from genuine co-movement without causation; the pattern is structurally unable to identify confounders.
Leaves the inference to the caller — 'correlation isn't causation' is cited everywhere and violated routinely, and the pattern has no structural defense against the upgrading.

Correlation.family_discussion: Paired with Causation as the foundational statistics distinction. Compare with Covariance (close cousin, different normalization), MutualInformation (nonlinear analogue), and Correlation-vs-Causation patterns explicitly guarding against the upgrade. Used by BayesUpdate (correlation as weak evidence), Investigation (correlation as starting lead), and Explanation (correlation as data to explain).

motivation.why_this_layer: pre-observation expectation freeze in group context
motivation.why_it_exists: Hindsight bias rewrites history — after observing the outcome, we 'knew it all along.' CounterfactualAnchor names the prediction-freezing move: commit an immutable anchor before observation, then measure the delta. The learning signal is genuine surprise, not a story fit to the data. Without it, agents silently revise their priors to match observations, destroying the calibration signal.
motivation.removability: Removable in contexts where calibration isn't tracked. Any serious learning or forecasting setup needs something like this — the delta between prediction and observation is the update signal, and without the immutable anchor there's no delta to measure.

usage.intended: freeze expectation BEFORE observation to measure true surprise.
usage.future: any "pre-commit prediction to prevent hindsight bias" mechanism.
usage.broad_contexts: prediction markets, forecasting discipline, A/B test hypothesis pre-registration, scientific pre-registration (OSF), experimental-design anchors.
usage.every_context_needs: pre-observation anchor, observation, delta-as-learning-signal, hindsight-bias prevention.
usage.varies: granularity (Duration per §3.17), retention policy (enum), anchor-update rules (immutable vs replaceable).

tensions: Anchor immutability (invariant) vs new information — if you learn something mid-observation that legitimately should update the prediction, the pattern forbids it.
Vague anchor vs specific anchor — the named failure mode 'vague anchor' means predictions like 'something will happen' pass the invariant while providing no falsification target.
Hindsight leakage — agents unconsciously adjust the anchor as data comes in; the invariant forbids explicit modification but can't prevent implicit reinterpretation.
tradeoffs: Gains: calibratable learning signal, hindsight-bias resistance, explicit commitment-before-observation.
Gives up: mid-observation learning. The immutability means you commit early and bear the cost of wrong commitments, which is precisely the point.
critique: Hindsight Leakage is the most important failure and the pattern has no structural defense — memory updates are opaque, and the anchor can be rationalized without being modified.
Vague Anchor failure mode is addressed by nothing in the invariants — 'anchor must be specific enough to be falsified' would help but isn't there.

Anchor Abandonment (ignoring large deltas as too uncomfortable) is a psychological failure the pattern names but can't prevent. Failure modes were previously jammed into one list entry (Hindsight Leakage + Vague Anchor + Anchor Abandonment run together); now split into three distinct entries.

CounterfactualAnchor.family_discussion: Calibration primitive paired with ConfidenceCalibrate (the aggregate update loop), BayesUpdate (the probabilistic substrate), and Prediction as the input. Compare with CommitmentDevice — CounterfactualAnchor is commitment of a prediction; CommitmentDevice is commitment of an action plan. Both use immutability to resist later revision.

motivation.why_it_exists: Most cognitive patterns are convergent — narrow toward a solution, satisfy constraints. Creative names the opposite mode: divergent thinking, remote association, pattern breaking. Without a named slot for this, agents default to the convergent mode that training reinforces, and genuinely novel solutions become structurally hard to produce.
motivation.removability: Removable if novelty isn't valued. The pattern earns its weight when the task requires generating genuinely new ideas rather than optimally combining existing ones. Naming it reserves the mode; without the name, callers don't distinguish 'be creative' from 'solve harder.'

usage.intended: cognitive mode focused on generating novel and valuable ideas.
usage.broad_contexts: Creative(Brainstorming), Creative(Design), Creative(Writing), as a modifier applied to other patterns.
usage.every_context_needs: marker semantic — descendants apply the "creative" tag.
usage.varies: contextual meaning of "creative" within domain.
usage.extensions: N/A — trait conversion means this is not a standalone pattern with descendants, but a tag other patterns carry.
notes: §3.18 converts Creative to `is_trait: true`. Broad-use confirms — the standalone pattern (without a concrete descendant) is too abstract; a Trait that concrete patterns carry is the right treatment.

tensions: Divergence vs evaluation — the creative mode specifically suspends judgment to generate; the paradox is that the output still has to be useful, which requires convergent evaluation later.
Remote association vs coherence — the further the associations, the more original the output and the less reliable the connection.
Pattern breaking vs reliability — breaking established patterns produces novelty and produces nonsense; the mode has no built-in filter for distinguishing them.
tradeoffs: Gains: a named slot for divergent thinking, explicit permission to suspend convergent pressure, a mode that complements the many convergent patterns.
Gives up: efficiency and reliability. Creative outputs are hit-or-miss by construction; 90% is noise, and the filter for the 10% lives outside the pattern.
critique: Almost entirely a stub — 'divergent thinking, remote associations, breaking patterns' is gestured at without operationalization.
No invariants, no failure modes — the pattern doesn't say what counts as creative vs just random, which is exactly the hardest question.
Conflates novelty (new) with value (useful); real creativity produces both, and the pattern doesn't say how.

Creative.family_discussion: Mode-pattern paired with Systematic (its convergent counterpart), ConceptBlend (a specific creative move), AnalogyBridge (another), and CreativeBlend. Compare with Abduction — Abduction produces hypotheses under constraints; Creative suspends constraints to explore. Both are generative, on different axes.

motivation.why_it_exists: Pure generation produces coherent-but-mundane output; ad-hoc novelty produces noise. CreativeBlend names the disciplined move: identify orthogonal concepts in context, fuse via ConceptBlend, add noise to escape local optima, then filter through a dual-check. Without the named pattern, 'be creative' reduces to 'generate, hope it's good.'
motivation.removability: Removable if novelty isn't valued. CreativeBlend earns its weight for tasks that require genuinely new combinations — ideation, design, problem reframing. Simpler generation patterns suffice for routine production where novelty would actually be harmful.

usage.intended: full creative pipeline — ConceptBlend + NoiseInjection with novelty/value gates.
usage.future: any ideation pipeline with quality gating.
usage.broad_contexts: structured-brainstorming with immediate filtering, product-idea generation pipelines, research-question generation with triage, art-ideation with critic loops.
usage.every_context_needs: ConceptBlend base, NoiseInjection for local-optima escape, dual-Check on Novelty + Value.
usage.varies: blend depth, noise temperature, gate strictness, iteration bound.

tensions: Divergence invariant (output unlike input) vs utility (must retain coherence) — the two invariants push in opposite directions; tension is the pattern.
Orthogonal concepts vs available concepts — the pattern demands orthogonal sources to fuse; real context often has only loosely-orthogonal material.
Noise injection vs structure preservation — too much noise destroys utility; too little prevents escape from local optima.
tradeoffs: Gains: structured novelty-production, explicit divergence and utility invariants, noise-injection that escapes local optima.
Gives up: determinism and reliability. CreativeBlend outputs are by design unpredictable; the dual-check filters some failures and can't catch all.
critique: Divergence threshold is unspecified — 'output similarity < threshold' defers the judgment to the caller, and getting it wrong produces either cosmetic variations or incoherent noise.
Orthogonal-concepts detection is itself a hard problem the pattern relies on — finding the orthogonal concepts in context is most of the work, and the pattern hand-waves it.
The dual-check is a downstream pattern; CreativeBlend without the dual-check is vulnerable to the coherent-but-wrong failure mode.

CreativeBlend.family_discussion: Generative-strategy pattern paired with ConceptBlend (the fusion primitive), NoiseInjection (the escape mechanism), and Creative (the umbrella mode). Compare with AnalogyBridge — AnalogyBridge maps one domain onto another; CreativeBlend fuses them. Different creative operations.

motivation.why_it_exists: Evaluation without explicit standards is vibes-based judgment. Criteria names the specific, referenceable standards used to judge success — 'under $50,' 'runs in under 100ms,' 'passes all tests.' Without the primitive, 'is this good?' has no cited answer, and every evaluation can disagree with every other.
motivation.removability: Non-removable. Every evaluation pattern (Judge, Critique, AcceptSpec, Validate) consumes Criteria or something isomorphic. Removing it forces every evaluator to carry its standards implicitly, which makes comparison across evaluations impossible.

usage.intended: specific standards used to judge success of an artifact.
usage.broad_contexts: acceptance criteria, rubric criteria, regulatory criteria, quality criteria, fitness criteria, performance criteria.
usage.every_context_needs: specific standards, target being judged, pass/fail or quantification rule.
usage.varies: criteria count, weighting, compensation rules (can one exceed offset another's failure), source (stakeholder vs derived).

tensions: Specific (measurable) vs rich (capture what matters) — the simplest criteria are measurable and shallow; the richest criteria are qualitative and hard to check.
Static vs evolving — criteria set at plan-time may not match what you discover matters during execution; evolving criteria mid-evaluation breaks reproducibility.
Independence vs coherence — criteria are often specified as a list (each independent) but really form a coherent shape (must be cheap AND fast, trade-offs allowed).
tradeoffs: Gains: citable standards for evaluation, shared vocabulary for 'what makes this good,' a substrate for Judge and Critique.
Gives up: subtlety. Explicit Criteria flatten the judgment; sometimes the unstated bar ('elegance,' 'fit,' 'taste') is doing the real work, and the pattern makes it illegitimate.
critique: Very thin mechanism — almost just a typed list. The interesting work (picking good criteria, resolving conflicts between them) lives outside the pattern.
No semantics for criteria compatibility — multiple criteria may be jointly unsatisfiable, and the pattern has no way to detect or express this.
Typically used as a bag of bullet points rather than a structured specification; the pattern doesn't resist this degradation.

Criteria.family_discussion: Substrate for Judge (scores against), Critique (produces feedback against), AcceptSpec (bounds against). Compare with Condition — Criteria are evaluation standards; Conditions are control-flow predicates. Both are 'things that evaluate,' at different operational points.

motivation.why_this_layer: generating qualitative strengths/weaknesses requires semantic understanding — cognitive
motivation.why_it_exists: Evaluation as a scalar score (Judge) loses the structure of what's good or bad. Critique names the descriptive variant: analyze against specific criteria, produce actionable assessment rather than a number. Without it, feedback collapses to 'this is 7/10' with no path to improvement, which is useless for refinement.
motivation.removability: Removable if you only need scores, but the refinement family (Reflexion, Refine, Iterate) depends on descriptive feedback. Critique is the feedback-structured output that makes improvement cycles possible; removing it collapses refinement to 'try again and hope.'

usage.intended: qualitative feedback generation — structured assessment produced from criteria.
usage.broad_contexts: peer review, design critique, code review, essay critique, art critique, policy analysis, clinical feedback.
usage.every_context_needs: target artifact, criteria, structured output (strengths, weaknesses, recommendations).
usage.varies: structure format, criteria source, depth, actionability requirement.

tensions: Descriptive (rich) vs scalar (comparable) — Critique is intentionally the first, which means its outputs don't easily compose into rankings.
Specific criteria (invariant: must reference criteria) vs emergent concerns — the pattern insists on criteria, which misses 'this is vaguely off but I can't say why.'
Actionable advice vs descriptive truth — sometimes the honest critique has no action (the artifact is fundamentally wrong concept); the pattern's shape pressures the critic to manufacture advice.
tradeoffs: Gains: structured feedback that feeds refinement loops, criteria-grounded critique, descriptive richness beyond a score.
Gives up: comparability (Critiques of two artifacts aren't easily ranked) and sometimes honesty (the bias toward actionable advice edits out 'this is fundamentally wrong').
critique: 'Nitpicking' is the most common failure mode — focusing on trivial details while missing structural flaws. The pattern can't force attention to the right level.
'Vague Praise' is the second-most-common — Critique that satisfies the invariants vacuously by naming criteria and giving no substance.
'Projection' (critiquing the artifact for not being what the critic would have built) is endemic; the pattern notes it without mitigating.

Critique.family_discussion: Produces Assessment, consumed by Reflexion and Refine. Sibling of Judge (scalar), Review (structured), and Evaluate (generic). Compare with AdversarialProof — Critique assesses quality; AdversarialProof searches for prohibited content. Both are structured-output verification.

motivation.why_this_layer: explicit formalization of implicit resonance — cognitive phase
motivation.why_it_exists: Soft patterns — implicit resonance, informal coordination, habits — can solidify into explicit obligations. Crystallize names the phase transition: agent A proposes crystallization based on history, agent B validates, consensus codifies the implicit into hard rules. Without it, the path from 'this just happens' to 'this is a rule' is ad-hoc and contested.
motivation.removability: Removable in single-agent contexts where nothing is shared. In multi-agent coordination, the soft-to-hard transition is real and needs a named primitive. Without it, norm formation is either silent (nobody agrees when it happened) or bureaucratic (formal legislation for every habit).

usage.intended: phase transition from implicit resonance to explicit contract.
usage.future: any "informal → formal" conversion when conditions are ripe.
usage.broad_contexts: norm-to-law transitions, team convention-to-policy, tacit knowledge → explicit documentation, prototype → production, case law formation, constitutional moments.
usage.every_context_needs: implicit behavior observation, consensus validation, codification mechanism, entropy-threshold check (don't crystallize prematurely).
usage.varies: resonance period (Duration, see §3.17), consensus requirement, reversibility post-crystallization.

tensions: Atomic transition (one transaction) vs gradual norm formation — the pattern forces discrete commit, but most norms form gradually; forcing atomicity loses the process.
Entropy threshold — below it, crystallize; above it, don't. The threshold is a judgment and the failure mode (premature crystallization) is exactly what happens when the threshold is wrong.
Illusory resonance — two agents thinking they agree when they don't; crystallization surfaces this disagreement, which is useful and painful.
tradeoffs: Gains: explicit path from informal norm to formal rule, consensus-requiring commit (both agents must sign), entropy-aware locking.
Gives up: reversibility (Crystallize produces Constitution-grade obligations that are hard to unwind) and sometimes honesty (the pressure to crystallize can force premature agreement).
critique: Illusory resonance is the most dangerous failure mode — agents perceive the same soft signal differently, crystallize, then discover the perception mismatch. The pattern surfaces this by failing, which is the honest move, but too late to avoid the process cost.
Entropy threshold is unspecified — what counts as "entropy" of a coordination context is itself a judgment.

Gloss fixed: previously rendered as literal "{{phase_transition}}" due to un-interpolated template token; now plain text. Orphan phase_transition dependency (declared but no longer used in any field after the gloss fix) was removed.

Crystallize.family_discussion: Norm-formation primitive paired with Resonate (the soft signal substrate), Constitution (the hard-rule output), and Consensus (the validation step). Compare with PhaseTransition — Crystallize is the social/epistemic phase transition (norms formalizing); PhaseTransition is the general physics-inspired primitive.

motivation.why_it_exists: Agents forget successful behaviors over time, especially if new training data drifts the distribution. CurriculumReplay names the self-reinforcement pattern: store high-scoring past outputs, replay them during idle cycles ranked by complexity. Without it, agents lose hard-won competence without any signal they've lost it.
motivation.removability: Removable — most agent systems don't do post-training self-reinforcement. The pattern is specifically for long-running agents with training loops who risk drift; in simpler setups it's overkill. Its value depends on whether drift is a real concern in your deployment.

usage.intended: self-supervised reinforcement — re-train on own high-scoring past outputs.
usage.broad_contexts: LLM self-distillation, RL experience-replay buffers, meditation on past successes, athletic replay training, habit reinforcement.
usage.every_context_needs: replay buffer of successful interactions, quality-ranking, sampling mechanism, fine-tune-during-idle semantic.
usage.varies: buffer size, ranking method, decay of old successes, update strategy.

tensions: Self-distillation (closed loop) vs external signal — training on your own outputs is the recipe for model collapse (the named failure mode); the pattern says to mitigate via complexity ordering and no-catastrophic-forgetting, which is a hope.
Easy-to-hard ordering vs realistic distribution — curriculum ordering is good for learning and bad for matching the distribution the agent faces in production.
Replay buffer size vs freshness — large buffers preserve diversity and lose recency; small buffers are fresh and prone to over-fitting.
tradeoffs: Gains: reinforcement of successful behaviors without external supervision, curriculum-ordered replay, a story for continuous learning.
Gives up: exposure to novel situations. Replay emphasizes what worked; agents that only replay risk never learning what should work in new conditions.
critique: Model collapse is the dominant failure mode and the pattern has no structural defense — self-distillation is known to degenerate without external signal, and the pattern essentially is self-distillation.
'Examples ordered by complexity' is a curriculum-learning idea; determining complexity rank is itself a non-trivial task the pattern doesn't specify.
'No catastrophic forgetting' is an invariant with no enforcement mechanism — preventing forgetting is a whole research area.

CurriculumReplay.family_discussion: Self-training primitive paired with Reflexion (deliberate feedback-driven revision), SelfDistillation (the broader technique), and PathwayMemory (reasoning trace memoization). Compare with ExperienceReplay (the RL cousin) — CurriculumReplay adds complexity ordering to the basic replay idea.

motivation.why_it_exists: Not every process is a DAG. Iterative refinement, self-correction, feedback control all require a topology that allows a process to revisit earlier states. Cyclic names the class of topologies that permit loops, with the crucial invariant that a termination condition must exist — otherwise 'iterative' becomes 'infinite.'
motivation.removability: Removable if your problem is fundamentally DAG-shaped. Many aren't — optimization, ML training, feedback control, interactive refinement all need cycles. The pattern is the named topology class for these, distinct from DAG which structurally forbids them.

usage.intended: topology permitting feedback loops.
usage.future: any topology with legitimate backward edges.
usage.broad_contexts: feedback-loop systems, iterative refinement, state machines with cycles, recursive optimization, control loops.
usage.every_context_needs: edge structure permitting backward references, loop-termination mechanism (explicit or implicit).
usage.varies: cycle count bounds, termination criteria, cycle detection, shared-state vs isolated-iteration.

tensions: Recurrence (the whole value) vs termination (the safety invariant) — every cycle must eventually exit, but without the cycle there's no iteration.
Explicit exit state vs implicit convergence — the pattern demands a defined exit; optimizing loops often don't have a crisp exit, they just slow down.
Cyclic topology vs reasoning hygiene — many reasoning patterns presume DAG structure for clarity; allowing cycles makes trace interpretation harder.
tradeoffs: Gains: support for iterative refinement, feedback loops, recursive optimization — the structural dual of DAG for non-DAG-shaped problems.
Gives up: simplicity of analysis. Cyclic graphs resist many static analyses (dependency-ordering, topological sort) that DAGs make trivial.
critique: The termination invariant is necessary and easy to violate — 'defined exit state' is a specification the caller must provide, and caller specifications frequently omit it.
Very thin — beyond 'has cycles, must terminate,' the pattern leaves structure to the caller. Real cyclic patterns (gradient descent, reflexion loops) build richer structure on top.
The pattern doesn't address cycle semantics — what does it mean to 'revisit a state'? Idempotent replay, stateful iteration, destructive re-entry are all distinct cases.

Cyclic.family_discussion: Topology-pattern counterpart to DAG. Foundational for Reflexion (iterative refinement), FeedbackLoop, and Iterate. Compare with Recurrence — Cyclic is the topology, Recurrence is the semantics; both name loop-shaped structure at different levels.

motivation.why_it_exists: When tasks can run concurrently but must respect precedence, DAG is the natural topology. Directed means dependencies flow one way; acyclic means no task waits on itself. Almost every build system, task pipeline, and dependency resolver is shaped like this — having DAG as a named pattern gives these a shared vocabulary.
motivation.removability: Non-removable as a topology class. Every dependency-resolution pattern uses DAG semantics; remove the name and the semantics still exist but without a shared handle. Given how widespread DAGs are, the value is mostly in naming.

usage.intended: directed acyclic graph topology — branching + merging, no cycles.
usage.broad_contexts: build systems, data pipelines, scheduling graphs, provenance graphs, task dependency graphs, workflow engines.
usage.every_context_needs: directed edges, acyclicity, parallel-execution potential, precedence respect.
usage.varies: node schema, edge labels, cycle-detection mechanism, stratification.

tensions: Acyclicity (structural safety) vs real dependency graphs — sometimes real workflows have cycles that need to be broken; DAG forbids them structurally.
Directed vs undirected — directedness is often the whole value; undirected dependency makes ordering ambiguous.
Single-direction edges vs bidirectional semantics — some dependencies are mutual (A needs B, B needs A at a different phase), and DAG can't express that.
tradeoffs: Gains: topological ordering, principled parallelism (independent nodes run concurrently), dependency-aware scheduling.
Gives up: cycles. DAG is specifically not the right topology when the problem has genuine feedback loops; use Cyclic instead.
critique: Very thin — the mechanism is two invariants (acyclic, directed). Everything else is inherited from graph theory.
No semantics for what nodes and edges represent — a DAG of tasks is different from a DAG of data flows, but the pattern doesn't distinguish.
The pattern names the structure without the operations (topological sort, reachability, longest path); these live in graph-theoretic patterns built on DAG.

DAG.family_discussion: Core topology primitive, paired with Cyclic (its feedback-allowing counterpart) and Graph (the general container). Foundation for Compose (which requires DAG shape), Chain (linear DAG), Pipeline (linear with side effects). Compare with Tree — Tree is DAG with single-parent constraint.

motivation.why_this_layer: passive attenuation models a physical damping property
motivation.why_it_exists: Unmoderated signal amplification produces oscillation and runaway — the control-theory failure mode. Dampen names the reduction primitive: negative feedback that reduces signal intensity in response to noise or resistance. Without it, feedback loops (Resonate, Compromise, BeliefUpdate) have no principled way to avoid oscillation.
motivation.removability: Very thin primitive; removable at the cost of callers inventing their own damping. The value is mostly in naming a primitive that many patterns reference. Compromise, Hysteresis, and backoff-style patterns all consume Dampen or isomorphic concepts.

usage.intended: passive attenuation of signal/force — negative feedback to prevent oscillation.
usage.broad_contexts: shock absorbers, electrical dampening, audio dampening, organizational politics dampening (cooling-off periods), alert suppression, over-eager response dampening.
usage.every_context_needs: signal being dampened, attenuation mechanism, resistance/noise source.
usage.varies: attenuation function, adaptive vs fixed dampening, target (signal, force, value).

tensions: Reduction vs signal preservation — dampen too much and the signal is lost; dampen too little and oscillation persists.
Negative feedback (stability) vs responsiveness — strong damping is stable and slow; light damping is responsive and potentially oscillatory.
Uniform reduction vs selective — dampen everything is simple; dampen specifically the noise is better and requires knowing which is which.
tradeoffs: Gains: a named stabilization primitive, explicit negative-feedback semantics, a shared handle for patterns that need to reduce intensity.
Gives up: nuance. The pattern's mechanism is essentially 'reduce'; the interesting question of 'reduce how, by how much, when' lives in the caller.
critique: Almost a stub — one sentence of mechanism, no invariants, no failure modes. The real work is always in the consuming pattern.
Negative feedback is the classic control-theoretic primitive; the pattern gestures at it without formalizing gain, phase, stability margin — the parameters that actually matter.
'In response to resistance or noise' conflates two different triggers — you might dampen because the system is pushing back (resistance) or because the signal is noisy; the responses differ.

Dampen.family_discussion: Foundational control primitive paired with Amplify (the inverse), Throttle (rate-limit variant), and Backoff (retry-specific damping). Used by Compromise (damp intensity), Hysteresis (damp transitions), and many resilience patterns. Compare with Entropy — both reduce, Dampen reduces magnitude, Entropy increases disorder.

motivation.why_this_layer: information hygiene between system and source
motivation.why_it_exists: Agents that ingest everything learn correlations they shouldn't and retain data they can't justify holding. DataMinimization names the information-hygiene discipline: filter before ingesting, map every retained field to a specific AcceptSpec requirement, drop sensitive data after intermediate use. Without it, privacy, compliance, and context-bloat all degrade.
motivation.removability: Removable only if you accept the consequences — privacy violations, compliance failures, correlation attacks on aggregated 'minimized' data. In agent systems that touch user or sensitive data, this pattern is non-optional; skipping it shifts the failure mode to post-hoc incident response.

usage.intended: ingest only what's strictly necessary — Principle of Least Privilege for data access.
usage.broad_contexts: GDPR data minimization, privacy-preserving ML, lean context management, medical-records minimization, zero-knowledge-where-possible.
usage.every_context_needs: pre-ingestion filtering, necessity-for-task determination, post-ingestion compression.
usage.varies: necessity definition, filter strictness, per-field vs per-document granularity.

tensions: Least privilege (invariant) vs 'just in case' retention — agents naturally want to keep everything because context is cheap to store and expensive to re-fetch; the pattern forbids this, which the named failure mode 'context hoarding' is exactly.
Per-task necessity vs reusable context — minimization is per-task-goal, which means the same agent with two tasks has to minimize twice; context sharing is structurally discouraged.
Correlation attack risk — minimized fields individually innocuous may combine to reveal PII; the pattern names this without providing a correlation-aware filter.
tradeoffs: Gains: privacy hygiene, compliance-aligned data handling, reduced context bloat, explicit necessity mapping via AcceptSpec.
Gives up: fluency. Agents can't 'just browse' the data they have; every field costs an explicit necessity argument.
critique: The Necessity invariant requires AcceptSpec-rich tasks; tasks without well-specified acceptance criteria can't support the invariant and the pattern has no fallback.
Correlation attacks are the sophisticated failure mode with no structural defense — the pattern minimizes per-field, but privacy is a combinatorial property.
Ephemeral processing (sensitive data dropped after intermediate use) depends on caller discipline — the pattern can't enforce the drop, only require it.

DataMinimization.family_discussion: Privacy/compliance primitive paired with PrincipalOfLeastAuthority (authorization analogue), BearerToken (capability-scoped access), and AuditTrail (what remains after minimization). Compare with ContextCompress — DataMinimization filters before ingesting; ContextCompress reduces after. Both manage information volume, at different operational points.

motivation.why_it_exists: Raw fact with no interpretation is qualitatively different from information (fact plus meaning). Datum names the pre-interpretive state — the thing you observed before your model colored it. Without the primitive, agents conflate observation with inference, losing the ability to say 'the datum was X, my interpretation is Y.'
motivation.removability: Very thin — a philosophical distinction between raw observation and interpreted information. Could be folded into Observation, but the 'no attached meaning' framing serves a specific purpose in epistemic patterns (BeliefTracking, Evidence, Anomaly) that want to distinguish the raw signal from its interpretation.

usage.intended: a single unit of raw unprocessed fact (singular of Data).
usage.broad_contexts: sensor readings, log lines, bytes, observations, raw measurements, tokens, events pre-interpretation.
usage.every_context_needs: existence (the unit IS something); distinctness from other data points.
usage.varies: encoding, unit type, precision, source attribution, timestamp attachment, structured vs unstructured.

tensions: No attached meaning vs theory-ladenness of observation — philosophy of science tells us all observation is theory-laden; Datum as 'pure fact' is an idealization.
Singular of Data — the word wants to be the atomic unit, but real 'atomic' observations are often already aggregates (an 'event' is often many subevents).
Existence vs interpretation — declaring a Datum is itself an interpretive act (you chose this was the fact to record), which the pattern's 'no meaning' framing hides.
tradeoffs: Gains: explicit separation of raw observation from interpretation, a substrate for pipeline stages that transform raw into interpreted.
Gives up: philosophical honesty — the pure-fact framing is aspirational; every real datum has interpretive commitments baked in.
critique: Almost a stub — the mechanism is half a sentence. The pattern's value is in its role in the type hierarchy, not in any operational structure.
'No attached meaning, just existence' is philosophically fraught; observation without context is rarer than the pattern suggests.
The Data/Datum distinction is grammatically correct and pedagogically useful; operationally, most systems use them interchangeably.

Datum.family_discussion: Foundational data primitive paired with Information (Datum plus meaning), Evidence (Datum supporting a claim), and Anomaly (Datum deviating from baseline). Compare with Observation — the two are nearly synonymous; Datum is the noun, Observation is the event.

motivation.why_this_layer: attenuation of untended value is a physical-law analogue
motivation.why_it_exists: Time-based attenuation as a physical-law analogue — without reinforcement, values fade. Essential for attention, relevance scoring, stale-data handling, and any time-sensitive signal. Makes the attenuation relationship (half-life, reinforcement, zero threshold) a shared concept so patterns that depend on it (attention budgets, memory decay, signal aging) reuse the same structure.
motivation.removability: Probably not. Many downstream patterns invoke decay semantics; without a pinned mechanism each redefines it locally. Structured-thinking criterion applies.

usage.intended: gradual value attenuation over time without reinforcement.
usage.broad_contexts: memory decay, cache TTL, pheromone decay in stigmergy, radioactive decay, attention decay, reputation decay, content freshness scoring.
usage.every_context_needs: current value, decay rate, time passage, reinforcement mechanism, zero-threshold action.
usage.varies: decay function (exponential, linear, custom), reinforcement magnitude, reset semantics, zero-threshold action.

tensions: Continuous vs discrete decay: exponential vs half-life-step vs threshold. The mechanism mentions half-life but allows different rates — descendants specialize.

Non-negativity vs zero-crossing behavior: the invariant forbids negative values but says 'zero threshold triggers state change or removal.' The boundary between 'near zero' and 'zero' is fuzzy for floating-point implementations.
Independent decay vs context-modulated: decay rate may depend on context (urgent items decay slower). The mechanism doesn't forbid this but doesn't name it either.
tradeoffs: Reinforcement-resetable buys simple operational model at the cost of excluding patterns where reinforcement only slows decay rather than resetting.
Half-life framing buys familiarity (physics intuition) at the cost of pinning to exponential decay — linear or other curves need descendants.
Zero threshold triggers state change buys discrete semantics at the cost of a non-smooth transition at the boundary.
critique: Premature Expiry is the named failure — half-life miscalibration is endemic.
The pattern has only one invariant ({{value}} never negative); richer invariants about monotonicity, reinforcement semantics, and threshold behavior would help.
Gloss fixed: previously rendered literal '{{state}}' token; now plain text 'Automatic expiration of stale state'.

Decay.family_discussion: Substrate pattern for time-attenuation. Paired with `Dampen` (magnitude attenuation independent of time) and `Hysteresis` (threshold-crossing with gap). Invoked by attention-allocation, memory, aging-based relevance patterns across the library.

motivation.why_it_exists: A first-class artifact for 'a committed choice, with its consequences acknowledged.' Without a named Decision type, every Gate-like pattern returns an ad-hoc enum and downstream code does not know whether a response represents 'we chose proceed' or 'we passed through.' Decision makes the commitment explicit, addressable, and auditable.
motivation.removability: No. Decision is Gate's output type; every flow-control primitive in the library lands its verdict here. Removing would collapse the verification stack's type distinctions — Status (Check), Score (Judge), Boolean (Validate), Decision (Gate) — each of which encodes different semantics.

usage.intended: the committed choice resulting from selection — an irrevocable selection artifact.
usage.broad_contexts: policy decisions, medical decisions, strategic decisions, resource-allocation decisions, decision-trees (output leaves), governance decisions.
usage.every_context_needs: the specific chosen option, reference to deliberation context, commitment semantic.
usage.varies: reversibility, precedent-setting power, audit trail, confidence of decision.
notes: §3.18 flagged Decision as Noun-with-Verb-mechanism. The §3.11-style rewrite preserves Decision as the artifact (committed choice) and lets `Decide` (if minted) be the Verb.

tensions: Selection vs process: the mechanism conflates Decision-as-artifact with Decision-making-as-process. A caller holding a Decision has the outcome but not necessarily the reasoning chain — auditability requires a separate Provenance attached by convention, not by the pattern.

Irrevocability vs reversibility: Once made, the decision cannot be unmade — but many real decisions are revisable (rate-limit recomputation, context shifts). The pattern's answer is that revisiting requires a new Decision, not unwinding the old — cleaner semantically, harder operationally.

Three-state (proceed/halt/debt) vs the Status three-state (Verified/Falsified/Unknown): both use three values but mean different things. Readers routinely conflate them. The library treats them as genuinely distinct — Decision is operational, Status is epistemic.
tradeoffs: Typed artifact buys routability (downstream systems can dispatch on Decision values) at the cost of forcing callers to import the enum and handle all three branches.
Irrevocability invariant simplifies reasoning (a Decision once made is stable) but rigidifies adaptive systems that want to revise in-flight.
Single-selection (must choose exactly one option) excludes plural or weighted decisions — tender/approve-partial, approve-subset — those need a richer pattern like `Allocation`.
critique: No failure modes listed. A foundational data-structure primitive should at least name Stale Decision (artifact outlives its validity window) and Phantom Option (selected option no longer exists).

'Debt' appears in Gate's mechanism but not in Decision's — the obligation semantics live implicitly between the two. The Decision pattern does not define what holding a debt-marked Decision means or requires of the holder.

The Select reference (`uses {{select}}`) implies Decision is the output of a selection act. But Decision is also used for opportunistic commits where no select step happens (a Gate's passthrough on proceed). The mechanism is ambiguous about whether Decision without a select history is valid.

Decision.family_discussion: Output of `Gate` and downstream artifact for every flow-control primitive in the library. Three-state semantics (proceed / halt / debt) distinguish it from `Status` (Check's three-state: Verified / Falsified / Unknown), `Boolean` (Validate's), and `Score` (Judge's). `DocumentedOverride` pairs with debt-marked Decisions at hard seams.

motivation.why_it_exists: Most interesting problems are too large to solve in one step. Decompose is the cognitive primitive for splitting a task into independent subtasks so each can be solved separately. The independence criterion is crucial — without it, 'decomposition' produces subtasks that interact, and solving each in isolation doesn't solve the whole.
motivation.removability: Non-removable for any solver above trivial scale. Decompose is the counterpart to Compose, and together they form the recursive-solving backbone that PolymorphicSolver, RootSolver, UniversalSolverTree all depend on. Remove it and you're left with monolithic solving.

usage.intended: split a task into independent subordinate parts where each part solved in isolation yields solution to whole.
usage.broad_contexts: algorithm divide-and-conquer, organizational task splitting, scientific problem decomposition, hierarchical planning, modular design.
usage.every_context_needs: task to decompose, independence criterion (subproblems don't interact), recursion base case.
usage.varies: decomposition axis, recursion depth, re-compose strategy.

tensions: Independence invariant vs real-world coupling — the pattern demands truly independent subproblems; most real decompositions have some coupling that the invariant treats as failure.
Axis of decomposition — the same problem can be decomposed along different axes (time, space, aspect), and the pattern doesn't prescribe which; choice matters enormously.
Depth of recursion vs integration overhead — deeper decomposition means smaller pieces but more assembly work; finding the right depth is the hard part.
tradeoffs: Gains: tractable solving for large problems, natural parallelism, principled recursion, clean pairing with Compose.
Gives up: problems with essential coupling (genuinely non-decomposable structures). Coupling leakage (the named failure) is exactly what happens when the decomposition axis was wrong.
critique: The independence invariant is almost always violated in practice — 'truly independent' is an ideal, and most decompositions have some acceptable leak.
