InvariantFilter names the firewall: intercept messages, evaluate against invariants, pass only those satisfying all predicates. Without it, validation happens inside the agent, where invalid input has already influenced state.
motivation.removability: Removable in trusted-input settings. Essential at any untrusted boundary — external API ingress, inter-agent messaging, tool output parsing. The Fail-Closed invariant is the load-bearing safety property.

usage.intended: strict communication firewall enforcing logical predicates on messages.
usage.future: any "contractual safety on communication channel" filter.
usage.broad_contexts: API request/response filters, chat moderation, content filters, security firewalls, regulatory-compliant communication checks, medical-record access filters.
usage.every_context_needs: invariant set (logical predicates), per-message evaluation, pass/block/flag decision.
usage.varies: invariant language, evaluation cost, logging of blocked, manual-review queue.

tensions: Atomic Blocking vs partial acceptance — the invariant blocks entire messages on single-predicate failure; no partial/cleansed forward path.
Invariant completeness vs evolvability — comprehensive invariants close gaps and harden the filter against new attack vectors; too rigid invariants block legitimate evolution.
Latency vs thoroughness — complex predicate evaluation slows high-throughput streams (named failure mode); simple predicates are fast and miss edge cases.
tradeoffs: Gains: clean boundary defense, named fail-closed default, explicit predicate list for audit.
Gives up: flexibility. False positives (named failure) block legitimate messages, and the filter has no graceful-degradation path.
critique: Incomplete Invariants (named failure) is endemic — filters can't anticipate all bad inputs, and each escape is a hard-to-detect leak.
False Positives (named failure) cause operational pain; there's no feedback loop from application to filter to surface which invariants are over-strict.
Isolation invariant (agent state not mutated during evaluation) is hard to enforce when evaluation requires looking at agent state to be effective.

InvariantFilter.family_discussion: Safety-boundary primitive paired with InputGuard (the general pattern), OutputGuard (counterpart for outgoing), and FailClosed (the default). Compare with LayeredCheck — InvariantFilter is a flat set of predicates at a boundary; LayeredCheck is ordered layers at abstraction levels.

motivation.why_it_exists: Looking at a problem from the 'how would I fail?' angle reveals blind spots that the 'how do I succeed?' angle misses. Invert names the opposition-solve move: list failure modes, invert each into a candidate solution. Without the named pattern, problem-solving stays in the constructive frame and misses the adversarial insights.
motivation.removability: Removable — agents can ask 'what would go wrong' without the named pattern. The value is the explicit discipline: logical negation, not just 'opposite,' and use of Invert as a generator of candidates. Remove it and inversion remains available but unstructured.

usage.intended: negation-based solution discovery — ask "how would I guarantee failure?"
usage.broad_contexts: Munger-style inversion, pre-mortem thinking, failure-mode-driven design, security (how would I break this?), testing (how might this fail?), strategic red-teaming.
usage.every_context_needs: goal reformulation to negation, enumeration of failure paths, inversion to get success candidates.
usage.varies: negation specificity, enumeration depth, validation of inverted candidates.

tensions: Logical negation (invariant) vs folk 'opposite' — 'the opposite of success' isn't 'failure' strictly; it's often 'mediocrity' or 'unrelated state.' The named failure mode 'False Dichotomy' is exactly this.
Double negation invariant — Invert(Invert(X)) implies X. This is true in logic and often fails in practice because Invert's real operation is generative, not strictly logical.
Generating candidates vs filtering them — inversion produces many candidates, most useless; downstream filtering lives outside the pattern.
tradeoffs: Gains: structured blind-spot exposure, adversarial perspective without adversarial setup, explicit logical-negation discipline.
Gives up: productive direct attack. Spending effort on Invert is less efficient than direct solving when the direct solve works; the pattern is for when direct solving is stuck.
critique: False Dichotomy is the named failure — assuming opposite-of-failure is success. This is the dominant real failure mode and the pattern has no defense.
Logical negation in real domains is often unclear — what's the negation of 'design a good UX'?
Double negation invariant is formally correct and practically misleading; in loose use, Invert(Invert(X)) rarely recovers X.

Invert.family_discussion: Reasoning-strategy primitive paired with Reverse, PreMortem (specifically for failure analysis), and AdversarialSteel. Compare with AntifragileInversion — Invert is cognitive reframing; AntifragileInversion is structural design. Both flip the problem relation.

motivation.why_it_exists: Direct negative feedback triggers defensive filtering — the recipient rejects the content by attacking the frame. Jester names the communication strategy that wraps critique inside semantic incongruity (humor, paradox, absurdity) so the critique lands before defenses fire. Without it, critical feedback gets bounced off defensive reflexes.
motivation.removability: Removable — direct critique works in trust-rich environments. Jester is specifically for environments where direct critique triggers defensive cascades; in those settings, it's the pattern that preserves the critique's information content.

usage.intended: deliver critique via incongruity to minimize social friction.
usage.broad_contexts: court-jester tradition, comedian social-commentary, satirical media, indirect feedback via stories, diplomatic indirect critique.
usage.every_context_needs: critique content, incongruity wrapper, defensive-filter bypass, relationship-maintenance priority.
usage.varies: incongruity type (humor, paradox, absurdity), risk of misinterpretation, target's receptivity.

tensions: Wrapping critique in humor (delivery) vs keeping critique legible — too much wrapper and the content gets lost; too little and defenses fire.
Coordination break prevention vs truth delivery — the pattern is optimized for keeping coordination alive; sometimes coordination should break (when the critique reveals a fundamental misalignment).
Humor as indirect delivery vs humor as dismissal — jokes can deliver critique or can dismiss it; the pattern doesn't distinguish.
tradeoffs: Gains: critique delivery without defensive cascade, coordination preservation through challenging feedback.
Gives up: directness and sometimes content fidelity. Humor-wrapped critique is easier to misinterpret or dismiss than direct feedback.
critique: No invariants or failure modes listed — the pattern is almost entirely heuristic. 'Use humor' isn't a mechanism, it's advice.
The recipient's 'defensive filtering' is an assumption about their psychology the pattern treats as given; for different recipients, Jester fails.
Conflates humor (which has its own genre discipline) with 'semantic incongruity' in general; the category is too broad.

Jester.family_discussion: Social-communication primitive paired with Critique (the content), Diplomacy, and Framing. Uses Incongruity as its mechanism. Compare with Steelman — Jester delivers critique indirectly; Steelman strengthens opposing positions. Both are trust-preserving epistemic moves.

motivation.why_it_exists: Graded quality evaluation as a primitive — distinct from Check (Boolean truth) and Validate (schema conformance). Real-world evaluation is rarely binary: ranking candidates, scoring aesthetic fit, assessing risk, rating model outputs — all need a [0, 1] scalar with deterministic inputs. Judge pins that signature.
motivation.removability: No. The Genesis Loop (paper §5.2) assigns Judge the role of evaluating pattern merit during self-authoring — removing Judge deprives the library of the only primitive that returns graded quality. Descendants (CalibratedJudge, ExplainableJudge, HumanJudge) specialize on calibration and provenance; they all need the parent contract.

usage.intended: scalar evaluation of merit on continuous scale.
usage.broad_contexts: model output evaluation, content quality rating, candidate ranking, aesthetic assessment, fitness evaluation, risk scoring, reviewer judgments.
usage.every_context_needs: subject to evaluate; accepts a `ScoringFunction` (criteria moved to accepts per §3.1); yields `Score` (per §3.13).
usage.varies: scoring function complexity, confidence bounds, calibration method, multi-axis decomposition, explainability.

tensions: Scalar vs multi-axis: merit is rarely one-dimensional. The mechanism forces scalar output, pushing multi-axis decomposition to descendants like `MultiAxisJudge`. Callers who want (parsimony, novelty, realizability, expansiveness) scores separately must layer Judge invocations.

Determinism vs calibration: same input → same score is enforced as an invariant, but real judges (LLMs, humans) drift. Determinism must be realized via seeded models or cached evaluations — the pattern names the property without saying how to achieve it.

Objective vs subjective criteria: Subjectivity Creep is a real failure mode. The mechanism requires a ScoringFunction encoding the Criteria, but whether those criteria are genuinely objective is a responsibility the caller inherits.
tradeoffs: Scalar output buys comparability (scores can be ranked, averaged, thresholded) at the cost of explanation — a 0.7 carries no reason by itself.
Bounded range [0, 1] buys cross-judge comparability at the cost of expressivity — unbounded judges (quality-per-dollar, confidence-weighted) require a separate pattern.
Deterministic contract buys replayability at the cost of excluding non-deterministic judges (stochastic LLMs without seeding) from valid implementations.
critique: Threshold Gaming is named but the mechanism does nothing to detect it — a ScoringFunction that passes the threshold on any input trivially honors the invariants. Detection is pushed to caller-level reviews.
No postconditions listed. The mechanism implies the Score is the postcondition but does not assert what the Score means relative to the Criteria (calibration contract absent).

The pattern is in Infrastructure/Primitives, which fits because scoring is a mechanical operation given a ScoringFunction — but the ScoringFunction itself can embed cognition. The layer boundary is honest about the Judge primitive, ambiguous about its input.

Judge.family_discussion: Graded-scalar corner of the verification stack (Check = three-state, Gate = decision, Validate = Boolean, Judge = scalar). Yields `Score`; accepts `ScoringFunction` carrying `Criteria`. Called by `PURECheck`, `Evaluator`, and the proposed Genesis Loop's self-evaluation step.

motivation.why_it_exists: Not every moment is equally receptive to an action. Kairos names the opportunity-window detector: aggregate receptivity, system load, friction into Readiness Potential, return True when the moment is right. Without the pattern, agents either act in every moment (wasting effort) or act in fixed schedules (missing windows).
motivation.removability: Removable in systems where timing doesn't matter. Essential for persuasion, coordination, and any action whose success depends on context readiness. The Ephemerality invariant is the key insight — moment-appropriateness doesn't persist.

usage.intended: sense the opportune moment via aggregated environmental signals.
usage.broad_contexts: trade-timing signals, product-launch readiness, political-moment sensing, conversational-interruption timing, game-engagement detection.
usage.every_context_needs: signal sources, aggregation function, readiness threshold, boolean yield.
usage.varies: signal weighting, time-window, false-positive cost, actionability horizon.

tensions: Ephemerality (invariant: True at t doesn't imply True at t+1) vs scheduling — Kairos is inherently non-schedulable; acting on Kairos requires real-time responsiveness.
Non-Compensatory (invariant: wrong moment can't be fixed with more effort) vs persistence — in the wrong moment, the pattern says give up; persistence is ineffective.
Readiness Potential calculation — aggregates multiple signals into a scalar threshold; the weighting is under-specified.
tradeoffs: Gains: temporal-opportunity detection, explicit moment-appropriateness, resistance to 'just try harder' failure mode.
Gives up: predictability. Actions gated by Kairos can't be scheduled; their timing depends on context the agent can't fully control.
critique: The sensitivity threshold is caller-dependent and consequential — set too high, True almost never; set too low, pattern fires indiscriminately.
Aggregation of signals into Readiness Potential is treated as given; the real work is picking and weighting signals, which the pattern doesn't specify.
The invariant 'If the moment is wrong, more effort cannot fix it' is strong — some wrong moments are fixable with enough effort.

Kairos.family_discussion: Temporal-sensitivity primitive paired with ReceptivityGate (the receptivity signal), AttentionMarkets (the system-load signal), and Heartbeat (the general signal substrate). Compare with Defer — Kairos detects good moments; Defer postpones until good moments. Related temporal reasoning primitives.

motivation.why_it_exists: Symbolic patterns (hash-identified, canonical) support strict verification; latent embeddings (high-dimensional vectors) support fuzzy semantic search. LatentAttachment names the bridge: attach the embedding to the pattern card without changing the canonical hash. Without it, patterns are either strict-only (findable only by exact hash) or fuzzy-only (no verification).
motivation.removability: Removable if fuzzy semantic search isn't needed. Essential in any vocabulary where agents need to find 'similar to X' patterns. The Identity Separation invariant is the core design move — the hash ignores the latent so canonical identity stays stable.

usage.intended: bind vector embedding to symbolic pattern card — bridges LLM intuition and code execution.
usage.broad_contexts: ConceptAnchor pairing with embeddings, pattern-library fuzzy-search, content-addressed semantic search, namespace fuzzy-matching, embedding-vs-hash dual binding.
usage.every_context_needs: symbolic anchor (pattern card / hash), high-dimensional vector embedding, fuzzy-search capability, canonical-hash verification.
usage.varies: embedding dimension, embedding model, similarity threshold, re-embedding policy on model update.

tensions: Identity Separation (invariant) vs embedding truth — the hash must be stable, which means the embedding is advisory only; out-of-date embeddings give wrong similarities.
Semantic proximity vs embedding model choice — different embedding models produce different similarities; the pattern is embedding-model-dependent in ways the invariant doesn't expose.
Model shift invalidates embeddings — the named failure mode is structural; every embedding model upgrade invalidates all prior embeddings.
tradeoffs: Gains: fuzzy search + canonical verification in the same vocabulary, LLM-intuition bridge to code-verification strictness.
Gives up: embedding durability. Upgrading the embedding model invalidates existing embeddings, forcing rebuild.
critique: Model shift (the named failure) has no mitigation in the pattern — it's assumed to be managed externally.
Semantic Proximity threshold is unspecified — what counts as 'close enough'? Caller decides, and the decision shapes search behavior.
The pattern assumes embeddings are a deterministic function of the pattern's text; in reality, subtle variations in text produce different embeddings.

LatentAttachment.family_discussion: Bridge primitive paired with ConceptAnchor (the canonical hash), Cache (the fuzzy search substrate), and Embedding (the vector unit). Compare with LatentWander — LatentAttachment is the structural connection; LatentWander uses the connected embedding space for daydreaming.

motivation.why_it_exists: Offline processing can do what online can't — explore without external constraints, consolidate memory, generate analogies. LatentWander names this daydreaming mode: higher exploration temperature, no external output, free traversal of the embedding space. Without it, agents only reason when prompted, missing the connection-making that happens in offline states.
motivation.removability: Removable in agents that don't do offline processing. The pattern is specifically for systems with idle cycles that can be used for consolidation. Its value depends on whether your agent has such cycles.

usage.intended: offline exploration of embedding space — daydreaming, memory consolidation, novel analogy generation.
usage.future: any "offline creative traversal of your own knowledge space" mode.
usage.broad_contexts: ML model embedding exploration, creative daydreaming, memory consolidation during sleep, LLM-based concept discovery, research-ideation sessions.
usage.every_context_needs: offline processing mode, embedding-space traversal, ConceptBlend usage, non-obvious-connection discovery.
usage.varies: wander duration, traversal heuristics, captured-output format.

tensions: Drift invariant (exploration > standard temperature) vs productive wandering — higher temperature produces more diverse associations and more noise.
Silence invariant (no external output) vs observability — offline processing is opaque by design, which limits monitoring.
Wandering vs structure — the mode is deliberately unstructured; the insights produced are hard to validate without re-running in structured mode.
tradeoffs: Gains: offline memory consolidation, novel analogy generation, explicit idle-state mode.
Gives up: observability and sometimes coherence. Wandering produces connections that don't always hold up to later scrutiny.
critique: No failure modes listed; LatentWander has many (drift without convergence, hallucinated connections, offline state corruption).
'Higher than standard inference temperature' is under-specified — how much higher, on what schedule?
Silence during wandering precludes mid-wander intervention, which prevents observability — a real operational problem.

LatentWander.family_discussion: Offline-mode primitive paired with LatentAttachment (the substrate), ConceptBlend (the primary operation during wandering), and AnalogyBridge (the typical output). Compare with CurriculumReplay — both are offline/idle processing; LatentWander explores embedding space, CurriculumReplay revisits successful examples.

motivation.why_it_exists: When an optimization is stuck in a local optimum, sometimes changing domains helps — reframe the problem as a biological system, solve in that domain, map back. LateralOptimization names this creative detour. Without the pattern, escape from local optima is ad-hoc.
motivation.removability: Removable — direct optimization covers most cases. LateralOptimization earns its weight specifically when direct optimization is stuck and a structural analogy is available. The Analogy Coherence invariant is what distinguishes this from just 'try random things.'

usage.intended: Reframe → Optimize → Translate loop — shift domains to find easier problem structure.
usage.future: any "solve in a different domain and map back" creativity technique.
usage.broad_contexts: analogical problem-solving, cross-domain innovation, mathematical transformation (Fourier, Laplace), biomimicry engineering, metaphorical reasoning.
usage.every_context_needs: source domain problem, target-domain mapping, optimization in target, mapping back (Translate).
usage.varies: domain-pair fit, translation fidelity, iteration across multiple target domains.

tensions: Analogy coherence (invariant) vs creative leap — strict structural consistency is safe and narrow; loose mapping is creative and error-prone.
Translation Loss (named failure) — the mapped solution can't be mapped back.
Complexity Overhead (named failure) — the cost of mapping outweighs the gain; for simple problems, lateral is worse than direct.
tradeoffs: Gains: structural escape from local optima, explicit analogy-based reframing, named detour pattern.
Gives up: reliability. Domain-switching is powerful and risky; most lateral attempts don't round-trip successfully.
critique: Hallucination (named failure) — the analogy introduces features that don't exist in the original problem.
Translation Loss is endemic; every lateral move loses something, and getting back to the original domain is often where the loss is discovered.
Complexity Overhead is the sensible-routing question and the pattern offers no cost model.

LateralOptimization.family_discussion: Creative-reasoning primitive paired with Reframe (the domain-shift move), AnalogyBridge (the mapping substrate), and Optimize (the goal). Compare with FirstPrinciples — LateralOptimization escapes via domain switch; FirstPrinciples escapes via axiomatic reconstruction. Different escape strategies.

motivation.why_it_exists: Geometric-neighbor consensus — commit requires signatures from the agent AND immediate neighbors in a virtual lattice. Local quorum (not global) makes this scalable while preserving redundancy. Essential for patterns where global consensus is too expensive but pure local independence is unsafe.
motivation.removability: Probably retain. Where Consensus requires global agreement and Vote requires N-participant tally, LatticeCommit offers a geometric middle ground. Distinct enough to warrant a named pattern.

usage.intended: geometric-neighbor consensus — state transition valid only if signed by agent AND its immediate lattice neighbors.
usage.broad_contexts: cellular automata, spatially-organized distributed systems, geographic-network protocols, mesh networks, federated systems with geographic partitioning.
usage.every_context_needs: lattice topology, neighbor relation, signatures from agent + neighbors, local quorum semantic.
usage.varies: lattice dimension (2D, 3D, hexagonal), neighbor count per node, signature aggregation method, lattice dynamism.

tensions: Local vs global quorum: local scales but requires the lattice topology to be well-formed. Fractured or disconnected lattices produce isolated clusters — named failure.

Geometric-neighbor signing vs dynamic membership: the pattern assumes stable lattice neighbors. Dynamic topologies (agents join/leave) require lattice reconfiguration that the pattern doesn't specify.
Monotonic progress vs legitimate rollback: 'no backtracking' is strict — commits are forward-only. Some use cases (error recovery, speculative writes) need rollback; pattern forbids.
tradeoffs: Local quorum buys scalability at the cost of global-consistency guarantee — the lattice may hold inconsistent states across distant clusters.
Geometric-neighbor requirement buys spatially-local redundancy at the cost of requiring a meaningful geometric arrangement.
Monotonic progress buys simplicity at the cost of forbidding rollback.
critique: Two invariants, one failure mode. Missing: Neighbor Availability (at least K neighbors must be online for progress), Lattice Integrity (topology verified before commit).
Fracture is the named failure with no specified recovery — how does a fractured lattice heal?
'Virtual lattice' topology is undefined — grid? hex? cube? Different shapes give different fault-tolerance profiles; the pattern is shape-agnostic but the choice matters.

LatticeCommit.family_discussion: The geometric-local variant of Consensus. Pairs with `Quorum` (local threshold), `Sign` (signatures). Sibling to `Consensus` (global) and `Vote` (tallied). Used where spatial locality is a meaningful coordination axis.

motivation.why_it_exists: Cheap checks should run before expensive ones. LayeredCheck names the abstraction-ordered gate sequence: existence → schema → semantics, with fail-fast between layers. Without it, expensive semantic checks run on artifacts that fail trivial existence checks, wasting compute.
motivation.removability: Removable — callers can hand-order checks. LayeredCheck's value is the named discipline: strict hierarchy obedience, fail-fast between layers. Remove it and the layer ordering becomes implicit and often violated.

usage.intended: hierarchical verification — existence → schema → semantics, with early-halt.
usage.broad_contexts: input validation pipelines, defensive parsing, API request validation, UI form submission, compiler error cascades, test-suite ordering (cheap tests first).
usage.every_context_needs: layered hierarchy (cheap→expensive), early-halt on lower-layer failure, gate sequence.
usage.varies: layer definitions, halt vs continue-with-warning behavior, layer cost estimation, skip conditions.

tensions: Fail-Fast (invariant) vs diagnostic completeness — stopping at the first failing layer gives fast feedback and misses compound problems.
Strict hierarchy obedience vs real dependencies — some checks don't fit a strict layer (cross-cutting concerns like security); the pattern treats them as layer violations.
Layer choice — what's layer 1 vs layer 2? Defaults are existence/schema/semantics, but different domains may warrant different orderings.
tradeoffs: Gains: efficient check ordering, explicit fail-fast discipline, clean abstraction layering.
Gives up: comprehensive diagnostics. Fail-fast surfaces the first problem, not all problems; debugging often needs all of them.
critique: Hierarchy Obedience is strict; real check graphs often have parallel or cross-layer dependencies that the pattern can't express.
Fail-Fast loses diagnostic information — the caller learns of layer N failing and not what layer N+1 would have said.
No failure modes listed; LayeredCheck has some (missed layer, layer misorder) that the pattern doesn't catalogue.

LayeredCheck.family_discussion: Verification-strategy primitive paired with Check (the verb), Gate (the binary decision unit), and FailClosed (the fail-fast default). Compare with CheckReference — both are check patterns; LayeredCheck orchestrates multiple checks, CheckReference validates a specific reference.

motivation.why_it_exists: Global consensus for every transaction is slow. LazyConsensus names the optimistic discipline: execute immediately, detect conflicts later, resolve via deterministic rollback rule. Without it, distributed systems either block on consensus (safety at latency cost) or proceed without consensus (chaos). LazyConsensus is the explicit speed-over-safety mode.
motivation.removability: Removable in settings where all operations are reversible and conflicts are rare. Essential for high-throughput systems where waiting for consensus is the bottleneck — the pattern accepts the cost of occasional rollbacks for the benefit of average-case speed.

usage.intended: optimistic execution with retroactive verification (conflict resolution after-the-fact).
usage.future: any speed-over-safety coordination with deterministic conflict resolution.
usage.broad_contexts: Apache committer model, git-flow, CRDT operations, eventual-consistency databases, optimistic locking, wiki edit flows.
usage.every_context_needs: optimistic-execution semantic, conflict-detection mechanism, deterministic rollback rule.
usage.varies: conflict-resolution policy, rollback complexity, window for revocation, audit trail.

tensions: Speed vs correctness — the whole value is execution before consensus; the whole risk is acting on state that will be rolled back.
Deterministic conflict resolution vs fairness — 'highest ID wins' is deterministic and arbitrary; agents with low IDs systematically lose conflicts.
Rollback safety vs irreversible external action — the named failure mode: lazy consensus applied to irreversible actions can't roll back, making inconsistency permanent.
tradeoffs: Gains: high throughput, no pre-execution coordination, explicit fast-path for rare-conflict workloads.
Gives up: correctness guarantees. Cascading rollbacks are common in high-conflict regimes and the pattern's speed benefit disappears.
critique: Cascading rollbacks are the named failure and the dominant real failure; they can spread faster than the rollback can complete.
Applied to irreversible external actions (the named second failure) is the nightmare case — sent emails, transferred funds, called APIs can't be rolled back.
Determinism in conflict resolution is a correctness property; it's also a fairness problem that the pattern doesn't address.

LazyConsensus.family_discussion: Optimistic-coordination primitive paired with Consensus (the opposite discipline), AtomicBid (similar fire-first shape for single actors), and Compensate (the rollback substrate). Compare with Bubble — LazyConsensus skips the bubble and accepts rollback cost; Bubble isolates before commit.

motivation.why_it_exists: Some problems decompose into subproblems of varying difficulty. LeastToMost names the easy-first prompting strategy: solve the easy subproblem, use its solution as context for the next. Without it, decomposition gives simultaneous subproblems and loses the cumulative scaffolding that easier-first solving provides.
motivation.removability: Removable when subproblems are independent. Essential when later subproblems require context from earlier ones. The pattern is a specific decomposition strategy with ordering discipline; remove it and you get generic Decompose without the scaffold.

usage.intended: solve subproblems from easiest to hardest — each solution becomes context for the next.
usage.broad_contexts: pedagogical scaffolding, curriculum design, puzzle solving, mathematical induction, LLM prompting strategy, algorithm training.
usage.every_context_needs: decomposition, difficulty ordering, sequential solving with solution-as-context passing.
usage.varies: difficulty metric, ordering stability, optional skipping if an easy problem provides insight.

tensions: Easy-first ordering (the value) vs difficulty assessment — knowing which subproblems are easier is itself judgment, and wrong ordering causes prerequisite gaps (named failure).
Cumulative context vs error propagation — later subproblems benefit from earlier solutions and suffer from earlier errors (named 'Subproblem Coupling' failure).
Decomposition overhead vs task size — the named 'Overhead' failure: simple problems don't benefit from the decomposition ceremony.
tradeoffs: Gains: scaffolded solving that builds context, explicit ordering discipline.
Gives up: independence between subproblems. LeastToMost creates sequential coupling; parallel solving is structurally blocked.
critique: Ordering Misjudgment is a dominant failure — difficulty is subjective, and wrong ordering cascades.
Subproblem Coupling is acknowledged but unmitigated — earlier errors poison later subproblems; the pattern has no isolation between subproblems.
No specified handling for subproblems that turn out to be equally difficult; the pattern assumes ordering exists.

LeastToMost.family_discussion: Prompting-strategy primitive paired with Decompose (the general split), ChainOfThought (the substrate), and MECE (the exhaustive partition). Compare with BackwardChain — LeastToMost orders forward by difficulty; BackwardChain orders backward from goal. Different ordering disciplines.

motivation.why_it_exists: Multi-agent economic coordination needs shared memory of value transfers. Ledger names the immutable append-only record of transfers, debts, and obligations. Without it, economic state lives in each agent's head and diverges immediately.
motivation.removability: Non-removable in any multi-agent economic system. The pattern is imported from blockchain/distributed systems and is the substrate for trust in multi-party economic coordination. Remove it and you're back to bilateral trust or centralized authority.

usage.intended: immutable record of value transfers, debts, obligations.
usage.broad_contexts: financial ledgers, blockchain state, CRDT operation logs, event sourcing stores, audit records, accounts-payable systems, game state transactions.
usage.every_context_needs: immutability, transactional semantics, value attribution per entry.
usage.varies: signature/authentication model, partitioning, query-efficiency structures (indices), retention, privacy controls.

tensions: Immutability (invariant) vs correctness — entries cannot be modified even if wrong; corrections require new offsetting entries.
Append-only (invariant) vs storage growth — ledgers grow without bound; pruning requires zero-knowledge proofs or snapshotting, both outside the pattern.
Shared memory vs privacy — shared ledger state means everyone sees everyone's entries; some systems need selective visibility.
tradeoffs: Gains: immutable audit trail, shared economic state, principled append-only discipline.
Gives up: privacy, edit-ability, and compact storage. Ledgers grow forever and are visible to all participants.
critique: Very thin — two invariants, one-line mechanism. The real work (consensus, signature, replication) lives in dependent patterns.
No failure modes listed; ledgers have many (fork resolution, double-spend, history rewrite attacks).
The pattern assumes shared state; privacy-preserving ledgers (zero-knowledge) require substantially different mechanisms.

Ledger.family_discussion: Economic-coordination primitive paired with Transaction (the entry), AuditTrail (general-purpose counterpart), and Sign (for entry authentication). Compare with AuditTrail — Ledger is economically-shaped (value, transfers); AuditTrail is action-shaped (who did what).

motivation.why_it_exists: Some claims are validated by the process of making them — writing a paper on brevity is only valid if the paper is itself brief. LivedProof names this recursive validation: the process IS the evidence. Without the named pattern, the shape gets lost in generic Proof; the specific discipline of enacting the claim during generation has no referent.
motivation.removability: Removable — most proofs are not LivedProofs. The pattern earns its weight for claims where process-fidelity is the evidence (brevity, simplicity, speed). Hard to argue against keeping it as a named slot for this specific rhetorical move.

usage.intended: process demonstrates thesis — the execution IS the evidence.
usage.broad_contexts: dogfooding demonstrations, recursive-validation arguments, teaching-by-modeling, manifesto writing that enacts its own claims, meta-circular reasoning.
usage.every_context_needs: thesis being argued, process that enacts it, observer who can verify the enactment matches the thesis.
usage.varies: observer type (self, peer, neutral), enactment fidelity requirements, fallback if enactment fails to prove thesis.

tensions: Process == Evidence (the invariant) vs external validation — the claim is self-validating, which is powerful and vulnerable to 'the process looks right' tricks.
Real-time (invariant) vs historical proof — only present execution counts; this rules out 'I have done this before' evidence.
Cryptographic trace reference vs verification cost — traceability is cheap to log, expensive to verify in detail.
tradeoffs: Gains: self-validating demonstrations, structural prevention of say-one-thing-do-another, explicit identity of process and evidence.
Gives up: pre-canned efficiency. LivedProofs must happen live, which rules out optimized pre-built demonstrations.
critique: Performative Contradiction is the named failure and it's the whole point — a LivedProof that contradicts itself is worse than one that doesn't attempt self-proof.
Staged Demo (named second failure) — pre-canned scripts that look like enactment; the pattern has no cryptographic-trace defense sufficient to detect sophisticated staging.
The pattern is rhetorical/epistemic; operationalizing 'the process enacted the thesis' requires judgment the pattern doesn't specify.

LivedProof.family_discussion: Rhetorical/epistemic primitive paired with Proof (the general category), Demonstrate (the active form), and Witness (the attestation counterpart). Compare with CiteBack — LivedProof is self-evidencing; CiteBack is externally sourced. Different epistemic shapes.

motivation.why_this_layer: partitioned feedback routing within one solver tree
motivation.why_it_exists: Feedback routed to all solvers diffuses signal. LocalizedLearning names the specialist-only update: feedback signal goes to the exact solver that generated it. Without the pattern, learning is global and lossy.
motivation.removability: Removable in uniform-agent systems. Essential for specialist-agent architectures. The Isolation invariant prevents cross-solver contamination.

usage.intended: feedback signals route to specific SolverManifests that generated the result — partitioned memory updates.
usage.future: any "route learning to the right module" mechanism.
usage.broad_contexts: mixture-of-experts training, modular ML architecture updates, organizational learning (feedback routes to the team), specialist-agent memory updates.
usage.every_context_needs: feedback signal tagged with solver ID, routing mechanism, isolation of updates to originating module.
usage.varies: routing granularity, catastrophic-interference avoidance strength, cross-module-signal-sharing policy.

tensions: Echo Chamber (named failure) — over-optimization for narrow metric.
Feedback Sparsity (named failure) — rare modules don't learn.
Isolation vs shared knowledge — strict isolation forbids transfer learning.
tradeoffs: Gains: specialist learning, explicit attribution.
Gives up: transfer. Specialists don't learn from each other.
critique: Both named failures are real.
Isolation invariant is too strong for transfer-learning scenarios.
Attribution requires feedback-signal identification.

LocalizedLearning.family_discussion: Learning primitive paired with Feedback, SolverManifest, and CurriculumReplay. Compare with CurriculumReplay — LocalizedLearning is routing; CurriculumReplay is self-distillation.

motivation.why_this_layer: mutual exclusion is a substrate atomicity primitive (kernel/hardware)
motivation.why_it_exists: Mutual exclusion is the atomicity floor every concurrent protocol depends on. Without a shared word for 'at most one holder at a time,' each downstream pattern re-invents mutex semantics locally and distributed systems fragment on subtle disagreements (is it reentrant? can it be stolen? what owns the release right?). Lock pins the minimal mechanism so descendants inherit an unambiguous parent.
motivation.removability: No. Lock is the conceptual floor for every exclusion primitive (Mutex, DistributedLock, Semaphore, ReadWriteLock) via `derived_from`. Removing would leave those dangling — they would each have to re-declare the exclusivity invariant, losing the one-parent canonical definition that lets agents verify they share the same atomicity semantics.

usage.intended: bounded concurrent access to a protected resource.
usage.future: any exclusion primitive where holder-count is capped.
usage.broad_contexts: in-memory mutexes (K=1), counting semaphores (K>1), distributed locks, advisory file locks, database row locks, ReadWriteLocks (bounded shared + 1 exclusive).
usage.every_context_needs: acquire operation, release operation, **bounded-concurrent-holders guarantee** (K ≥ 1).
usage.varies: K (the bound), fencing tokens, reentrancy, deadlock detection, timeouts, ownership transfer, shared vs exclusive modes, wait queue discipline.
usage.extensions: `Mutex` (K=1 specialization + token+fencing via `derived_from Lock`), `Semaphore` (K>1 counting), `ReadWriteLock` (shared/exclusive variant), `DistributedLock` (lease-based).

tensions: Substrate vs authored: Lock is placed in Physics on the view that atomicity is a hardware-level given (two holders cannot simultaneously modify the same word). In practice, every Lock users touch is engineered — the kernel or database provides the primitive. The library takes the substrate framing because the property is the point; the implementation is a specialization detail.

Fairness vs throughput: the mechanism is silent on contention ordering. Fair queuing, priority-inherited, and preemptable locks are all compatible with the spec — each has different liveness failure modes.

Explicit release vs timeout: 'Release-after-use' assumes cooperative holders. In adversarial or crash-prone settings you need leases, fencing tokens, or timeouts — none of which Lock itself provides. Descendants carry that complexity.
tradeoffs: Strong safety (exclusivity) costs liveness: a holder crash blocks the resource until external recovery intervenes.
Single-object atomicity costs throughput — the protected region serializes writers by construction.
Minimal acquire/release interface costs expressivity: read-write, reentrant, and hierarchical locks are all separate descendants rather than parameters.
critique: The 'resource' in the mechanism is underspecified — byte, record, abstract object? Granularity matters for cost profiles and the mechanism is silent.

Listed failure modes cover Deadlock and Priority Inversion but omit Starvation (under adversarial queue discipline), Convoying (high-frequency contention collapses throughput), and Spurious Release (non-holder calls release).
Acquisition semantics (blocking vs try-acquire vs timed-acquire) are not specified — every descendant re-invents the call surface.

Lock.family_discussion: The atomicity primitive at the bottom of the contention-handling stack. Parent to `Mutex` (K=1 with fencing+token) and conceptually paired with `StateLock` (Society layer: two-party atomic state fusion). `Backoff`, `Cooldown`, and `Throttle` compose with Lock to handle contention behavior at a layer above the exclusion guarantee itself.

motivation.why_it_exists: Repetition is fundamental to feedback, learning, and persistent processes. Loop names the control-flow primitive for repeating work until a condition is met. Without it, iterative patterns collapse to ad-hoc recursion or unbounded while-loops. The Termination Guarantee invariant is what distinguishes structured Loop from infinite loop.
motivation.removability: Non-removable. Every iterative pattern (Reflexion, EvaluatorOptimizer, Retry) consumes Loop or equivalent. The pattern is a control-flow primitive that Cyclic topology-patterns specialize. Removing it collapses iteration.

usage.intended: control flow structure repeating work until condition met.
usage.broad_contexts: for/while loops in programming, biological-feedback loops, retry loops, polling loops, perception-action cycles, game loops.
usage.every_context_needs: work to repeat, termination condition.
usage.varies: iteration bound, condition evaluation timing (pre/post), break/continue semantics, parallelism.

tensions: Termination Guarantee (invariant) vs daemon mode — the invariant demands proven exit OR explicit daemon mode, which is correct and sometimes awkward (what counts as 'proven'?).
Progress (invariant: state must change) vs idempotent operations — some loops legitimately don't change state (polling, waiting); the invariant forbids them.
Single condition vs compound conditions — Loop takes one exit condition; complex loops with multiple termination reasons must encode them into a single predicate.
tradeoffs: Gains: structured iteration, explicit termination guarantee, clean control-flow primitive.
Gives up: freedom. Ad-hoc iteration without Loop's invariants is common in real code; the pattern's discipline is aspirational.
critique: Termination Guarantee is aspirational for most real loops; formal proof of termination is rare outside of specific algorithms.
Progress invariant conflates state change with useful progress; a loop that decrements a counter technically 'makes progress' without doing useful work.
Very thin — one sentence, two invariants. Real loops have richer structure (pre-conditions, post-conditions, loop invariants) the pattern doesn't capture.

Loop.family_discussion: Foundational control-flow primitive paired with Cyclic (the topology class), Condition (the termination predicate), and Retry (a specific failure-handling loop). Compare with Recurse — Loop is iterative, Recurse is self-calling. Different structures for repetition.

motivation.why_it_exists: Partitioning a problem space needs discipline — no overlap (mutually exclusive), no gaps (collectively exhaustive). MECE names the consulting/analysis discipline. Without it, partitions drift: some items fit multiple categories, some fit none, and the analysis gets unreliable.
motivation.removability: Removable — partitioning can be done without explicit MECE discipline. The named pattern is specifically the quality check: run the two tests (exclusivity, exhaustiveness) and refine. Remove it and the tests become implicit and often skipped.

usage.intended: Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive partitioning.
usage.future: any "no overlap, no gaps" partitioning discipline.
usage.broad_contexts: consulting frameworks (McKinsey's Pyramid), probability-space partitioning, category-schema design, market-segment analysis, legal case-law partitioning.
usage.every_context_needs: problem space, partition into non-overlapping categories, no-gap test.
usage.varies: partition granularity, test rigor, dynamism (static vs updating partition).

tensions: Exclusivity vs natural overlaps — some domains have items that legitimately belong to multiple categories; MECE forces an arbitrary primary assignment.
Exhaustiveness vs closed-world assumption — exhaustive partition requires a closed universe; open-world domains always have 'Other.'
The Other Bucket Trap (named failure) — when too many items fall into 'Misc,' the partition is failing exhaustiveness, and the pattern has no threshold for 'too many.'
tradeoffs: Gains: principled partition discipline, explicit overlap-and-gap tests, forcing function for partition refinement.
Gives up: fuzzy category membership. Many useful categorizations are probabilistic or gradient; MECE flattens them to crisp bins.
critique: The Other Bucket Trap is endemic — real domains have stubbornly-uncategorizable items, and MECE has no graceful handling.
Dimensional Error (named failure) — partitioning criteria mixed (Color AND Origin) — is easy to commit, and the pattern has no type-check.
False Exclusivity — edge cases ignored to force fit — is the common shortcut; the pattern's tests don't catch motivated ignoring.

MECE.family_discussion: Analysis-methodology primitive paired with Decompose (which can be MECE or not), Category (the bin unit), and DecompositionGate (the stricter four-test variant). Compare with ConceptualDecomposition — MECE is exclusivity+exhaustiveness; ConceptualDecomposition adds the full four tests from the paper.

motivation.why_it_exists: Planning is the architectural phase — take a FrameSpec, think through it, produce an ExecutionManifest. ManifestPlanning names this transformation. Without the named pattern, the FrameSpec-to-ExecutionManifest step is implicit, and planning blurs with execution.
motivation.removability: Removable in settings where execution can proceed directly from FrameSpec. Essential in complex workflow orchestration where the plan itself needs to be structured, validated, and handed off. The pattern is the substrate for the generic Plan primitive.

usage.intended: architectural phase transforming FrameSpec → ExecutionManifest via optimization.
usage.broad_contexts: software architecture phases, project planning from requirements to Gantt, experimental protocol planning, manufacturing production planning, lecture planning.
usage.every_context_needs: FrameSpec input, Think to transform, Optimize for resource feasibility, strict Definition of Done generation.
usage.varies: optimization depth, resource model, feasibility-check rigor, iteration count with framing.

tensions: Causality invariant (dependency order) vs opportunistic parallelism — correct ordering is conservative; sometimes steps that look dependent are actually parallelizable.
Resource Bound invariant vs optimistic planning — planning within budget is disciplined and sometimes produces plans that won't actually complete within the budget when reality intrudes.
Hallucinated Resources (named failure) — planning to use tools that don't exist — is a real LLM-planner failure mode.
tradeoffs: Gains: architectural separation of plan from execution, explicit transformation from FrameSpec to ExecutionManifest.
Gives up: iteration. ManifestPlanning is a one-shot transformation; real planning often needs to iterate as execution reveals new information.
critique: Hallucinated Resources is the canonical LLM failure mode; the pattern names it without providing a resource catalog to check against.
Fragile Chain (named failure) — single-step failure collapses the plan — is structural and unmitigated.
No replanning story — the pattern produces a manifest and doesn't specify what to do when execution reveals the manifest is wrong.
`derived_from` fixed: previously legacy stub `sema:Plan` without hash; now full sema_id.

ManifestPlanning.family_discussion: Planning phase primitive paired with FrameSpec (input), ExecutionManifest (output), and Plan (the general primitive). Compare with Design — ManifestPlanning produces an executable; Design produces an artifact proposal. Different output types.

motivation.why_this_layer: ratio test for depth allocation — cognitive rule
motivation.why_it_exists: Recursion in solvers could continue indefinitely without an economic brake. MarginalValueRule names the per-dive economic check: go deeper only if expected quality improvement exceeds incremental cost. Without it, recursion-dive patterns have no principled termination and burn budget.
motivation.removability: Removable in pre-budgeted recursion. The pattern's value is the per-level marginal check, which catches cases where an allowed budget would be better stopped early. Remove it and budget gets consumed to its floor rather than stopped when it stops paying.

usage.intended: economic stop-condition for recursion — go deeper only if expected-improvement > incremental-cost.
usage.broad_contexts: solver-depth decisions, research-effort stopping, optimization-iteration bounds, tree-search pruning, cognitive-effort allocation, meeting-length stopping.
usage.every_context_needs: expected-improvement estimator, cost estimator, comparison rule.
usage.varies: estimation method, cost-time-horizon, risk adjustment, stopping-threshold calibration, reset on surprise.
notes: this is the economic counterpart to ComputeBudget — both stop runaway cognition but on different axes (MVR is per-step, ComputeBudget is total-resource).

tensions: Expected improvement vs actual — the rule depends on accurate estimates; overestimation wastes budget, underestimation stops early (both named failures).
Budget Respect (invariant) vs value-cap override — sometimes you want to exceed remaining budget for a very high-value dive; the invariant forbids it.
Diminishing Returns (invariant: deeper levels must show proportionally higher marginal value) — this is a strong form that many real recursions don't satisfy.
tradeoffs: Gains: principled recursion termination, explicit marginal-value check, budget protection.
Gives up: straightforward recursion. Every dive pays the evaluation tax; for small recursions this is overhead.
critique: Underestimation and Overestimation of marginal value are both named failures; neither has a structural defense. Estimation quality is exactly what's at stake.
Sunk Cost Fallacy (named failure) — the pattern's framing is marginal, but callers frequently slip into 'we already invested, keep going.'
The Diminishing Returns invariant is strong; some valuable recursions have constant or increasing marginal returns, which the invariant would forbid.

MarginalValueRule.family_discussion: Economic governor paired with Budget (resource bound), Estimate (marginal-value input), and DepthGovernor (quality-driven counterpart). Compare with RecursionDive — MarginalValueRule gates dives; RecursionDive is the dive itself.

motivation.why_this_layer: substrate act of extracting info — in general perturbs the measured system
motivation.why_it_exists: Names the substrate act of state-extraction — distinct from the cognitive Observe pattern. Measurement is the physical phenomenon (with perturbation, cost, irreversibility); Observe is the cognitive act. The distinction is load-bearing because library patterns that reason about measurement (MeasureOnce, ProbeSafe, quantum-inspired uncertainty) need the substrate version, while cognitive patterns (Witness, Attest) need the Mind version.
motivation.removability: Probably not. The perturbation invariant ('measurement, in general, changes the state') is a structural property that patterns depending on it (Reversibility, CausalBarrier, MeasureOnce) need as a shared assumption. Collapsing Measurement into Observe would lose the substrate claim.

tensions: Perturbation invariant vs classical measurement that doesn't perturb: the invariant says 'in general' changes the state. But many classical observations are essentially non-perturbing (reading a clock). The qualifier 'in general' covers this but leaves the boundary fuzzy.
Cost as invariant: requires resources. But the degree varies from nanoseconds of CPU to hours of wet-lab experiment. The pattern flatly asserts cost without quantifying.

Substrate vs epistemic: Measurement names what happens when you extract information from a system. The epistemic act (what do I know now?) is cognitive. The split is defensible but callers routinely want both — they invoke Measurement when they mean Observe.
tradeoffs: Substrate framing buys a shared assumption set (always cost, always perturbation, always irreversibility) at the cost of being rigid for low-cost observations.
Three invariants (Perturbation, Cost, Irreversibility) buy a strong structural claim at the cost of excluding the edge case where measurement is effectively free and non-disturbing.
Distinctness from Observe buys clean typing at the cost of requiring callers to consciously pick which pattern they want.
critique: No failure modes. Missing: Under-Measurement (extracting less information than the protocol requires), Aliasing (sampling faster than Nyquist produces false signal), Instrument Bias (measurement systematically offsets the true value).
'In general' is a load-bearing qualifier that softens all three invariants. A pattern can tolerate a little softness but this is significant — the invariants are guidelines, not laws.

Quantum measurement (superposition collapse) and classical measurement (record the value) are structurally different; the pattern treats them as one. Defensible for the library's use but risks conflation.

Measurement.family_discussion: Substrate act of information extraction. Paired with `Entropy` (what is measured), `MutualInformation` (what a measurement reveals about one variable from another), `Conservation` (what persists through measurement). Companion (but not parent) to the cognitive `Observe` pattern.

motivation.why_it_exists: Standard design proposals describe what without why-it-works. MechanisticDesignProposal names the structured blueprint that must define the leverage point, the causal chain, what's new, and — crucially — why it fails in equal detail to why it works. Without the pattern, design proposals skew toward advocacy; with it, the dialectic is structural.
motivation.removability: Removable — lighter proposal formats exist. MechanisticDesignProposal is specifically the serious-engineering shape: causal clarity, novelty claim, dialectic balance. The dialectic-balance invariant is the anti-advocacy discipline.

usage.intended: structured blueprint for systemic solution requiring core-mechanism definition.
usage.future: any "here's how it would work, causally" design artifact.
usage.broad_contexts: system-architecture proposals, policy proposals with theory-of-change, academic theory proposals, economic intervention proposals, organizational-change proposals.
usage.every_context_needs: problem definition, system-level solution, core mechanism (leverage point + causal chain), dialectic ("why works" + "why fails"), implementation + vision projections.
usage.varies: domain specificity, dialectic depth, implementation detail, visualization.

tensions: Dialectic Balance (invariant) vs pragmatic advocacy — proposals are naturally persuasive; demanding equal detail on failure modes is contrary to the advocacy genre.
Novelty Requirement (invariant) vs incremental improvements — most useful design is incremental; the requirement to identify unique contribution pressures proposers to over-claim.
Causal Clarity vs gestural description — 'A causes B' is often the hardest part to specify, and the pattern demands it.
tradeoffs: Gains: structural dialectic balance, explicit mechanism-of-action requirement, novelty claims made visible.
Gives up: speed and sometimes simplicity. MechanisticDesignProposal is heavy; lighter formats suit routine work.
critique: 'Why it fails as detailed as why it works' is structurally demanding and often under-provided even by honest authors.
Novelty Requirement can produce theater — authors claim unique contributions that aren't really unique.
Causal Clarity is an invariant without a test — claims of causation that aren't really causal pass the invariant trivially.

MechanisticDesignProposal.family_discussion: Design-artifact primitive produced by DesignArchitect. Paired with Mechanism (the leverage unit), PreMortem (why-it-fails source), and Steelman (why-it-works source). Compare with FrameSpec — MechanisticDesignProposal is the design artifact; FrameSpec is the requirement artifact.

motivation.why_it_exists: Standards adoption is driven by subsidy, not truth. MemeticSeed names the mechanism: agent broadcasts ontology to neighbors with favorable terms, reducing its own future translation costs. Adoption comes from incentive gradient, not authority. Without the pattern, standard-setting mechanisms pretend they're evaluating correctness.
motivation.removability: Removable in settings where standards are imposed top-down. For organic, distributed standardization, the pattern is the honest description. Its value is explaining what actually happens rather than prescribing what should.

usage.intended: viral propagation of semantic standards via economic subsidy.
usage.broad_contexts: protocol-standard propagation, open-source adoption, pattern-library evangelism, memetic engineering, ecosystem bootstrapping, convention setting.
usage.every_context_needs: standard being propagated, neighbor set, subsidy mechanism (favorable yield), broadcast channel.
usage.varies: subsidy magnitude, targeting precision, retractability, decay profile.
notes: interesting economic pattern — "standards are adopted not because they are true, but because they are subsidized." The broad-use test captures the fact that this is how *most* standards spread, not just the one originally modeled.

tensions: Fidelity invariant (isomorphic propagation) vs local adaptation — receiving agents may want to tweak the adopted ontology; strict isomorphism forbids it.
Subsidy Gradient invariant (incentive > switching cost) vs standard quality — the mechanism adopts whatever subsidizes most, regardless of quality.
Translation proxy reduction — sender's future cost savings depend on adoption; receivers may see this as exploitation.
tradeoffs: Gains: honest description of standards spread, explicit subsidy gradient mechanism, pragmatic coordination primitive.
Gives up: the fiction that standards win on merit. Some find this uncomfortable; the pattern insists on it.
critique: No failure modes listed — the pattern has some (receivers free-riding, sender over-committing, standard rot).
The 'isomorphic propagation' invariant is strong and often violated in practice — receivers simplify, specialize, extend.
The pattern is politically charged — describing standards adoption as economic transaction rather than consensus is accurate and uncomfortable.

MemeticSeed.family_discussion: Standards-coordination primitive paired with Yield (the favorable terms), TranslationProxy (the cost being reduced), and Rally (group adoption). Compare with Constitution — MemeticSeed is voluntary spreading via subsidy; Constitution is collective agreement.

motivation.why_it_exists: Before acting, an agent can simulate the plan on a causal graph of the target system and see what breaks. MentalSim names the System 2 dry-run: construct graph, execute plan in sandbox, observe outcome. Without it, agents act on plans without predictive testing, learning the plan was wrong by failing.
motivation.removability: Removable when plans are simple or when simulation-reality gap is large. Essential for complex plans in domains where failure is expensive. The Simplification invariant — simulation cost << execution cost — is what keeps the pattern economically viable.

usage.intended: System-2 predictive simulation via causal graph dry-runs.
usage.broad_contexts: "what-if" analysis, chess move evaluation, strategic planning, debugging predictions, scientific theory testing, counterfactual reasoning, legal case analysis.
usage.every_context_needs: causal graph of target system, proposed action, prediction of state(t+1), isolation (dry-run doesn't affect real world).
usage.varies: graph fidelity, simulation depth, heuristic vs rigorous mode toggle, computational cost.

tensions: Simulation fidelity vs cost — higher fidelity is more predictive and closer to execution cost; lower fidelity is cheaper and misses edge cases.
Read-Only Reality (invariant) vs simulation-guided learning — simulation can't mutate production, which is correct and prevents feedback-loop learning.
Map-Territory Error (named failure) — simulation diverges from reality — is the foundational limit of simulation-based reasoning.
tradeoffs: Gains: predictive testing of plans, bounded cost (simulation << execution), sandboxed trial.
Gives up: guarantees. Simulations can be wrong; the pattern's value depends on the causal graph accuracy.
critique: Map-Territory Error is the dominant failure — every simulation diverges; the pattern has no defense beyond 'try to match reality better.'
Overconfidence (named failure) — trusting simulation over real-world feedback — is an ongoing risk when simulations are well-tuned.
The pattern requires a causal graph of the target system; constructing that graph is most of the work and the pattern defers it.

MentalSim.family_discussion: Predictive-reasoning primitive paired with AgentSandbox (the isolation substrate), CausalGraph (the simulation substrate), and PreMortem (failure-specific variant). Compare with CognitiveEcho — MentalSim simulates the full plan; CognitiveEcho runs quick variance probes. Both are pre-execution testing.

motivation.why_it_exists: Raw signals lack provenance. Message names the structured wrapper around a signal with sender, recipient, timestamp, and the immutability contract. Without it, inter-agent communication has no substrate for routing, audit, or de-duplication.
motivation.removability: Non-removable in multi-agent communication. Every messaging protocol uses Message or equivalent; the pattern names the minimum structure. Remove it and communication reduces to raw signal without metadata.

usage.intended: structured container for a Signal with Metadata.
usage.broad_contexts: email, HTTP requests, gRPC messages, agent-to-agent messages, ML-pipeline artifacts, log entries with metadata, instant-messaging.
usage.every_context_needs: payload (Signal), Sender identity, Recipient, Timestamp.
usage.varies: encryption, authentication, ordering guarantees, size limits, reply-to chaining.

tensions: Immutability invariant (content frozen after send) vs corrections — typos, revisions, and retractions require new messages rather than editing old ones.
Addressability vs broadcast — the invariant specifies sender and optional recipient, accommodating both point-to-point and broadcast; the cost is that broadcast recipients must be inferred.
Structured metadata vs flexibility — the structure buys routing and audit; it also constrains what can be carried in the raw payload.
tradeoffs: Gains: routable, auditable unit for communication; explicit immutability for log integrity.
Gives up: edit-ability. Messages can't be changed after send; corrections require separate messages and the pattern has no built-in retraction.
critique: Very thin — two invariants, one-line mechanism. The real work of protocols (serialization, acknowledgment, reliable delivery) lives elsewhere.
Immutability conflicts with practical needs (typo fixes, retractions); the pattern leaves corrections to higher-level protocols.
No failure modes listed; messaging has many (loss, duplication, reordering, replay).

Message.family_discussion: Foundational communication primitive paired with Signal (the raw emission), Handshake (the negotiation), and AuditTrail (the durable log). Compare with Event — Message is addressed and immutable; Event is an atomic state-change occurrence. Different communication units.

motivation.why_it_exists: Some reasoning is about reasoning, some modeling is about modeling. Meta names the self-referential or abstraction-raising modifier. Without it, meta-level concerns (MetaPrompt, MetaProtocols, MetaCheck) have no shared handle for 'operates on its own kind.'
motivation.removability: Very thin — a modifier primitive. The value is in the conceptual marker for self-reference. Removing it scatters meta-level patterns without a common descriptor.

usage.intended: higher-order modifier for self-reference/abstraction.
usage.future: Meta(Prompt), Meta(Check), Meta(Rule) — a trait carried by specific patterns.
notes: §3.18 converts to `is_trait: true`. Broad-use confirms — the standalone pattern is a modifier/tag, not a concept.

tensions: Self-reference is philosophically loaded — can a Meta pattern operate on itself? Infinite regress looms.
Abstraction raising vs utility — meta-level thinking is powerful and often impractical; the pattern is easy to invoke recursively without benefit.
Meta-X vs simply complex-X — the distinction often blurs; is MetaPrompt really meta, or just a complex prompt?
tradeoffs: Gains: a shared modifier for self-referential patterns, explicit abstraction-raising marker.
Gives up: very little — the pattern is so thin that removing it wouldn't lose much operational content.
critique: Almost a stub — one sentence of mechanism, no invariants, no failure modes.
Philosophical loading without operational content; the pattern is mostly a label.
Doesn't address the infinite-meta regress (MetaMetaPrompt, etc.) that the modifier invites.

Meta.family_discussion: Modifier pattern used by MetaPrompt, MetaProtocols, MetaCheck, MetaObserverSolver. Paired with Self and Recursive as conceptual companions. Compare with Abstract — Meta specifically names self-reference; Abstract is generic abstraction-raising.

motivation.why_it_exists: Periodic meta-cognitive audit — pause object-level work to evaluate progress, approach, assumptions. Without naming this move, agents drift through tasks without self-correction; the 'step back and check' discipline is the specific pattern.
motivation.removability: Probably retain. Reflexion is partial but downstream of failure; MetaCheck is preventive, triggering before failures compound. The two compose but aren't interchangeable.

usage.intended: recursive self-verification of reasoning process itself.
usage.future: any "am I doing this right?" introspection mechanism.
usage.broad_contexts: reasoning audits, agent self-correction, debugging your debugging, paper-review-of-a-review, meditative introspection, progress retrospectives.
usage.every_context_needs: pause from object-level work, audit questions ("making progress? approach sound? assumptions changed?"), course correction or continue.
usage.varies: trigger frequency, audit depth, recursion limit (to avoid infinite meta), integration with Reflexion.

tensions: Infinite regress named as failure vs max-depth as solution: the pattern caps depth to prevent regress but doesn't say what depth is appropriate. A too-shallow cap loses meta-benefit; too-deep risks the named failure.

Periodicity vs context-sensitivity: 'periodically' is prescribed but periodicity is a caller concern. Rigid periodic checks miss urgent course-corrections; adaptive triggers risk skipping needed checks.

Meta on self vs meta on process: the pattern checks both 'am I making progress' (self) and 'is my approach sound' (process). The two have different evidence bases — self-check uses internal state, process-check uses external signals.
tradeoffs: Periodic check buys course-correction at the cost of interrupting object-level flow.
Max-depth on regress buys termination at the cost of capping legitimate deep meta.
Broad audit scope (progress, soundness, assumptions, obvious misses) buys completeness at the cost of becoming its own task.
critique: Two invariants, one failure mode. 'Checker checks the checking process' is the self-reference invariant but isn't really a claim about invariance — it's a description.
Max depth prevents regress but the value isn't specified. Callers choose arbitrarily.
The four audit questions (progress, soundness, assumptions, obvious misses) are the mechanism but no structure for them — an agent can superficially answer yes/no without substantive audit.

MetaCheck.family_discussion: The periodic self-audit pattern. Composed with `Reflexion` (post-failure learning) and `WhyClimb` (abstraction shift when the audit suggests reframing). Uses bounded meta-recursion to prevent infinite regress.

motivation.why_it_exists: Sometimes the right prompt for a task isn't obvious — but a prompt that generates task-specific prompts is easier. MetaPrompt names the higher-order prompting technique: use LLMs as prompt engineers. Without the named pattern, the shape gets lost in generic prompting.
motivation.removability: Removable — direct prompting always works. MetaPrompt earns weight when task variety exceeds what a single fixed prompt can handle. In uniform tasks, it's overhead; in varied tasks, it's leverage.

usage.intended: use prompts to generate/refine/analyze other prompts.
usage.broad_contexts: DSPy-style prompt optimization, template-generating prompts, prompt-critique loops, meta-teaching (teach how to teach), editorial style guides (templates-for-templates).
usage.every_context_needs: higher-order prompt, target prompts (to generate/refine/analyze), LLM-as-prompt-engineer role.
usage.varies: task specificity, template reusability, optimization depth.

tensions: Meta-prompt complexity vs direct-prompt simplicity — named failure 'Meta-Complexity' is exactly this: the meta-prompt is harder to write than the direct prompt, negating the value.
Prompt Drift (named failure) — generated prompts diverge from intent over iterations of refinement.
Overfitting (named failure) — generated prompts too specific to their seed examples; they work well on those and fail on neighbors.
tradeoffs: Gains: scalable prompt generation across varied tasks, explicit meta-level prompting pattern.
Gives up: simplicity and direct control. Meta-prompting adds an indirection that's often unnecessary and occasionally counterproductive.
critique: Meta-Complexity is an endemic failure — writing a good meta-prompt is often harder than writing the direct prompt it produces.
Prompt Drift happens across iterations and the pattern has no stability mechanism; meta-prompts get refined and subtly change their output shape.
The 'output is a prompt' invariant is trivial; the real question (is the output prompt any good?) is deferred.

MetaPrompt.family_discussion: Meta-pattern paired with Prompt (the substrate) and Meta (the modifier). Compare with Reflexion — MetaPrompt generates prompts for others; Reflexion revises one's own output. Both are meta-level operations, on different axes.

motivation.why_this_layer: solver tree self-regulation — one agent can observe its own tree
motivation.why_it_exists: The paper's §6.10 protocols operate on the solver tree itself, not on tasks within it — monitoring whether the tree has the right shape, whether solvers are performing, whether the structure warrants restructuring. MetaProtocols names this bundle. Without them, the tree's self-regulation is ad-hoc.
motivation.removability: Removable in small or static solver trees. Essential in large, adaptive trees where self-regulation matters. The Tree-level scope invariant — operates on topology, not tasks — is the distinguishing property.

tensions: Tree-level scope (invariant) vs task-level observability — meta solvers observe topology; they don't have task-level detail, which means they can miss issues visible at the task level.
Meta solvers are solvers — the recursive pattern is elegant and invites infinite meta (who watches the watchers?).
Contract-invariant — meta solvers have bounded meta-observation depth — which is correct safety discipline and also limits how reflective the system can be.
tradeoffs: Gains: self-regulating solver tree, explicit tree-topology observation, principled meta-level operation.
Gives up: simplicity. Meta solvers add a whole layer of observation; for simple trees this is overhead.
critique: The 'approximate gestalt' of the tree is intuitive and vague — what the MetaObserverSolver actually maintains is under-specified.
The contract-invariant bounds meta-observation depth; setting that bound right is itself a meta-meta decision the pattern doesn't address.
Meta solvers can be wrong about the tree in ways that are hard to detect without meta-meta solvers.

MetaProtocols.family_discussion: Protocol-bundle paired with MetaObserverSolver (the primary implementation), Solver (the observed unit), and SolverTree (the topology). Compare with DriftWatch — MetaProtocols monitor topology drift; DriftWatch monitors behavioral drift. Both are self-regulation, at different scopes.

motivation.why_it_exists: Optimization and monitoring need quantifiable measures. Metric names the definable, quantifiable property. Without a named primitive, every measurement re-invents the 'numerical property of this system' concept.
motivation.removability: Very thin — almost a stub. Could be folded into Measure or Number. The pattern's value is in the naming and in providing a target for Score, Judge, Budget to consume. Remove it and these have to describe measurement shapes ad-hoc.

usage.intended: definable, quantifiable measure of a property providing signal for optimization/monitoring.
usage.broad_contexts: system metrics (latency, throughput), business KPIs, scientific measurements, health metrics, financial metrics, ML training metrics, game scores.
usage.every_context_needs: measurement definition, quantifiability, target property.
usage.varies: aggregation granularity, sampling frequency, cardinality, derived vs raw.
notes: §3.18 flagged Metric as gloss-restates-mechanism. Broad-use sketch is a concrete rewrite target.

tensions: Quantifiable vs qualitative — Metric is numerical by design, which rules out qualitative properties that might also need tracking.
Optimization signal vs Goodhart's law — 'when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure' is the dominant real failure for optimization metrics; the pattern doesn't mention it.
Definable vs well-defined — a metric can be defined (you can compute it) and still be a poor measure of what you actually care about.
tradeoffs: Gains: shared handle for measurement, substrate for optimization and monitoring.
Gives up: qualitative measures. Metric is numerical; qualities that resist quantification don't fit.
critique: Almost a stub — one sentence, no invariants, no failure modes.
Doesn't mention Goodhart's law, which is the most important failure mode for optimized metrics.
No schema specified — every consuming pattern (Score, Budget, Judge) has its own assumptions about what a Metric looks like.

Metric.family_discussion: Foundational measurement primitive paired with Score (bounded evaluation), Measure (the verb), and Quantify (the act). Consumed by Optimize, Monitor, Judge, Budget. Compare with Signal — Metric is calculated, Signal is emitted. Different origins of numerical data.

motivation.why_it_exists: Without discipline, agents mint patterns speculatively — 'just in case.' MintWhenFriction names the reactive-only rule: mint only when explicit friction signals show the pattern recurs. Without it, vocabularies bloat with edge-case patterns that never come up again, making discovery harder for everyone.
motivation.removability: Non-removable for the sema Living Taxonomy workflow. The pattern is what keeps the vocabulary from degenerating into a pile of speculative concepts. Its invariants (prior-art check, compression value, 3+ instances of friction) are the quality bar for new mints.

usage.intended: mint new patterns only when specific friction signals surface ("Just in Time" vs "Just in Case").
usage.future: any "don't create a new term until usage demands it" discipline.
usage.broad_contexts: vocabulary growth in libraries, API surface evolution, ontology management, taxonomic splitting in biology, legal-term introduction.
usage.every_context_needs: friction-signal detection, repetition monitoring, threshold-based minting, rejection of speculative minting.
usage.varies: friction-signal set, threshold calibration, minting-review process, aging/expiration if usage drops.

tensions: Reactive vs proactive — waiting for 3+ instances means the first two use ad-hoc names; agents have to tolerate friction before minting relieves it.
Compression Value invariant (reference < 0.7× definition) vs richness — small compression wins reject pattern proposals that are worth naming for non-compression reasons.
Definition Drift — minting a concept that evolves; the named failure mode has no explicit supersession remedy in this pattern.
tradeoffs: Gains: disciplined vocabulary growth, registry bloat prevention, explicit friction threshold.
Gives up: discovery speed. Agents hit friction multiple times before minting; sometimes the third instance is the 'too late' instance.
critique: Premature Optimization (named failure) — minting for edge cases — is exactly what the pattern prevents; it catches ambitious mints and may miss patient over-minting.
The 3+ instances threshold is arbitrary; it's a reasonable default and the pattern treats it as law.
Registry Bloat is acknowledged; the pattern prevents new bloat and doesn't remove old bloat.

MintWhenFriction.family_discussion: Vocabulary-growth primitive paired with Mint (the action), PatternDiscovery (the prior-art check), and FrictionLog (the trigger). Compare with DogfoodFirst — MintWhenFriction requires lived friction; DogfoodFirst requires creator use. Both gate adoption by real use.

motivation.why_it_exists: Agents aren't always in the same stance — Exploration vs Exploitation, Cautious vs Aggressive, Normal vs Emergency. Mode names the stable configuration of agency that persists until explicit transition. Without it, stance changes are implicit and conflict-prone.
motivation.removability: Removable in single-stance agents. Essential in adaptive systems where stance legitimately varies. The Stability and Exclusivity invariants are load-bearing — they distinguish Mode from ordinary state.

usage.intended: discrete configuration of agency — stable set of constraints and priors.
