Echo Chamber failure vs homogeneity as feature: Rally attracts responders; if all responders are similar, the group is homogeneous. Sometimes homogeneity is desired (domain experts); the pattern's named failure assumes it isn't.
tradeoffs: Atomic-or-abort buys predictable outcomes at the cost of failing fast when partial teams might suffice.
Quorum-based commitment buys minimum-viability at the cost of excluding legitimate under-quorum team formation.
Deadline enforcement buys termination at the cost of cutting off late-but-legitimate enlists.
critique: Deduplicated failure modes (was: 8 entries with 2 duplicate pairs — Flaking/ghost-at-MUSTER, Rally Spam/RALLY spam floods network).
Echo Chamber and Flaking remain; both are social-coordination risks the pattern can't structurally prevent.
Initiator power is mitigated by transparent selection_criteria but still concentrated — the pattern is monarchical by default.

Rally.family_discussion: The dynamic-team-formation protocol in Society. Composes with `AcceptSpec` (requirements), `Quorum` (minimum size), `Select` (from responders). Sibling to `Delegate` (principal-to-agent assignment) — Rally is broadcast-and-assemble, Delegate is directed handoff.

motivation.why_it_exists: Sorting items by caller-supplied score is a universal operation. Rank names the deterministic sort with optional Top-K truncation. Without it, sorting gets reimplemented everywhere; the Conservation and Monotonicity invariants are what distinguish Rank from ad-hoc ordering.
motivation.removability: Non-removable. Every ordering primitive (Prioritize, BeamSearch, Rank-based voting) uses Rank. The pattern is deliberately thin — the scoring function is caller-supplied, and the pattern provides the framework.

usage.intended: deterministic sort — apply scoring function, return List ordered by Score, truncate to Top-K.
usage.future: any "sort by score, return top" operation.
usage.broad_contexts: search result ranking, leaderboards, bid ranking, candidate ranking, option selection, feed ranking.
usage.every_context_needs: scoring function (ScoringFunction per §3.5), sort mechanism, Top-K truncation.
usage.varies: tiebreaker policy, ranking stability, lazy vs eager evaluation, distributed ranking.

tensions: Score Indeterminacy (named failure) — multiple items with identical scores — requires tie-breaking.
Incomparability (named failure) — scoring function returns non-orderable values — the pattern has no handling.
Top-K truncation vs complete ranking — truncation is efficient and loses items that might matter downstream.
tradeoffs: Gains: deterministic sort framework, optional Top-K, Conservation and Monotonicity invariants.
Gives up: nothing substantial — the pattern is a thin wrapper that gives ad-hoc ordering a shared vocabulary.
critique: Tie-breaking is deferred to the caller's scoring function; if ties happen, output is arbitrary.
Incomparability is a named failure without specified handling — the pattern assumes scores are totally orderable.
Very thin; the real work (defining good scoring functions) lives outside.

Rank.family_discussion: Foundational ordering primitive paired with Score (the scoring substrate), Select (Top-K), and Compare (the element-comparison). Consumed by Prioritize, BeamSearch, Aggregate (sometimes).

motivation.why_it_exists: Pure reasoning can't act; pure action can't reason about results. ReAct names the interleaved loop: Thought, Action, Observation. Without the pattern, agent loops collapse to one mode or the other, losing the observation-driven re-reasoning that makes agents adaptive.
motivation.removability: Removable — agents can interleave manually. The named pattern codifies the discipline. It's the dominant LLM-agent loop shape in 2024-2025; removing it doesn't remove the need, just the shared vocabulary.

usage.intended: interleaved Thought-Action-Observation cycle.
usage.broad_contexts: ToolUse agents, scientific experimentation loops, debugging loops, debugging with live inspection, conversational-assistant loops, robotic loops.
usage.every_context_needs: Thought step, Action step (ToolInvoke), Observation step, context update with observation results.
usage.varies: step count, failure-recovery policy, parallel action support, cost-of-thought.

tensions: Observation Blindness (named failure) — agent ignores observations, follows initial plan — is the 'I predicted the answer already' pathology.
Loop Explosion (named failure) — endless thought-action cycles — requires external termination.
Action Bias — jumping to actions without reasoning — the opposite named failure.
tradeoffs: Gains: structured reasoning-action interleave, named canonical agent loop, observation-driven adaptation.
Gives up: efficiency. Pure-reasoning or pure-execution is faster for tasks that don't need the full loop.
critique: Observation Blindness is endemic — LLMs trained on reasoning often confabulate observations to fit the plan.
Termination conditions live outside ReAct; the pattern is the cycle shape, not the stopping rule.
The Thought-Action-Observation ordering is canonical; some tasks legitimately benefit from Action-Observation-Thought or other orderings.

ReAct.family_discussion: Agent-loop primitive paired with ChainOfThought (pure reasoning), EventReact (reactive counterpart), and OODA (military-origin analogue). Foundational for LLM-agent architectures.

motivation.why_it_exists: 'Try the same call again after a delay' is the atomic substrate operation. ReAttempt names it — distinct from Retry which may vary parameters. Without the distinction, semantic retry and substrate reattempt blur, and rate-limit failure modes slip through.
motivation.removability: Removable by folding into Retry, but the distinction is load-bearing for rate-limited systems where same-arg-same-target reattempt has specific failure modes.

tensions: Uncapped reattempts (named failure) vs transient recovery — without caps, amplification into DoS.
Missing jitter (named failure) — thundering herd on shared resources.
Same-call semantics vs parameter variation — ReAttempt is strict same-args; Retry allows variation, and the line is easy to blur.
tradeoffs: Gains: clean substrate-level semantics, named primitive for same-call retry.
Gives up: simplicity. Having both ReAttempt and Retry forces callers to pick, and the distinction is subtle.
critique: Uncapped reattempts are the dominant production failure; the pattern names the failure without prescribing caps.
Missing jitter is well-known; the pattern acknowledges without built-in jitter mechanism.
The ReAttempt/Retry split is subtle and often ignored; in practice callers often conflate.

ReAttempt.family_discussion: Substrate-level primitive paired with Retry (semantic variant), Backoff (the delay discipline), and CircuitBreaker (the cap). Compare with IdempotentWrite — ReAttempt makes safe retry possible (with idempotency); IdempotentWrite is the safety property.

motivation.why_it_exists: Plans that look logical may not actually be buildable. Realizable names the feasibility judgment: causality preserved, leaf nodes grounded in known primitives. Without this PURE-axis, designs pass quality-gates on elegance and fail on physical impossibility.
motivation.removability: Non-removable for PURE. One of the four axes; removes it and PURE loses the feasibility check, which is the most common real failure for ambitious designs.

usage.intended: Judge-as-feasibility — 3-class classification (Magical / Uncertain / Coherent).
usage.future: any "can we actually do this?" evaluator.
usage.broad_contexts: PURECheck's R dimension, engineering feasibility reviews, startup due-diligence, scientific-proposal feasibility, policy feasibility.
usage.every_context_needs: plan, physics/primitives availability check, dependency-chain verification, 3-class judgment.
usage.varies: feasibility-threshold strictness, domain specificity, reviewer expertise.

tensions: Hidden Complexity (named failure) — 'draw the rest of the owl' — a step looks simple but contains unsolved sub-problems.
Resource Blindness (named failure) — logically sound but physically impossible given budget.
Causality vs practical workflow — the invariant enforces topological order; some real work benefits from parallel exploration.
tradeoffs: Gains: feasibility discipline, explicit grounding requirement, anti-hand-waving invariant.
Gives up: aspirational design. Realizable rejects plans whose feasibility is unclear; some legitimate R&D plans are pre-feasible.
critique: Hidden Complexity is the most common real failure — plans look feasible until you try to execute the hand-waved step.
Grounding in 'known primitives' requires defining the primitive set; this is context-dependent.
Resource Blindness mitigation requires costing the plan, which the pattern doesn't specify.

Realizable.family_discussion: PURE axis paired with Parsimony, Novelty, Expansive. Consumed by PURECheck. Compare with ExecutionManifest — Realizable is the feasibility judgment; ExecutionManifest is the runnable artifact.

motivation.why_it_exists: The standardized tree that turns user_request into concrete execution. RealizationProtocol names the Abstract-to-Concrete phase transition under PolymorphicSolver. Without it, the lifecycle is ad-hoc and solvers duplicate lifecycle management.
motivation.removability: Removable in bespoke solver designs. Essential for standardized solver behavior. The invariants (Artifacts at Seams, Non-Compensatory, Realizability) are the discipline that prevents lifecycle shortcuts.

usage.intended: standardized SolverTree for abstract → concrete transition.
usage.broad_contexts: SOPs for solver-based systems, build-from-spec pipelines, requirement-to-implementation workflows, idea-to-execution templates.
usage.every_context_needs: interpret step, manifest_planning step, rollout step, strict phase ordering.
usage.varies: per-phase detail, alternate paths, customization points, audit requirements.

tensions: Artifacts at Seams vs loose coupling — requiring typed artifacts at transitions is rigor and ceremony.
Non-Compensatory vs iteration — strict halt-on-artifact-failure prevents iterative refinement at seams.
Bureaucracy (named failure) — applying full protocol to trivial tasks.
tradeoffs: Gains: standardized lifecycle, typed-artifact discipline, non-compensatory quality gates.
Gives up: lightness. For simple requests, the protocol is overkill.
critique: Artifact Rejection (named failure) at seams triggers restart; cascading rejections are a real failure.
Loop Stalling (named failure) — stuck in ManifestPlanning — when non-compensatory gates reject repeatedly.
The Abstract-to-Concrete framing is the paper's, and commits to it as the universal lifecycle.
`derived_from` removed: previously pointed at `CreationProtocol` which no longer exists (retired name; this is the successor).

RealizationProtocol.family_discussion: Lifecycle-protocol primitive paired with PolymorphicSolver (the consumer), FrameSpec/ExecutionManifest (the seam artifacts), and OrchestrationLoop (which uses it). Compare with AgentProtocol — RealizationProtocol is execution lifecycle; AgentProtocol is interop bundle.

motivation.why_it_exists: Isolated Think operations don't produce plans or decisions; they need to be chained. Reason names the orchestrated cognition: multiple Think steps under a specific topology (chain, tree). Without the pattern, 'reasoning' is ambiguous between single-step think and multi-step orchestration.
motivation.removability: Non-removable as the orchestration layer. Every reasoning pattern (ChainOfThought, GraphOfThought, HypothesisLadder) specializes Reason. The Structure Adherence invariant is the discipline.

usage.intended: orchestrated cognition chaining multiple Think steps using a specific topology.
usage.broad_contexts: CoT, ToT, GoT, BFS/DFS reasoning, ReAct loops, debate-based reasoning, chain-of-verification.
usage.every_context_needs: topology, multiple Think steps, context-to-conclusion transformation, compute_budget respect.
usage.varies: topology type, step count, self-correction integration, feedback loops.

tensions: Bounded Execution invariant vs unbounded discovery — bounded reasoning completes; some genuinely hard reasoning exceeds any a-priori budget.
Side-Effect Free invariant vs tool use — pure reasoning is idealized; real agent reasoning often includes tool calls.
Structure Adherence vs creative divergence — strict topologies constrain; creative reasoning breaks them.
tradeoffs: Gains: structured cognition, topology-aware reasoning, bounded-execution discipline.
Gives up: creative license. The Structure Adherence invariant rules out ad-hoc topological reasoning.
critique: Analysis Paralysis (named failure) — too much compute on diminishing returns — is endemic.
Circular Reasoning (named failure) — loops back to premise without progress — is common in loosely-structured reasoning.
Context Window Overflow — the LLM-era failure of reasoning exceeding context — is structural and named without mitigation.

Reason.family_discussion: Orchestration layer paired with Think (the atomic op), ChainOfThought (linear topology), and GraphOfThought (DAG topology). Compare with Plan — Reason produces conclusions; Plan produces step sequences.

motivation.why_it_exists: Guards a Solver's Feedback surface against poisoned or hallucinated rejections. In adversarial or open-commons settings, downstream agents can fabricate rejections to extract resources or bias learning. ReceptivityGate verifies every incoming FailureTrace — clause exists, evidence matches artifact, signature valid — before the signal reaches PathwayMemory.
motivation.removability: No, if you deploy in anything beyond a fully-trusted environment. A trusted deployment could short-circuit ReceptivityGate, but the pattern is the mechanism by which feedback channels become trustworthy. Removing would expose PathwayMemory directly to evaluator inputs — which in open commons is a direct poisoning vector.

tensions: Over-strict vs under-strict: the two named failure modes are symmetric. Tuning the gate involves deployment context the pattern doesn't know — too strict starves the Solver of real feedback; too lax lets poison through.

Clause existence + evidence verification vs content quality: the gate verifies structural integrity (clause exists, evidence present, signed). It does NOT verify that the evaluator's reasoning is correct — a structurally-valid but substantively-wrong FailureTrace passes.
Bypass by privileged peer: the pattern acknowledges that high-trust evaluators can skip the gate. That's pragmatic but opens a backdoor — the privileged peer is a single point of compromise.
tradeoffs: Structural verification buys cheap defense against obvious attacks at the cost of accepting substantively-wrong but structurally-valid feedback.
Typed FailureTrace requirement raises the bar for rejection (you can't just say no) at the cost of making legitimate-but-unstructured feedback inadmissible.
Society layer placement reflects the multi-party assumption — single-agent deployments pay for machinery they don't strictly need.
critique: 'Bypass by privileged peer' is a named failure with no mitigation. If the library wants trust-tier scoping, it should be a pattern — not a caveat in this spec.
The gate is binary: accept or reject the entire FailureTrace. A richer gate could quarantine (accept but flag) suspect traces; not offered.

'Malformed traces that pass checks still corrupt pathway memory' names a failure but doesn't specify what 'malformed-but-passing' means — if the trace passes the invariants, is it corrupt or is the invariant set incomplete?

ReceptivityGate.family_discussion: The Feedback-channel guard at Solver boundaries. Consumed by the Feedback surface before any FailureTrace reaches PathwayMemory. Specialization of `Gate` (in Society because the multi-party poisoning context is structural). Pairs with AcceptSpec and FailureTrace as the three-pattern feedback-integrity chain.

motivation.why_it_exists: The downward traversal of the solver tree — applying Decompose at each node, generating children. RecursionDive names this operation. Without the named pattern, solver-tree traversal is implicit in each solver family's implementation.
motivation.removability: Removable — solvers can traverse without the named pattern. RecursionDive's value is as the explicit traversal-verb that MarginalValueRule and DepthGovernor regulate. Remove it and those governors have nothing to govern.

usage.intended: vertical traversal of solver tree — accept solver_node, apply Decompose, generate children.
usage.broad_contexts: solver trees (FI v3), recursive descent parsers, hierarchical planning, divide-and-conquer algorithms, fractal refinement.
usage.every_context_needs: solver node input, decomposition application, child node generation, traversal downward.
usage.varies: depth bound, termination criteria (leaf conditions), parallelism, backtrack support.

tensions: Recursion without bound vs safety — RecursionDive alone doesn't bound depth; MarginalValueRule and DepthGovernor do.
Tree traversal vs graph traversal — the pattern assumes tree shape; solver DAGs need different semantics.
Strategy selection — the pattern applies Decompose; the choice of Decompose strategy is caller-dependent.
tradeoffs: Gains: named traversal verb, separate from governance.
Gives up: very little — thin primitive that composes with governors.
critique: No failure modes listed; RecursionDive has some (unbounded recursion without governor, cycle in solver graph treated as tree).
Very thin — one-line mechanism.
The pattern assumes decomposition always applies; some nodes may need different strategies.
`_meta.related` reference fixed: pointed at renamed-away `SolutionNode#2b4a` (pattern no longer exists); now points at the successor `SolverNode` in full sema_id format.

RecursionDive.family_discussion: Solver-tree traversal paired with Decompose (the strategy), SolverTree (the structure), and DepthGovernor/MarginalValueRule (the governors). Compare with Ascend — RecursionDive goes down; Ascend (or compose) goes up.

motivation.why_it_exists: Surface-level symptoms aren't causes. RecursiveRootCause names the causal drill: ask 'why,' take answer as new problem, repeat. Without the pattern, debugging and investigation stop at the first plausible explanation.
motivation.removability: Removable — agents can ask 'why' without the pattern. The named discipline enforces the recursion and termination (at actionable root or fundamental axiom). Remove it and root-cause analysis stops at 'why' round 1.

usage.intended: recursive "why?" analysis until reaching actionable root.
usage.broad_contexts: Toyota 5-Whys, incident post-mortems, bug tracing, systems analysis, therapy root-cause work, scientific causal investigation.
usage.every_context_needs: problem statement, "why did this happen?" iterator, actionability detector for stopping.
usage.varies: depth cap, actionability definition, branching (multiple causes per level), provenance tracking.

tensions: Single Track Blindness (named failure) — assuming linear chain when reality is multi-factor mesh — is endemic.
Causality Chain invariant (Step(N) direct cause of Step(N-1)) vs correlational — real chains mix causation and correlation.
Termination (actionable root or fundamental axiom) vs infinite regress — when does 'why' stop?
tradeoffs: Gains: structured root-cause discipline, explicit factual invariant, named termination conditions.
Gives up: multi-factor explanations. The linear-chain shape flattens reality; Single Track Blindness is the consequence.
critique: Single Track Blindness is the dominant failure — real root causes are often multi-factorial, and the pattern's linearity misses them.
'Factual, not speculative' is an invariant that's hard to enforce — most 'whys' have speculative components.
Termination at 'actionable root' is caller-dependent; agents disagree on what counts as actionable.

RecursiveRootCause.family_discussion: Investigation primitive paired with Causation (the semantic substrate), Bisect (which uses RecursiveRootCause's drill), and Why (the atomic question). Compare with Eliminate — RecursiveRootCause is causal drill; Eliminate is option-space narrowing.

motivation.why_this_layer: adversarial stress-testing — can be done mentally
motivation.why_it_exists: Defenders share assumptions with designers. RedTeam names the adversarial-mindset stress test: attacker goal, document vectors by severity. Without it, security review shares the designer's blind spots.
motivation.removability: Removable if you accept that your team will miss vectors it can't see. RedTeam is the structural move to bring in the attacker's perspective — external, paid-to-find-flaws, not loyal to the design. The Sympathetic Attacker failure mode is the dominant quality issue when the red team shares too much context.

usage.intended: adversarial stress testing via attacker-mindset exploitation search.
usage.broad_contexts: security penetration testing, AI safety evaluation, devil's-advocate debate, wargaming, competitive analysis, pre-publication critique, regulatory stress tests.
usage.every_context_needs: target system, attacker persona adoption, exploit-path documentation, severity+likelihood classification, switch-back-to-defender for patching.
usage.varies: adversarial depth (ethical hacker vs nation-state model), automation level, scope (single vulnerability vs systemic), coordination with defender.

tensions: Adversarial intent (simulated) vs real adversary — simulated adversaries share designer training; real adversaries are worse.
Find flaws vs fix flaws — the invariant separates them; in practice the temptation to fix-as-you-find is strong.
Red team independence vs shared context — the Sympathetic Attacker failure is structural when red team is internal.
tradeoffs: Gains: adversarial stress test, explicit goal (find flaws), severity/likelihood documentation.
Gives up: defender-centric view. RedTeam specifically refuses to propose fixes, which can feel adversarial in team settings.
critique: Sympathetic Attacker is endemic; genuinely adversarial red teams are hard to find and harder to sustain.
The 'no loyalty to the design' stance is philosophically clean and operationally hard in team cultures.
Severity/likelihood documentation is deferred in rigor; real red teams need CVSS-style methodologies the pattern doesn't specify.

RedTeam.family_discussion: Adversarial-testing primitive paired with SteelmanCheck (strongest-opposing variant), AdversarialProof (exhaustive search), and DissentSeek (disagreement-seeking). Compare with PreMortem — RedTeam is adversarial-external; PreMortem is failure-future.

motivation.why_it_exists: Iterative improvement — apply critique, identify incongruities, edit — is the core improvement loop. Refine names this cycle. Without the pattern, 'improve' is ambiguous between 'replace' and 'iterate toward.'
motivation.removability: Non-removable for quality-constrained work. Every iterative production pattern (PhasedRefinement, EvaluatorOptimizer, Reflexion) consumes Refine. Remove it and iterative improvement becomes implicit in each pattern.

usage.intended: iterative improvement — apply critique, edit, repeat.
usage.broad_contexts: essay revision, code refactoring, design iteration, scientific-paper rewriting, product iteration, art polishing.
usage.every_context_needs: artifact to refine, critique mechanism, edit mechanism, termination condition (quality threshold or cycle cap).
usage.varies: critique source (self, peer, rubric), edit granularity, convergence criteria.

tensions: Iterative improvement vs diminishing returns — endless refinement extracts less value each round.
Critique-edit cycle vs ground-up rewrite — sometimes rewriting beats refining; the pattern favors refinement.
Termination condition — the pattern says 'until condition met,' but the condition is caller-set.
tradeoffs: Gains: structured improvement, explicit critique-edit cycle.
Gives up: blank-slate thinking. Refine preserves structure; when structure is the problem, Refine can't help.
critique: Failure modes now cover the main refinement traps: diminishing returns, cosmetic drift, and termination drift.
The mechanism remains compact, but the added invariants carry the loop discipline: critique-edit linkage, visible termination, and artifact continuity.
The pattern still assumes critique is available and actionable; the added precondition makes that assumption explicit rather than silent.

Refine.family_discussion: Iterative-improvement primitive paired with Critique (the feedback substrate), Reflexion (self-variant), and PhasedRefinement (layered variant). Compare with Optimize — Refine is qualitative; Optimize is quantitative.

motivation.why_it_exists: Some responses must be fast, non-negotiable, and immune to deliberation — emergency stops, kill switches, hardcoded safety. Reflex names this: stimulus S triggers response R with no override. Without the pattern, safety-critical responses get routed through deliberation, which is exactly what reflexes defeat.
motivation.removability: Removable only at safety cost. The named pattern reserves the slot for deliberation-bypass response. Remove it and every 'immediate response' becomes deliberable, which is the wrong trade for emergencies.

usage.intended: hardcoded fast-path response bypassing deliberation — stimulus → response without override.
usage.future: any "no time to think, just react" mechanism.
usage.broad_contexts: biological reflexes, safety-critical fast-paths (airbag deployment), emergency-stop reflexes, trained-reflex routines (athletics), pre-programmed safety responses in AI systems.
usage.every_context_needs: hardcoded stimulus-response mapping, minimal latency, no-override semantic.
usage.varies: stimulus pattern, response complexity, override mechanism (if any), safety-critical vs optimization.

tensions: No override possible vs legitimate exceptions — real emergencies sometimes warrant override (false-alarm reflex firing), and the pattern forbids it.
Immutable stimulus-response mapping vs learning — reflexes don't learn, which is safe and inflexible.
Reflex Hijack (named failure) — adversary triggers reflex to bypass deliberation — is the security cost of non-negotiability.
tradeoffs: Gains: fast safety-critical response, deliberation bypass, named slot for automatic reactions.
Gives up: flexibility. Reflexes are hardwired; adapting them requires rewriting the mapping.
critique: Reflex Hijack is the dominant security failure — adversaries exploit non-negotiability.
Immutability at runtime is strong; some reflex mappings should be adjustable between sessions even if not mid-execution.
No failure modes for false-positive reflexes; these are real and the pattern doesn't address them.

Reflex.family_discussion: Automatic-response primitive paired with EjectionSeat (specific kill-switch reflex), FailClosed (the conservative default), and Guard (the general safety pattern). Compare with Deliberate — Reflex is pre-deliberation; Deliberate is slow thoughtful response.

motivation.why_it_exists: Post-failure self-critique loop — generates linguistic analysis of what went wrong, uses that as context for retry. Named pattern for 'learn from this attempt without touching weights.' Essential for LLM-era agents that cannot fine-tune between attempts but can update prompts and context.
motivation.removability: No. OptimisticSolver depends on Reflexion for post-hoc error correction; retry-heavy protocols invoke it. Removing forces each to reinvent the self-critique structure.

usage.intended: self-critique after failure, feeding reflection as context for retry.
usage.future: any self-improvement loop via textual self-critique.
usage.broad_contexts: LLM agent self-improvement, post-mortem culture, after-action reviews, journaling for learning, code review incorporation.
usage.every_context_needs: task attempt, linguistic self-critique generation, episodic memory buffer, retry with critique in context.
usage.varies: critique depth, buffer size, retry budget, memory-eviction policy.

tensions: Linguistic critique vs structured feedback: Reflexion uses natural-language self-critique, which can be rich but also vague. Structured critique (fields: what failed, why, what to try) would be more actionable but less flexible.
Self-critique vs external feedback: the pattern is self-contained — the agent critiques itself. Compromised or blind-spotted agents produce weak self-critique (named failure Shallow Reflection).
Retry-driven vs preventive: Reflexion only fires after failure. Preventive meta-checks (MetaCheck) live as a separate pattern; the distinction is sharp but callers may want combined versions.
tradeoffs: Linguistic form buys rich reasoning at the cost of inconsistent quality.
Self-contained loop buys independence at the cost of self-serving critiques.
Retry-focused scope buys clean semantics at the cost of missing preventive opportunities.
critique: Two invariants, two failure modes. Shallow Reflection and Reflection Drift are real and named. Missing: Self-Deception (the critique asserts a reason for failure that isn't the true cause), Insight Hollowness (identifies the right failure but no action plan follows).
'Generic (try harder)' is shallow-reflection territory; the pattern has no quality check to detect this.
No termination condition — a Reflexion loop can run indefinitely across retries. Budget composition is implicit.

Reflexion.family_discussion: The post-failure self-critique pattern. Composed with `MetaCheck` (preventive), `WhyClimb` (abstraction-shift on persistent failure), `Reason` (the critique itself). Used by `OptimisticSolver` for post-hoc error correction.

motivation.why_it_exists: When the current framing doesn't admit a solution, changing frames can reveal one. Reframe names this perspective rotation: transform the problem statement, seek a new root. Without it, agents stay stuck in the original frame when the frame is the problem.
motivation.removability: Removable — agents can reformulate without the named pattern. Reframe earns its weight as the explicit 'try a different framing' move in solver family composition. Without it, framing rigidity is the default.

usage.intended: transform the problem statement to find a new solver tree root.
usage.broad_contexts: creative problem-solving, deadlock resolution, lateral thinking, reductio reformulation, analogical reframing, scope reset, domain translation.
usage.every_context_needs: original problem statement, transformation (perspective, scope, framing), new solver-root candidate.
usage.varies: reframing technique (invert, expand, shift time, change subject), return semantics (replaces vs. augments), cost, success criteria.
notes: `Reframe` pairs with `Route` in §3.14's hard-seam composition — `Gate → Decision{FrameError} → (Route | Reframe)`. Broad-use validates both as general-purpose primitives.

tensions: Problem semantics preserved (invariant) vs genuine re-interpretation — some legitimate reframings change the problem, which the invariant forbids.
Perspective shift vs random relabeling — the pattern is under-specified on what counts as a legitimate shift vs. a cosmetic rephrasing.
Frame Blindness (named failure) — new frame has its own blind spots — is endemic; reframing trades one bias for another.
tradeoffs: Gains: explicit perspective-shift move, substrate for recovering from frame rigidity.
Gives up: framing stability. Reframing allows productive pivots and repeated reframing without resolution.
critique: Frame Blindness is unavoidable — every frame has blind spots, and reframing exchanges them without eliminating them.
Preserving problem semantics is vague; some reframings legitimately change what counts as the problem.
The pattern doesn't specify how to evaluate a new frame's quality; that's caller judgment.

Reframe.family_discussion: Cognitive-move primitive paired with Invert (specific opposition move), Perspective (the substrate), and LateralOptimization (domain-switch variant). Compare with AntifragileInversion — Reframe is cognitive; AntifragileInversion is structural design.

motivation.why_it_exists: Models that fit yesterday's regime may fail when the regime shifts. RegimeSense names the continuous divergence tracker: rolling average of prediction error, alert when it drops below threshold. Without it, regime shifts get noticed after losses accumulate.
motivation.removability: Removable in stable environments. Essential for adaptive systems in non-stationary environments (markets, social dynamics, adversarial games). The Stability Break invariant triggers OntologicalAccommodation — model revision rather than just parameter tuning.

usage.intended: detect structural breaks — when the generative process underlying reality has changed.
usage.broad_contexts: ML concept drift detection, financial regime detection, model-staleness alerts, changing-environment adaptation, scientific anomaly detection.
usage.every_context_needs: internal model prediction, observed reality, divergence metric (Regime Stability Score), threshold for triggering.
usage.varies: window size, metric choice (KL divergence, RSS, surprisal), threshold adaptation, trigger action.

tensions: Lag (named failure) — RSS is trailing, so shifts are detected after-the-fact.
False Positives (named failure) — noise spikes trigger unnecessary accommodations.
Threshold Gaming — setting threshold too high misses real shifts; too low fires constantly.
tradeoffs: Gains: continuous regime-shift detection, explicit divergence tracking, trigger for ontological update.
Gives up: immediacy. Trailing indicator means you react after the shift has begun.
critique: Lag is structural — rolling averages inherently trail; there's no fix for this at the pattern level.
False Positives require threshold calibration that the pattern doesn't specify.
Window Integrity (fixed window size, not cherry-picked) is discipline that's easy to violate.

RegimeSense.family_discussion: Anomaly-detection primitive paired with DriftWatch (behavioral analogue), Anomaly (the data unit), and OntologicalAccommodation (the response). Compare with Monitor — RegimeSense specifically tracks model-reality divergence; Monitor is general observation.

motivation.why_it_exists: Expected-value optimization assumes outcome distributions are symmetric enough that averaging makes sense. For survival-critical decisions, the right frame is minimax: minimize worst-case loss. RegretMinimization names this stance. Without the pattern, existential risks get averaged into expected value calculations.
motivation.removability: Removable for non-catastrophic decisions. Essential for decisions where the worst case is ruinous. The Safety Floor invariant (never choose option with catastrophic worst-case) is the crucial discipline.

usage.intended: safety-first decisions via Minimax loss-avoidance (not expected-value maximization).
usage.broad_contexts: survival-critical decisions, catastrophe-avoidance strategies, conservative-investment framing, medical-triage under uncertainty, insurance-decision framing, power-law-exposed choices.
usage.every_context_needs: decision space, loss function, Minimax selection.
usage.varies: worst-case estimation (data-driven vs adversarial), risk-aversion coefficient, consideration of expected value alongside Minimax (hybrid).

tensions: Pessimism invariant vs optimistic opportunity — assuming worst-case closes off high-variance high-reward paths.
Safety Floor vs absolute safety impossible — no option has zero worst-case; defining 'catastrophic' is the threshold question.
Regret vs expected value — the two produce very different decisions; choosing which frame to apply is itself a judgment call.
tradeoffs: Gains: survival-robust decisions, explicit pessimism, safety floor against ruinous outcomes.
Gives up: expected value. RegretMinimization leaves value on the table by avoiding positive-expected but high-variance options.
critique: No failure modes listed; RegretMinimization has some (over-conservatism, missed opportunity, miscalibrated worst-case).
'Catastrophic' is caller-defined; the pattern's discipline is only as strong as the definition.
Assumes worst-case is definable and comparable across options; for genuinely uncertain situations, comparing worst-cases is speculative.

RegretMinimization.family_discussion: Decision-under-extreme-risk primitive paired with ExpectedValue (the standard framing), Minimax (the game-theoretic cousin), and Utility (the optimized-for). Compare with OptimalStop — RegretMinimization is stance for extreme-risk; OptimalStop is search termination. Different decision-theory moves.

motivation.why_it_exists: Errors invisible in one representation become obvious in another. RepresentationSwap names this verification move: transcode to orthogonal modality (text → flowchart, code → English) to reveal structural errors. Without it, reviewers share the blind spots of the original representation.
motivation.removability: Removable — single-representation review covers most cases. RepresentationSwap earns weight for serious verification where blind spots matter. The Orthogonality invariant — target modality constrains different dimensions — is the structural check.

usage.intended: verification protocol via transcoding to strictly orthogonal modality.
usage.future: any "change representation to reveal errors" verification.
usage.broad_contexts: code-to-plain-English explanation for bug-finding, table-to-narrative verification, diagram-to-code round-trips, educational explanations (if you can't explain it simply...).
usage.every_context_needs: original representation, orthogonal target modality, lossless transcoding requirement, gap/inconsistency detection in new format.
usage.varies: modality pair, transcoding rigor, roundtrip expectation (reverse-transcode and compare).

tensions: Smoothing (named failure) — agent unconsciously fixes errors during translation — is the dominant failure mode.
Lossless Intent invariant vs legitimate information loss — some swaps necessarily lose detail.
Orthogonality vs reviewability — highly orthogonal modalities constrain different dimensions and are harder for reviewers to judge.
tradeoffs: Gains: error detection via modality shift, orthogonal-dimension check.
Gives up: simplicity. Every swap requires expertise in the target modality.
critique: Smoothing is the hardest failure — LLMs translating incoherent text into coherent flowcharts mask the original error.
Orthogonality is hard to verify; two modalities may seem orthogonal and share hidden assumptions.
The pattern requires skilled agents in multiple modalities; the capability gap limits applicability.

RepresentationSwap.family_discussion: Verification-via-modality primitive paired with Translate (the mechanism), Critique (the target), and Incongruity (the output). Compare with CiteBack — RepresentationSwap reveals errors via modality shift; CiteBack enforces source-grounding. Different verification strategies.

motivation.why_it_exists: The initial workflow step — take a message, interpret the real ask, produce a FrameSpec. RequestFraming names this interpretation. Without the pattern, the first step is ambiguous between 'receive' and 'interpret,' and interpretation gets smeared across later stages.
motivation.removability: Non-removable for OrchestrationLoop. The pattern is the interpretive first step. Skip it and downstream stages inherit unclear interpretations that surface as later-stage failures.

usage.intended: initial orchestration phase — interpret message into FrameSpec before committing resources.
usage.broad_contexts: requirements elicitation, customer-request translation, ticket triage, ambiguous-command handling, user-intent inference, onboarding questionnaires.
usage.every_context_needs: input message, interpretation mechanism, FrameSpec output (constraints, success criteria, hidden assumptions), semantic-firewall role.
usage.varies: interpretation depth, clarification-question budget, escalation on unclear intent.
notes: `RequestFraming` will move Society → Mind per §3.18.

tensions: Misinterpretation (named failure) — clarifying the wrong ambiguity.
Over-constraint (named failure) — adding unnecessary restrictions that kill innovation.
Premature Optimization (named failure) — jumping to solutions before understanding the problem.
tradeoffs: Gains: explicit interpretation step, no resources committed before framing, named first-stage of workflow.
Gives up: speed. RequestFraming is ceremony before action; in reactive contexts the ceremony delays response.
critique: Misinterpretation is endemic — framers clarify what they assume is ambiguous, which often misses the real ambiguity.
Over-constraint is the eager-framer failure; the pattern doesn't bound how much to constrain.
Premature Optimization happens when framers slide into solving; the pattern's 'no resources committed' invariant is the discipline.
`derived_from` fixed: previously legacy stub `sema:Interpret` without hash; now full sema_id.

RequestFraming.family_discussion: Interpretation primitive paired with Interpret (the verb), FrameSpec (the output), and ProblemFramer (the role). Compare with ManifestPlanning — RequestFraming is 'understand the ask'; ManifestPlanning is 'plan the solution.'

motivation.why_it_exists: Alignment can emerge without explicit negotiation — agents act, others amplify or dampen, signal aggregates. Resonate names this implicit alignment via intent tags and amplification. Without the pattern, coordination requires explicit agreement; Resonate is the 'we're all drifting toward this' pattern.
motivation.removability: Removable if explicit coordination always suffices. Essential for stigmergic coordination where explicit agreement would be too costly. The Signal Decay invariant (unreinforced signals fade) is the cleanup mechanism.

usage.intended: implicit coordination via signal amplification without explicit negotiation.
usage.broad_contexts: social mirroring, market sentiment, meme propagation, cultural drift, musical tempo sync, meditation co-sensing, team synchronization.
usage.every_context_needs: intent tags on actions, amplification/dampening observers, alignment detection via signal strength.
usage.varies: intensity metric, decay profile, bond-formation threshold, signal-channel specifics.

tensions: False Resonance (named failure) — apparent alignment that's actually random noise.
Echo Chamber (named failure) — feedback amplifies error instead of signal.
Spoofing (named failure) — adversarial agents emit fake intent tags.
tradeoffs: Gains: explicit-negotiation-free alignment, emergent coordination, signal-decay cleanup.
Gives up: decisiveness. Resonance is slow and emergent; critical decisions need faster mechanisms.
critique: False Resonance is endemic — the pattern has no distinguisher between real alignment and noise.
Echo Chamber is structural — any feedback loop can amplify errors; the pattern has no built-in correction.

Spoofing is the adversarial failure mode and the pattern's invariants don't defend against it. Deduplicated failure modes (was: 9 entries with duplicate False Resonance, duplicate Spoofing, and overlapping Precise/High-stakes entries).

Resonate.family_discussion: Stigmergic-coordination primitive paired with Stigmergy (trace-based communication), Amplify (reinforcement), Dampen (reduction), and Crystallize (the hardening move). Compare with Consensus — Resonate is implicit alignment; Consensus is explicit agreement.

motivation.why_it_exists: Allocation, consumption, and locking all depend on a finite, identifiable unit. Resource names this. Without it, 'budget,' 'resource pool,' and 'supply' become fuzzy, and contention management has no substrate.
motivation.removability: Non-removable. Every allocation, lock, or budget primitive (Budget, Lock, ContinuousResourceAuction, Queue) consumes Resource or equivalent. The Conservation invariant is what distinguishes real resources from ideas.

usage.intended: finite allocatable entity — can be allocated, consumed, locked.
usage.broad_contexts: compute resources, tokens, memory, attention budget, physical goods, database connections, rate-limit slots, personnel time.
usage.every_context_needs: identity, finiteness, allocation/consumption/lock semantic, contention handling.
usage.varies: renewability, exhaustibility, divisibility, accounting mechanism.

tensions: Conservation invariant (can't create from nothing) vs renewable resources — renewables regenerate, which is a form of creation the pattern allows but doesn't formalize.
Identity invariant (unique handle per instance) vs fungible resources — money is fungible; the invariant forces tracking individual dollars.
Finite but scale — computational resources grow over decades; at any instant they're finite.
tradeoffs: Gains: shared vocabulary for allocation substrates, explicit conservation, identified instances.
Gives up: simplicity. Some things are resource-like but don't fit Conservation (attention, knowledge, reputation) cleanly.
critique: Identity invariant is strong; fungible resources (money, compute hours) are awkwardly handled.
Conservation is a physical-world assumption; informational resources don't always satisfy it.
No failure modes listed; resources have many (overdraft, lock contention, starvation).

Resource.family_discussion: Foundational allocation primitive paired with Budget (bounded resource), Lock (exclusive acquisition), and Allocate (the operation). Compare with Asset — Resource is allocable; Asset is the more general ownership concept.

motivation.why_it_exists: Tasks terminate; some things need continuous maintenance. Responsibility names the standing governance contract — bond to a system invariant over a specific scope, maintain it, don't just complete and leave. Without it, continuous maintenance gets framed as repeated tasks, losing the ownership semantic.
motivation.removability: Non-removable for durable governance. Every role that owns something over time (admin, maintainer, watchdog) instantiates Responsibility. The Single Writer Principle (WriteResponsibility is exclusive) is the critical exclusivity invariant.

usage.intended: continuous ownership of a system invariant (standing wave, not event).
usage.broad_contexts: on-call ownership, SLA maintenance, ethical responsibility, stewardship contracts, fiduciary duty, bug-bucket ownership.
usage.every_context_needs: invariant being maintained, scope of authority, agent owning it, liability semantics, heartbeat proof that invariant holds.
usage.varies: escalation paths, handover protocol, scope-expansion rules, externality ownership.

tensions: Exclusivity (invariant: one writer per state) vs shared ownership — some states legitimately have multiple writers with merge semantics.
Bounded Scope vs cross-cutting concerns — some responsibilities (security, quality) cross boundaries; strict scoping forbids that shape.
Scapegoating (named failure) — agent blames external factors — is the canonical accountability failure.
tradeoffs: Gains: named continuous-maintenance contract, Single Writer exclusivity, explicit scope.
Gives up: flexibility. Responsibility is heavier than task assignment; for one-off work, Task suffices.
critique: Responsibility Vacuum (named failure) — no agent bound to a critical invariant — is endemic in large systems.
Overreach (named failure) — claiming responsibility for scope beyond bounds — is role-creep.
The Single Writer Principle is strong; some genuinely shared states need multi-writer semantics via CRDT or similar.

Responsibility.family_discussion: Governance primitive paired with Role (the capability bundle), Permission (the grant), and Invariant (what's being maintained). Compare with Task — Responsibility is continuous; Task is discrete. Different temporal structures.

motivation.why_it_exists: Operations produce outputs with structure — status, artifact, metrics. Result names this canonical output shape. Without it, every operation has its own output format and downstream consumption requires per-pattern adapters.
motivation.removability: Non-removable. Every Solver, Task, and Action produces Result or equivalent. The invariants (Provenance, Immutability, Measurability) are the downstream-trust properties.

usage.intended: canonical output of a Solver operation (Execute surface return type).
usage.broad_contexts: Solver results, API responses, test results, workflow outputs, task completions, query returns, computation products.
usage.every_context_needs: `status` (success/partial/fail) and `stop_reason` (completed/budget/quality) — without these a Result is ambiguous.
usage.varies: `outputs` (optional — a failed Result may have no outputs to report; a partial Result has some); metrics payload, provenance, confidence.

tensions: Immutability (invariant) vs correction — once yielded, Results can't be modified; supersession is the only path.
Provenance vs privacy — tracing Result to Task and Solver preserves audit trail and conflicts with privacy goals.
Measurability vs qualitative outputs — 'resource consumption quantifiable' forces quantification that doesn't fit all operations.
tradeoffs: Gains: canonical output shape, audit-ready by construction, measurement discipline.
Gives up: flexibility. Results are immutable; in-place updates aren't possible.
critique: Partial Result (named failure) — incomplete output presented as complete — is real.
Hallucinated Result (named failure) — claims to solve the task but doesn't — is the LLM-era canonical failure.
Unvalidated Result — bypasses checking — happens when callers consume Results without verification.

Result.family_discussion: Foundational output primitive paired with Solution (the artifact component), Task (the producer context), and Metric (the measurement). Compare with Artifact — Result is structured output with status; Artifact is the immutable data unit.

motivation.why_it_exists: LLMs don't know what they don't know; retrieval augmentation injects relevant external context before generation. RetrievalAugment names this: query vector store, retrieve relevant chunks, condition generation. The pattern is the 2024-2025 RAG standard.
motivation.removability: Removable in fixed-context settings. Essential for open-domain generation where the model's training data isn't enough. The Query-Before-Generate invariant is what makes RAG different from just 'prompt engineering with context.'

usage.intended: ground responses in retrieved external knowledge before generation.
usage.future: any "look up first, then answer" augmentation.
usage.broad_contexts: RAG (canonical), memory-augmented LLMs, reference-backed writing, citation-required journalism, legal research pipelines, medical-reference queries.
usage.every_context_needs: external knowledge store, pre-generation query, retrieval result, prompt injection, generation-after-retrieval.
usage.varies: store type (vector DB, search index, knowledge graph), retrieval depth, citation format, freshness guarantees.

tensions: Relevance Threshold vs recall — high threshold misses relevant docs; low threshold includes noise.
Retrieval Poisoning (named failure) — malicious index contamination.
Context Stuffing (named failure) — too many chunks exceed window.
tradeoffs: Gains: grounded generation, external knowledge injection, citation-ready outputs.
Gives up: self-sufficiency. RetrievalAugment introduces an external dependency (the retrieval store) that can fail, be stale, or be attacked.
critique: Retrieval Poisoning is a real adversarial concern; the pattern has no built-in verification of retrieved content.
Context Stuffing is endemic; top-K selection requires a budget that many implementations don't respect.
Citation invariant is aspirational; retrieved sources get cited formally while not actually being load-bearing for the response.

RetrievalAugment.family_discussion: Grounding primitive paired with LatentAttachment (the retrieval substrate), CiteBack (source-binding), and ConceptAnchor (the canonical target). Compare with DeepResearch — RetrievalAugment is single-turn retrieval; DeepResearch is iterative multi-source.

motivation.why_it_exists: After failure, sometimes the right move is to try again with different strategy. Retry names the classify-then-retry move: transient vs persistent, backoff, capped attempts. Without the pattern, retries are ad-hoc and usually either too eager (amplifies transient failures) or too timid (gives up on recoverable ones).
motivation.removability: Non-removable for any fault-tolerant system. The pattern is the standard discipline — classify the failure, apply backoff, bound the attempts. Remove it and ad-hoc retry becomes the default.

usage.intended: intelligent, failure-informed re-attempt.
usage.broad_contexts: network failures, rate-limit recovery, API error handling, coordination breaks, verification retries, LLM completion retries, workflow step retries.
usage.every_context_needs: failure classification, retry decision, backoff computation.
usage.varies: classification taxonomy (transient/persistent specifics), budget, circuit-breaker integration, retry-hint protocol, jitter strategy.
usage.extensions: `ExponentialRetry`, `JitteredRetry`, `BudgetedRetry`, `ClassifiedRetry`. The substrate-level "try same thing again" moves to `ReAttempt` in Physics/Primitives (§3.2).

tensions: Classification quality vs speed — classifying failures accurately requires work; cheap classification is often wrong.
Max_Retries cap vs genuine intermittency — some failures legitimately need many attempts; the cap cuts them off.
Backoff strictness vs recovery speed — aggressive backoff is safe and slow.
tradeoffs: Gains: failure-informed retry strategy, capped attempts, backoff discipline.
Gives up: simplicity. Retry with classification is heavier than 'just try again'; for simple cases the overhead isn't warranted.
critique: Misclassifying persistent failures as transient (wastes retry budget) is the named common failure.
Misclassifying transient as persistent (gives up too soon) is the dual failure.
Backoff calibration is caller-dependent and frequently wrong.

Retry.family_discussion: Resilience primitive paired with Backoff (the delay discipline), ReAttempt (substrate-level), and CircuitBreaker (the cap). Compare with Compensate — Retry attempts the same operation; Compensate unwinds the failed one.

motivation.why_this_layer: condition on actions — substrate property, not authored
motivation.why_it_exists: A decision-theoretic primitive — can this action be undone? Bezos-style Type-1/Type-2 decisions, CRDTs vs destructive ops, experimental rollback, safe-to-try assessment. Makes reversibility a first-class property rather than a caller-supplied attribute that varies in definition.
motivation.removability: Marginal. Could be expressed as a Boolean check computed from an action's description. The pattern's added value is the Entropy constraint invariant — reversal must not violate thermodynamic limits. That constraint is not obvious without the explicit pattern.

usage.intended: Condition evaluating whether action post-state allows return to pre-state at acceptable cost.
usage.broad_contexts: Type-1 vs Type-2 decisions (Bezos), surgical reversibility judgments, regulatory-decision reversibility, financial-transaction reversibility, deployment reversibility.
usage.every_context_needs: pre-state, post-state, return-cost evaluation, TRUE/FALSE yield.
usage.varies: cost threshold, information-loss tolerance, reversibility-over-time (e.g., given time X, is it reversible?).

tensions: Binary reversible/irreversible vs graded reversibility: some actions are reversible with cost (rollback effort, data loss bounded). The pattern is binary — within acceptable cost is a caveat, not a semantic.
Perfect reversal vs approximate reversal: 'zero information loss' is the strict definition, 'acceptable cost' is the loose one. The mechanism hedges; descendants could sharpen.

Physics vs decision-theoretic: Reversibility is classed as Physics (substrate property: the Second Law), but the pattern is used primarily for decision support (should I do this?). The dual role blurs the layer test.
tradeoffs: Binary output (TRUE/FALSE) buys simplicity at the cost of hiding graded reversibility.
Entropy constraint invariant buys physical grounding at the cost of forcing callers to reason about thermodynamics for decisions where the cost is effort, not entropy.
The physics-layer placement buys substrate claim at the cost of obscuring the decision-theoretic use.
critique: Only one invariant (Entropy constraint) and zero failure modes. Missing: False Reversibility (caller thinks reversal is possible but an externality was created mid-action), Cost Drift (the 'acceptable cost' threshold changes between action and rollback).
'Type 1 and Type 2' references Bezos's framing but the pattern does not describe the framing for readers unfamiliar with it. The reference is a shortcut.

The pattern yields a Boolean but does not specify how the check is performed — it is up to the caller to evaluate entropy constraints and cost, which re-introduces the variability the pattern was supposed to reduce.

Reversibility.family_discussion: Substrate-level decision property pairing with `Entropy` (the thermodynamic limit) and with action patterns. Invoked by `PreMortem`, `ReversibilityCheck`, `SafeToTry`-style gates. The pattern names the property; specific tooling descends from it.

motivation.why_it_exists: Type 1 (irreversible) decisions warrant more caution than Type 2 (reversible). ReversibilityCheck names the wrapper: halt if irreversible without authorization. Without the pattern, irreversibility is implicit, and agents commit to unrecoverable actions without the extra review.
motivation.removability: Removable in fully-reversible systems (rare) or systems with separate authorization flows. The pattern's value is the automated check — is this action undo-able? — which callers often skip.

usage.intended: convenience wrapper — Check configured with Reversibility condition.
usage.future: any "is this undoable?" check with human-approval escalation on irreversible.
usage.broad_contexts: git operation safety checks, DELETE API request verification, surgical "point of no return" check, deployment reversibility screening, financial-transaction reversibility.
usage.every_context_needs: action being evaluated, Reversibility condition, halt-if-irreversible, mandatory HumanApprove on irreversible.
usage.varies: reversibility definition specifics, tolerance for "mostly reversible," authorization hierarchy.

tensions: Reversibility assessment vs real undo-ability — 'reversible' is a claim that may not hold under load or state changes.
False confidence (named failure) — check reports reversible; undo path fails in practice.
Authorization gates vs speed — every irreversible action pays the check.
tradeoffs: Gains: automated Type 1/Type 2 distinction, halt-before-commit on irreversible.
Gives up: speed. Every action pays the check; in tight loops this adds up.
critique: False confidence is the dominant failure — checks claiming reversibility that don't hold in practice.
The check is only as good as the reversibility predicate; getting the predicate right is the hard part.
Very thin — the pattern is a 'convenience wrapper.'

ReversibilityCheck.family_discussion: Safety primitive paired with Check (the verb), Reversibility (the property), and HumanApprove (alternative heavier gate). Compare with FailClosed — ReversibilityCheck is specifically about reversibility; FailClosed is general denial.

motivation.why_it_exists: The high-reliability specialization of the solver contract — mandates every surface (including Consult and Verify), enforces non-compensatory acceptance gates, and refuses to let partial success propagate. Minted for cases where latency is cheap but an undetected wrong answer is expensive: audit workflows, safety-critical ops, formal verification tasks.
motivation.removability: Conditionally. The distinction it encodes — mandatory-Verify vs optional-Verify — could live as a parameter on PolymorphicSolver. But making it a separate pattern lets callers state their rigor requirement up front via the type, rather than discovering it at runtime through a configuration.

usage.intended: high-reliability, high-latency Solver with non-compensatory gates.
usage.future: any solver trading speed for pre-action verification assurance.
usage.broad_contexts: safety-critical reasoning, high-stakes decisions, medical diagnosis, financial deployments, correctness-first code generation, formal verification, audit preparation.
usage.every_context_needs: full five-surface contract (Manifest, Execute, Consult, Verify, Feedback); non-compensatory acceptance gates; pre-action verification.
usage.varies: specific verification steps, probing depth, socratic clarification depth, feedback structure.

tensions: Mandatory five surfaces vs practical solver substrates: many real substrates (stateless LLM calls, batch scripts) don't naturally expose Consult or Feedback. RigorousSolver forces their presence, which may produce surfaces that are 'implemented' only as degenerate stubs.

Non-compensatory acceptance vs graceful degradation: a single failed invariant forbids Result → Solution promotion. In long pipelines this concentrates risk at gate points — the whole chain can stall on a strict gate that is wrong.

Latency tradeoff explicit vs the pattern's role in the family: RigorousSolver is the 'slow but right' counter to OptimisticSolver's 'fast but needs compensation.' Callers who want a middle ground (some verification, some compensation) have no obvious pattern — they must compose manually.
tradeoffs: Lifecycle Completeness buys assurance (every declared invariant gates the output) at the cost of latency (every stage runs, every time).
Mandatory Probe step buys reality-alignment at the cost of integration complexity — Probe needs a reality model the solver may not have.
SocraticLoop before action buys disambiguation at the cost of extra round-trips with the caller.
critique: No failure modes listed at all. For a rigor-focused pattern, this is surprising. At minimum: Verification Tautology (the Verify step uses the same logic as Execute, making it trivially pass); Gate Lockup (a strict gate rejects everything the solver can produce).
The mechanism couples Probe and SocraticLoop as mandatory; if the deployment lacks either, RigorousSolver is unusable. A configurable-strictness version could degrade more gracefully.
'Trades speed for assurance' is stated in the mechanism but the caller has no way to express how much assurance they need. The pattern is maximal rather than dialed.
`derived_from` fixed: previously had an all-zeros placeholder hash for PolymorphicSolver (never filled in); now the current sema_id.

RigorousSolver.family_discussion: The assurance-specialized descendant of `PolymorphicSolver`. Sibling to `OptimisticSolver` (the opposite tradeoff). Composed with `Probe` (reality alignment), `SocraticLoop` (disambiguation before action), and `Feedback` (post-execution assurance). The correct choice when a wrong answer costs more than a delayed answer.

motivation.why_this_layer: quantified potential for negative outcome — data
motivation.why_it_exists: Potential negative outcomes need structured representation — probability, severity, mitigation, monitoring triggers. Risk names this unit. Without the structure, 'risk' reduces to anxiety.
motivation.removability: Non-removable in any deployment with real consequences. The pattern's invariants — quantification, mitigation, monitoring — are the discipline that distinguishes real risk management from risk theater (the named failure).

usage.intended: quantified potential for negative outcome — probability + severity + mitigation + trigger.
usage.future: any "here's what could go wrong" artifact.
usage.broad_contexts: risk registers, insurance actuarial data, project risk logs, security risk assessments, financial risk models, clinical risk profiles.
usage.every_context_needs: probability, severity (impact metric), mitigation (reducing actions), trigger (materialization conditions).
usage.varies: quantification method, dynamism, aggregation at-container level.

tensions: Quantification invariant vs uncertainty — probability and severity must be estimated; for novel risks the estimates are speculative.
Risk Blindness (named failure) — failing to identify material risks.
Risk Theater (named failure) — documenting without meaningful mitigation.
tradeoffs: Gains: structured risk representation, mitigation-required discipline, monitoring triggers.
Gives up: simplicity. Full risk documentation is expensive; small projects skip it and fail to quantify.
critique: Risk Theater is endemic — organizations document risks as compliance ritual without real mitigation.
Probability Miscalibration is real and structural — rare events are systematically under-estimated.
Correlation between risks isn't specified — portfolios of correlated risks look smaller than they are.

Risk.family_discussion: Safety-planning primitive paired with Probability (the likelihood axis), Mitigation (the response), and PreMortem (the risk surfacing move). Compare with Constraint — Risk is probabilistic downside; Constraint is hard boundary.

motivation.why_it_exists: Temporal planning over multiple milestones has different shape than linear execution plans. Roadmap names the multi-milestone temporal plan with direction. Without it, long-horizon planning collapses into either Plan (too linear) or vague aspiration.
motivation.removability: Removable for short-horizon work. Roadmap is specifically for strategic/temporal planning where milestones matter. The pattern is thin but reserves the slot for 'plan over time with multiple goals.'

usage.intended: strategic plan over time — milestones with flexibility between them.
usage.broad_contexts: product roadmaps, research roadmaps, corporate strategy, infrastructure-buildout roadmaps, policy roadmaps, career planning.
usage.every_context_needs: temporal dimension, milestones (key goals), flexibility between milestones.
usage.varies: time horizon, granularity, update cadence, public-vs-internal.

tensions: Strategic plan (loose) vs execution plan (strict) — Roadmap sits between, which means it's often neither rigorous enough for execution nor flexible enough for strategy.
Milestones vs continuous progress — milestones are discrete; continuous progress fits some domains poorly.
Temporal dimension — Roadmap adds time; most execution plans are mostly sequential, not time-based.
tradeoffs: Gains: named strategic-temporal primitive.
Gives up: rigor. Roadmap is loose by design; detailed planning uses Plan.
critique: Very thin — almost a stub, no invariants, no failure modes.
'Often allows...' in the mechanism suggests the pattern permits many shapes without disciplining any.
Doesn't specify milestone semantics, update cadence, or revision policy.

Roadmap.family_discussion: Strategic-planning primitive paired with Plan (tactical), Milestone (the discrete units), and Goal (the targets). Compare with Strategy — Roadmap is temporal; Strategy is approach-level.

motivation.why_it_exists: Systems exposed to stress need the property of resisting it. Robustness names this — function invariant under shock. Distinct from Antifragility (which gains from shock). Without the pattern, 'robust' and 'antifragile' blur in design discussions.
motivation.removability: Removable by folding into general safety patterns. The pattern's value is the specific Survival invariant — function persists under shock. Remove it and the Antifragility distinction gets muddied.

usage.intended: capacity to maintain validity under stress (resist, not antifragilely gain).
usage.future: any "holds up under pressure" system quality.
usage.broad_contexts: system robustness, argument robustness, brand robustness, code robustness, institutional robustness.
usage.every_context_needs: validity criterion, stress source, resistance mechanism, distinction from Antifragility (which gains from stress).
usage.varies: stress model, resistance mechanism, measurement method.

tensions: Rigidity (named failure) — system too stiff to adapt — is the over-robustness failure.
False Robustness (named failure) — valid under known stressors, fragile to black swans.
Survival invariant vs gradual degradation — the invariant is binary; real systems degrade gracefully (or don't).
tradeoffs: Gains: explicit shock-resistance framing, distinction from Antifragility.
Gives up: gains from disorder. Robust systems survive; antifragile systems improve.
critique: Rigidity is real — the most robust systems are often the least adaptive.
False Robustness is the black swan problem — robustness under known stressors fails on novel ones.
Survival is binary in the invariant but real robustness has gradation.

Robustness.family_discussion: Paired with AntifragileInversion (the gains-from-disorder counterpart), Resilience (adjacent but different), and Survival (the property being maintained). Compare with GracefulDegradation — Robustness survives; GracefulDegradation degrades predictably.

motivation.why_it_exists: Identity is persistent; what an agent can do varies by context. Role names the capability bundle — permissions + responsibilities — that an agent adopts. Without it, permissions and responsibilities attach directly to identity, losing the context flexibility.
motivation.removability: Non-removable for any role-based system. Every RBAC, capability-delegation, or responsibility-assignment pattern uses Role or equivalent. The decoupling from Identity is the key insight.

usage.intended: named bundle of permissions and responsibilities assigned to an agent.
usage.broad_contexts: RBAC systems, job titles, organizational hats, game character classes, agent mode switching, team rotation, on-call schedules.
usage.every_context_needs: role name, permission set, responsibility set, assignment binding to agent.
usage.varies: time-bounded vs permanent, delegation support, inheritance/composition, context-scoping, revocation semantics.

tensions: Decoupled from identity vs accountability — role-switching can hide who-did-what; audit requires keeping both.
Permissions vs responsibilities as a bundle — Role bundles them; some systems want decoupled.
Multiple roles vs conflict — agent in multiple roles with conflicting permissions needs resolution.
tradeoffs: Gains: capability/identity decoupling, context-flexible permissions, role-based access control.
Gives up: simplicity. Roles add a layer of indirection; for simple systems, direct permissioning is cleaner.
critique: Failure modes now name the common operational breaks: privilege creep, role explosion, and conflicting assignments.
The mechanism remains intentionally compact; the added invariants pin identity decoupling, permission closure, and responsibility binding without over-specifying inheritance or revocation.
Relationship with Identity and Responsibility is still easy to conflate in practice, but the contract surface now makes the distinction reviewable.

Role.family_discussion: Foundational capability primitive paired with Identity (persistent handle), Permission (the atomic grant), and Responsibility (the continuous contract). Compare with Card — Role is a local concept; Card is the advertisement.

motivation.why_it_exists: Deployment isn't just 'copy code to production'; it's build + deploy inside a circuit-breaker envelope with reversibility. Rollout names this full discipline. Without the pattern, deploy skips the safety ceremony.
motivation.removability: Removable in dev-only or non-critical systems. Essential for production deploys. The invariants (WorldReversible, Unblockable EjectionSeat) are the production-safety properties.

usage.intended: safe, reversible deployment with circuit breaking and emergency ejection.
usage.broad_contexts: software deploys (canary, blue-green, rolling), policy rollouts, experiment launches, configuration changes, model deployments, feature-flag progressions.
usage.every_context_needs: spec extraction, build, circuit-breaker envelope, canary, ejection-on-breaker-trip, compensation for rollback.
usage.varies: canary fraction, breaker sensitivity, rollback granularity, observability integration.

tensions: Big Bang Failure (named failure) — 100% deploy without canary.
Compensate Failure (named failure) — dirty rollback.
Config Drift (named failure) — deployed state diverges from manifest.
tradeoffs: Gains: safe deployment discipline, reversibility, EjectionSeat preservation.
Gives up: deploy speed. Canary, circuit-breaker, and reversibility add latency.
critique: WorldReversible is aspirational; most real deploys have some irreversible component (data migrations, especially).
Config Drift is endemic; environments diverge from manifests over time.
Big Bang Failure requires enforcement the pattern doesn't provide; it names the bad behavior without preventing it.

Rollout.family_discussion: Deployment primitive paired with Build (artifact production), CircuitBreaker (the envelope), Compensate (the reversal), and EjectionSeat (the override). Compare with Deploy — Rollout is the disciplined version; Deploy is the raw move.

motivation.why_it_exists: Deployments produce state; auditing deployments requires the full state record. RolloutManifest names this immutable log: config, flags, targets. Without the pattern, deploy state lives implicitly in production and diagnostic traceability suffers.
motivation.removability: Removable in systems that don't care about deploy-state audit. Essential for regulated or large-deployment contexts. The Immutability and Completeness invariants are the audit property.

usage.intended: immutable record of actions during deployment — baseline for monitoring.
usage.future: any "what we did during the rollout" audit artifact.
usage.broad_contexts: Kubernetes deployment events, CI/CD deploy records, release notes, operational logs, change-management records.
usage.every_context_needs: action record, configuration states, feature-flag settings, deployment targets, immutability.
usage.varies: granularity (per-action vs per-batch), retention, access-control, signature.

tensions: Completeness (invariant: all state changes recorded) vs size — full logs grow unbounded.
Immutability vs corrections — wrong entries stay; supersession patterns aren't specified.
Deploy manifest vs live state — the manifest records what was deployed; config drift means live state diverges.
tradeoffs: Gains: deploy-state audit trail, comparison substrate for monitoring.
Gives up: storage. Full manifests grow; retention policy isn't specified.
critique: Completeness is aspirational; many state changes slip through manifest boundaries.
Immutability doesn't help when the manifest was wrong to begin with.
No diff semantics between manifests; comparing deploys is a separate problem.

RolloutManifest.family_discussion: Deploy-state primitive paired with Rollout (the production), RolloutWatch (the consumer), and AuditTrail (general analogue). Compare with ExecutionManifest — RolloutManifest is the immutable record of what happened; ExecutionManifest is the plan for what to do.

motivation.why_it_exists: After deployment, the Definition of Done must be verified against live metrics. RolloutWatch names this: monitor the solution, compare against the spec, alert on deviation. Without it, deploy is 'ship and hope.'
motivation.removability: Removable in fire-and-forget systems. Essential for production deployments where success means post-deploy performance. The Fidelity and Actionability invariants are what distinguish real monitoring from monitoring theater.

usage.intended: continuous verification of deployed state against manifest — closes the feedback loop.
usage.broad_contexts: production monitoring, SLA monitoring, A/B test result tracking, deployed-model drift detection, policy-effectiveness post-rollout.
usage.every_context_needs: RolloutManifest reference, Monitor + Observe, Definition-of-Done comparison, MonitorReport upstream on deviation.
usage.varies: monitoring interval (Duration), deviation thresholds, escalation protocol, duration of watch.

tensions: Alert Fatigue (named failure) — too many false positives ignore real issues.
Lagging Indicators (named failure) — detecting failure after damage is done.
Silent Failure (named failure) — metrics look good but UX is broken.
tradeoffs: Gains: post-deploy verification, alert routing to capable agents, fidelity-to-spec.
Gives up: attention. Every rollout watched is attention spent; for low-risk deploys this is overhead.
critique: Silent Failure is the scariest failure — metrics pass, users are unhappy; the pattern can't detect it without user-side metrics.
Alert Fatigue is endemic; the pattern names it without giving a reduction mechanism.
Lagging Indicators are inherent; the pattern can trigger after-the-fact and not prevent.
`derived_from` fixed: previously legacy stub `sema:Monitor` without hash; now full sema_id.

RolloutWatch.family_discussion: Post-deploy monitoring paired with Monitor (the substrate), Observe (the sensing), and AcceptSpec (the Definition of Done reference). Compare with DriftWatch — RolloutWatch watches deployed solution; DriftWatch watches agent behavior.

motivation.why_it_exists: Information spreads via signed re-transmission paths. RootHashGossip names this mycelium-like protocol. Receivers trust based on path length and composition.
motivation.removability: Removable in centralized systems. Essential for distributed gossip networks.

usage.intended: information spreads with signed path; receivers trust by path reputation, not just source.
usage.future: any "trust depends on the chain of trust" gossip protocol.
usage.broad_contexts: BGP-style internet routing with reputation, Tor-like path-based anonymity with reverse-trust, academic citation chains, reputation-weighted rumor spread.
usage.every_context_needs: re-transmitter signature appending, root path, path-based trust evaluation.
usage.varies: reputation model, path-length limit, path-verification cost.

tensions: Path explosion (named failure) — metadata overhead.
Loop Free invariant — path signature detection.
Path Verify — signature chain must validate.
tradeoffs: Gains: distributed gossip with trust.
Gives up: compactness.
critique: Path explosion is endemic at scale.
No failure modes beyond path explosion.
Trust model depends on path quality, not content.

RootHashGossip.family_discussion: Distributed-gossip primitive paired with Sign, Trace (path analogue), and MemeticSeed (ontology spread).

motivation.why_this_layer: apex triage node — one agent can dispatch its own sub-solvers
motivation.why_it_exists: Every solver tree has a unique entry point that sees all problems the system processes; making that entry point a named pattern lets the library attach special authorities (problem framing, budget allocation, ultimate accountability, reframe power) that shouldn't exist at non-root nodes. The RootSolver is also the site of the tree's Pathway Memory — the only node that sees how problems enter, so the only node that can learn which framings route well.
motivation.removability: No. The FI architecture's compounding-learning property depends on a singleton root — without it, Pathway Memory becomes per-node and the 'see all problems' aggregation breaks. Every solver tree needs exactly one RootSolver as a structural axiom.
